01-01.body:
“The party’s over. It’s time to call it a day.” — Judy Garland

When we got here, it felt like our lives had fallen apart. We didn’t plan on things like divorce, only seeing our kids sometimes, or having a bank account that looks like it’s on life support. We used to drink for fun. And for a while, it worked. We felt free, confident—like we finally fit somewhere. But then the fun stopped, and after life started pushing back, it became clear we’d gone too far this time.

Some of us heard about the friend who went to AA, and now they’re like a different person. Change is possible. Part of us wondered if maybe we weren’t too far gone—if maybe it could work for us too. Anything has to be better than going back to drinking. We don’t want to go back. We’re tired of pretending things are okay when they’re not. It was fun—now it’s not. Strange how long it took us to admit that the fun was killing us.

When did you first realize it wasn’t fun anymore—and what helped us take the next step instead of going back?
01-01.title: January 1 – It Was Fun — Now It’s Not

01-02.body:
“Our best efforts to drink like other people always led us deeper into trouble. We could no longer escape the truth that liquor had us licked.” — Little Red Book, p. 17

Drinking got suckier. Looking back, we don’t even know exactly when it changed. It used to be fun. Loud nights, good laughs, that easy kind of escape. Then something flipped. It started feeling heavy. We couldn’t drink enough to feel good, and we couldn’t stop long enough to feel normal.

We’d wake up with that pit in our stomach, already knowing we said or did something stupid again. Deep down, we knew this was taking a toll on us, and that part scared us. It felt like watching a slow-motion wreck and not being able to hit the brakes. We could see it getting worse, but we kept pretending it wasn’t. That lie felt safer than quitting.

Now, sitting in AA, we’re starting to see the truth about our drinking.

What lie kept us drinking when we already knew the truth?
01-02.title: January 2 – It Got Suckier

01-03.body:
“That’s gonna leave a mark.” — Tommy Boy

No matter what we tried, it still sucked. Some of us quit booze and switched to pills instead. It worked for a while. We felt in control again. Then one day we felt so good we decided to drink booze on top of the pills. That one hurt. It wasn’t just our bodies that took the hit, it was our confidence. We thought we had this handled, and we proved to ourselves we didn’t.

The bruises fade, but the memories don’t. It’s hard to forget that kind of proof that we can’t control this thing.

The people in AA have shown us that life doesn’t have to be a string of meaningless drunken nights.

How many times do we have to get hurt before we finally believe we can’t win?
01-03.title: January 3 – That’s Gonna Leave a Mark

01-04.body:
“If I keep doing things my way, I’ll end up on the highway — broke down again.” — Imaginary Friend, “Same Old Road”

Our way didn’t work. We tried cutting back, switching drinks, switching crowds, making promises. Every plan blew up in our face. It was like juggling fire and acting surprised when we got burned. We kept thinking we could outsmart the same problem that had beaten us every time.

Every time we swore we’d do better, we did worse. We don’t trust our own plans anymore, and maybe that’s a good start.

How much longer do we need to keep proving our way doesn’t work?
01-04.title: January 4 – My Way Didn’t Work

01-05.body:
“I want to learn the ways of the Force and become a Jedi like my father.” — Luke Skywalker, Star Wars (1977)

We’re here because we don’t want our lives to suck anymore. We got tired of waking up every day feeling like we lost another round. Someone we used to drink with went to AA, and now they’re like a completely different person. Calmer. Happier. They’ve got their life together and this peaceful kind of presence. Nothing seems to shake them the way it used to. We don’t fully understand how they did it, but we want some of that.

When we sit in a meeting, things seem to suck a little less. A lot of the people we meet in AA are actually happy. Not fake happy, but steady. Like they’ve found a way to deal with life on life's terms instead of running from it.

Wanting a better life is easy. Doing what it takes can be scary.

What if this really could work for you… and the only thing in the way is you?
01-05.title: January 5 – I Don’t Want My Life to Suck Anymore

01-06.body:
“I get knocked down, but I get up again. You’re never gonna keep me down.” — Chumbawamba (1997)

Something about sitting in a meeting makes the noise in our heads calm down. We don’t always know what it is. Maybe it’s hearing people talk about the same things we swore we’d never say out loud. Maybe it’s just not feeling alone for an hour.

We used to think nobody could understand what it’s like in our heads, but these people do. We’ve picked up some things in meetings that have actually helped. When we listen, it starts to feel like maybe we don’t have to keep figuring this out on our own.

Peace used to feel uncomfortable. Quiet can be harder than chaos.

What would it look like for us to not do this alone, just for today?
01-06.title: January 6 – It Doesn’t Hurt as Much Here

01-07.body:
“We’re all pretty bizarre. Some of us are just better at hiding it, that’s all.” — The Breakfast Club (1985)

When I first walked into a meeting, I thought everyone was judging me. I sat in the back, arms crossed, ready to bolt. But something weird happened — people smiled at me anyway. Nobody cared what I looked like or how bad I’d messed up. They just nodded, like they already knew. The only requirement to be here is a desire to stop drinking — and I have that. These other people do too. So maybe I belong here after all. Belonging feels good, but I know how fast shame can talk me back out the door. I earned my seat here. Am I willing to keep coming back?

What helps you remember that you’ve earned your seat here?
01-07.title: January 7 – I Think I Belong Here

01-08.body:
“Living one day at a time freed us from fear of the future and regret over the past.” — The Little Red Book, p. 29

When I first heard people say one day at a time, I didn’t get it. My head was always racing! What about next week, next month, the rest of my life? Thinking that far ahead used to crush me.

But when we just focus on today, it’s not so bad. We can do today. We don’t have to figure out forever. Just stay sober until my head hits the pillow tonight.

Some days we still try to live next week in my head, and that’s when the peace slips away. The future’s not asking for our attention right now. Today is.
01-08.title: January 8 – One Day at a Time Works

01-09.body:
“Each morning sober is a victory we once thought was impossible.” — The Little Red Book, p. 31

Waking up without a hangover still throws me off. I used to open my eyes and instantly check for the damage! The texts, the guilt, the empty bottles. My head would already hurt before my feet hit the floor.

Now we wake up and it’s quiet. Our heads don’t hurt. Our stomachs aren't twisting. We can actually remember where our keys are. There’s no panic, no damage control, no piecing together the night before. Just morning.

It feels good to wake up in the clear. And sometimes that can be scary. Because it’s easy to forget how bad it used to be. This is what better feels like. No hangover. No shame. Just another sober morning we once thought was impossible.

Does waking up without a hangover still feel weird?
01-09.title: January 9 – No Hangover Today

01-10.body:
“Life moves pretty fast. If you don’t stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.” — Ferris Bueller’s Day Off (1986)

I’m doing this for me. Not because I have it all figured out, but because I’m tired of feeling sick and tired. There are hiccups along the way, but I’m keeping an open mind about this journey. I love being not hungover. I love remembering what I said last night. I love waking up clear. But sometimes I forget how bad it used to hurt, and that’s when I start thinking I can coast. I’m willing to do whatever it takes to keep this feeling — because for the first time in a long time, I actually want to be here. Am I still doing this for me, or am I slipping back into proving it to everyone else?

What’s one small thing that’s been better since AA got between you and your next drink?
01-10.title: January 10 – I’m Doing This for Me

01-11.body:
“The less I know the more I learn.” — The Revivalists

Keeping an open mind wasn’t always easy. A lot of us came in to AA as a know-it-all, interrupting, talking over people, not listening, waiting for our turn to talk. That mentality used to include the idea of how to drink without wrecking our lives. Meanwhile people were telling us to slow down. Then, after nothing we tried worked, we finally started listening to people in AA. The more we stopped comparing, and tried to relate, the more they'd make sense. We don’t have to believe everything we hear, but we can stay open-minded. When we keep an open mind, we stop falling into the same old traps that keep us stuck. The second we think we’ve got this all figured out, we start slipping backward.

What’s one thing you’ve learned by listening to someone different from you?
01-11.title: Jsnusty 11 – Keeping an Open Mind

01-12.body:
“Every little thing is gonna be all right.” — Bob Marley, “Three Little Birds” (1977)

We’ve heard the Serenity Prayer at every meeting since we got here. At first, it was just something we said on the way to the coffee.

Lately, we’ve been listening.

“Serenity to accept…” — not our favorite, but probably needed.
“Courage to change…” — yeah, we could use some of that.

Some days we don’t feel serene at all. But we say it anyway. Maybe it starts working before we fully believe it.

Are we willing to keep saying it until it does?

What line is sticking with us today?
01-12.title: January 12 – Trying to Mean It

01-13.body:
JANUARY 13 – Nothing But the Truth

“The first rule of Fight Club is: you do not talk about Fight Club.” — Fight Club (1999)

I had my own Fight Club going for years, and rule number one was the same — don’t talk about it. Don’t talk about the bottles hidden behind the detergent, or the way I’d drink just enough to feel “normal.” Don’t mention how I’d wake up at 3 a.m. with my heart racing, swearing I’d never do it again — then do it again by noon.

I lied to everyone, especially myself. I thought I was protecting people, but what I was really protecting was King Alcohol — ruler of my life, destroyer of my peace. I obeyed every command.

The night I finally told the truth, it broke me wide open. It wasn’t some polite confession; it was messy, snotty, desperate — the kind where all that comes out is, “I can’t do this anymore.” But in that wreckage, something moved. It felt like a match got struck inside me — not the kind that burns things down, the kind that shows you there’s still something left to rebuild.

Sometimes honesty still stings, but it’s better than living in the dark.

What’s something you don’t have to hide anymore because you’re sober?
01-13.title: January 13 — Nothing But the Truth

01-14.body:
JANUARY 14 – The Beat Down

“You got knocked the f— out!” — Friday (1995)

Willingness doesn’t start with fireworks; it usually starts with exhaustion. I didn’t decide to get sober — I just ran out of other ideas. There’s a strange grace in that collapse, the kind that sneaks in between panic and surrender. I was beat into a state of reasonableness. I used to think I’d change once I understood everything. Turns out, I only got willing when I finally stopped pretending I knew everything. A Higher Power can work with a broken “I don’t know.” It can’t do much with a person hellbent on pretending everything is fine. The trick is, I can forget that fast. Am I willing to keep coming back?

What finally helped you walk through the door the first time?
01-14.title: January 14 – The Beat Down

01-15.body:
JANUARY 15 – Same Willingness, Different Direction

“You can’t stop what’s coming.” — No Country for Old Men (2007)

I used to be willing to do anything to get drunk — lie to my family, hide booze in places they wouldn’t find, drunk-drive across town at 2 a.m. — whatever it took. I called it commitment back then, but it was really just selfish desperation dressed up like freedom.

When I got sober, I thought willingness meant being good, saying yes to everything, or trying to look like a saint. But it’s the same muscle — it just finally points toward life instead of death. The question isn’t whether I have willingness; it’s what I’m feeding it.

I used to chase the drink with fire in my gut. Now I try to chase sobriety with that same hunger. Some days, though, I still feel the pull to chase the wrong thing. That old energy doesn’t disappear — it just waits for direction.

What’s one thing you’re willing to try today that you wouldn’t have tried before?
01-15.title: January 15 – Same Willingness, Different Direction

01-16.body:
JANUARY 16 – Soft Doesn’t Mean Weak

“It’s not about how hard you hit. It’s about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward.” — Rocky Balboa (2006)

I used to think willingness was a weakness people could take advantage of. I’d spent years proving I could handle myself, hiding pain behind sarcasm or tearing other people down. The idea of letting go felt like volunteering to lose. But real willingness isn’t about being a doormat — it’s about being teachable. It’s laying down my “I got this” mentality. The strength I have now didn’t come from fighting harder; it came from finally admitting I didn’t have to fight. Some days, though, I still catch myself tightening up, mistaking softness for surrender. Am I willing to stay teachable today?

What’s something you used to think was weakness that turned out to be strength?
01-16.title: January 16 – Willingness Doesn’t Mean Weakness

01-17.body:
JANUARY 17 – Debate Club Is Over

“We had to stop fighting everybody and everything.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 103

For a long time, I thought I was open-minded — I just quietly argued with everything I heard. I nodded in meetings while running a full debate in my head. I wasn’t listening; I was defending. That kind of “willingness” looks cooperative on the outside but never leads anywhere new.

What finally shifted wasn’t understanding — it was action. I didn’t suddenly agree with the suggestions. I just got tired enough to try one and see what happened. That’s where growth showed up. Not in winning arguments, but in laying them down. The old tools I trusted — self-reliance, control, fixing things my way — had worked just enough in life to fool me. They just didn’t work on alcoholism.

Real willingness still makes me uncomfortable. It means doing something before I’m convinced it’ll work. It means staying alert for complacency — that sneaky voice that says, You’ve got this now. I don’t. I never did. What I have is a daily choice: keep debating, or experiment with trust.

Willingness didn’t make me stronger overnight. It just made me teachable again. And that’s been enough to keep me moving.

Meeting starter:
Was there a suggestion you argued with for a long time — then finally tried — and realized the argument was the only thing holding you back?
01-17.title: January 17 – Debate Club Is Over

01-18.body:
JANUARY 18 – Willing to Be Willing

“God asks only that we become willing — not that we understand. The light enters through the smallest opening in a heart that stops arguing.” — Father John Doe

There were days I didn’t even want to be willing — I just wanted the pain to stop. People in meetings said, “Pray for the willingness to have willingness,” and I thought they were out of their minds. But I tried it anyway. Somewhere between the eye roll and the quiet moment, something shifted. I started praying for the smallest crack in the delusion of my alcoholism so I could see it. That’s all willingness really is — a crack big enough for light to get in. I don’t have to want to change perfectly; I just have to stop pretending I’m fine and let something help me. Some days I still fight that help, as if holding on to misery proves I’m in control. Am I willing to pray for willingness when I don’t feel it?
01-18.title: January 18 – Willing to Be Willing

01-19.body:
JANUARY 19 – Stop Lying

“The truth will set you free, but first it will piss you off.” — Gloria Steinem

I once asked a guy in a meeting, “How do you practice rigorous honesty?” He said, “Stop lying.” I laughed, but he didn’t. I thought honesty was about confessing every thought that crossed my mind, but he meant something simpler — stop twisting facts to make myself look good. I used to lie to survive; eventually I lied out of habit. Sometimes it’s not even a full lie — it’s exaggerating a story just enough to look better, tougher, or more interesting. But recovery isn’t about becoming a saint — it’s about catching myself before the lie becomes the story. When I stop spinning things and just tell the truth, I start to feel lighter. Still, sometimes I wonder — if I drop the act completely, will people still like me?

Where am I still trying to make the truth look better than it is?
01-19.title: January 19 – Stop Lying

01-20.body:
JANUARY 20 – H.O.W. to Wake Up

“It’s never too late to be who you might have been.” — George Eliot

The Big Book says the three keys to a spiritual awakening are Honesty, Open-mindedness, and Willingness — H.O.W. Simple enough, but I spent years complicating it. I was working the promises to try and get the steps. Doesn’t work like that. I thought spirituality was something you achieved once you stopped being a mess. Turns out, it starts because I’m a mess.

Honesty was my first crack of light. Open-mindedness kept it from closing. Willingness gave me the courage to walk toward it. The Big Book also says we began to get results even when we only had a willingness to believe — not a full understanding, not proof, just the tiniest opening.

It’s not about becoming holy — it’s about becoming real. Every day I get to practice the H.O.W. of waking up instead of the why me of staying stuck. Some days I forget, and that’s okay. I just start again.

What does keeping it simple look like for you right now?
01-20.title: January 20 – H.O.W. to Wake Up

01-21.body:
JANUARY 21 – We Stay Sober

“You’re not alone, even if you feel like you are. You just haven’t met your people yet.” — Unknown

I’ve been coming to meetings regularly now, and things are starting to feel different. The shakes are gone. My head’s a little clearer. For the first time in a long time, I can actually sit still.

One night I looked around the room and it hit me — everyone there had one really, really bad night that brought them to AA, just like me. Nobody showed up on the wings of victory. We all came in looking for answers. I thought I was different. Turns out, I was just alone.

The first word of the First Step is We — and that word saved my life. I don’t have to figure this thing out by myself anymore. There’s help all around me if I’m willing to take it. All I really have to do is keep coming back.

And still, there are days I drift back into that old thinking — trying to handle life solo, forgetting what brought me here in the first place. That’s when I need the reminder: I get drunk… we stay sober.

Where do you still catch yourself trying to do this alone — even though you know better now?
01-21.title: January 21 – We Stay Sober

01-22.body:
JANUARY 22 – The Power of We

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.” — African Proverb

Somewhere along the way, "We" started to matter. It wasn’t just the word that opens the First Step — it became a lifeline. I used to think my strength was doing things alone. Turns out, alone was killing me.

Now I sit in rooms full of people who understand exactly what that feels like. When one of us is hurting, someone else shares something that lands dead-on. I’ve come to believe that’s how this thing really works — we lend each other faith when we’re short on it.

We isn’t a crowd; it’s a current. When I stay connected, I stay sober. And still, there’s a voice that whispers, You don’t need them anymore. That voice always shows up right before I drift. When I hear it, I know I need the we most.

If someone came in tonight without a single phone number, what would you want them to leave with before they walk out the door?
01-22.title: January 22 – The Power of We

01-23.body:
JANUARY 23 – Admitted

“We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics. This is the first step in recovery.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 30

I’ve admitted to the group that I’m an alcoholic. I might not understand the power in that just yet, but I admitted it anyway. Saying it out loud hit different — like hearing my own voice confirm what I’d been dodging for years.

I still ask myself, have I fully admitted it to myself, though? That’s where it can get tricky. I crossed a line with drinking, and trouble followed. A lot of my friends still drink like I did, but they seem to be able to stay out of trouble. I don't have a full view of their lives, just what I see on the outside, so maybe they can, maybe they can’t — but the fact is I couldn’t. It finally caught up to me. Alcohol hurt me. I got tired.
 The hardest part isn’t saying I’m powerless — it’s meaning it.

It’s not about being worse than anyone else. And once I could finally admit that, I didn’t have to keep pretending it was all under control. Admitting it to myself didn’t fix everything, but it cracked the door wide open.

Admitting it is surrendering it. And for the first time in a long time, I’m ready to move on and take responsibility for my alcoholism.

Have I really admitted this to myself, or am I still hoping I can drink like other people one day?
01-23.title: January 23 — Admitted

01-24.body:
January 24 – Silencing the Alarm

"Same old story, same old song and dance.” — Aerosmith

At some point, we became the people who “fixed” the alarm by taking the battery out of the smoke detector. It wouldn’t stop beeping, so we pulled the Power. Problem solved, right? Except now it couldn’t warn us if the house was actually on fire. It was quiet—but useless.

That’s how it is with problem drinkers. Somewhere down the line, the battery slipped out, and we are the last ones to realize it. Friends and family tried to tell us, “You might want to slow down.” But we got used to the smoke. We got used to the lifestyle of living in fire. The noise of our own denial was easier to live with than the truth that something was burning.

We didn’t lose control overnight—it just got quieter. A little less warning, a little more smoke, until eventually the flames were surrounding us and we finally started to feel the heat.

Powerless doesn’t mean we're weak; it means the system that was supposed to keep us safe stopped working a long time ago. We can’t fix it by pulling the power again. We need to find the right battery to put back in.

What alarms have I silenced in my life just because I didn’t like the sound of them?
01-24.title: January 24 – Silencing the Alarm

01-25.body:
January 25 – The Broken Off Switch

“I can’t stop. It’s like a car crash — I can’t look away.” — Fight Club

Once we take a drink, something in us flips and we can’t flip it back. The Big Book describes it as the phenomenon of craving, an allergy to alcohol. Nowadays, we can just tell ourselves our off switch is broke. It doesn’t go from on to off — it goes from on to mor-on, and there ain't a damn thing any alcoholic can do to stop it once they have one in them.

After that first one, our bodies light up like a short circuit. Our nerve endings fire and scream “more!” and no amount of willpower stops it. We've tried. We tell ourselves, this time I’ll stop after two, but that’s just the mental obsession lying to us again — the same lie that keeps us testing a theory we have already proved wrong so many times.

We used to think we needed more willpower. Turns out we needed honesty. Weakness says try harder. Powerlessness says stop pretending.

How many times do I have to flip the same broken switch before I believe it’s not going to work?
01-25.title: January 25 – The Broken Off Switch

01-26.body:
January 26 – One Drink, No Chance

“Once the acetone accumulates in their body — and that begins to happen with only ONE drink — they will crave more.”

We used to think “powerless” just meant we made bad choices. Like if we tried harder, we could drink like everybody else. But some of these AA guys who really understood the science behind alcoholism explained it to us in a way that finally clicked.

They said only a small chunk of people — maybe twelve percent — have the body of an alcoholic. It’s not just attitude or behavior; it’s physical. The liver and pancreas of an alcoholic processes alcohol way slower than normal, sometimes at only one-third the speed. So when a normal drinker has a drink, their body breaks it down and moves on. But when someone with alcoholism drinks, the chemical that alcohol turns into — acetone — doesn’t clear out. It hangs around in our systems and makes us crave more.

By the time we're halfway through the first one, the choice to drink alcoholically isn't a choice anymore, it's a physical need. The phenomenon of craving has already taken control. That’s why “just one” never worked — it was never just one. Once the physical allergy is triggered, we're off and running, no matter how much we swore we wouldn’t.

The wild part? This never changes. It only gets worse. That’s not depressing to us anymore — it’s proof that we're not crazy, we're just wired differently. And now that we know that, we can stop trying to drink like someone we're not.

Am I willing to entertain the possibility that I’m actually bodily different than other people when it comes to drinking — and if so, what would it mean to finally accept that?
01-26.title: January 26 – One Drink, No Chance

01-27.body:
January 27 – Someone We Didn’t Want to Be

“It’s like I’m watching my life from the cheap seats.” — Reality Bites

Looking back, our lives didn’t just get messy — they got strange. We’d wake up after a bender and think, Who is this guy? Why did I do that? I know better. How the hell do I get out of this? Somewhere in our life, we started crossing lines we swore we'd never cross. We lied to people we cared about, made promises we couldn’t keep, and called it “getting by.”

We used to think “unmanageable” meant total chaos — flashing lights, jail time, the crash-and-burn stuff. But now we see it showed up quieter, earlier, before we could even recognize it — pretending everything was fine while it all slipped through our fingers. We weren't out of control in the dramatic sense — We were just quietly losing the ability to steer. Every fix we tried only made the mess worse.

Life had become centered around survival — keeping things from falling apart, holding people at arm’s length so they wouldn't see how much we drank, maintaining the delusion. Underneath it all, We were scared — scared of being found out, scared that we had no purpose in life. We weren’t bad people. We were just sick and tired of being sick and tired, lost, and afraid to admit it.

It wasn’t only the drinking that broke us — it was everything that came with it. Our dishonesty, our need to control, our endless reruns of good intentions followed by regret. Step One isn’t about failure; it is about recognition. The life we built on self-will wasn’t sustainable. It never was.

Am I still trying to convince myself I can steer this thing alone, even when I’ve already seen where that road leads?
01-27.title: January 27 – Someone We Didn’t Want to Be

01-28.body:
January 28 – The Invisible Line

“Everything was beautiful, and nothing hurt.” — Kurt Vonnegut, Slaughterhouse-Five

We don’t need a Jellinek Curve to tell us this whole drinking thing has a pattern. We lived it. It builds us up, makes us feel bulletproof — then tears us down and takes everything we have. At first it’s all laughs, long nights, and good stories. Then somewhere along the way, the fun starts taking more than it gives. And before we even realize it, the line we swore we’d never cross is already miles behind us.

For a long time, we thought we still had choices. We thought we could slow it down, switch drinks, or prove we weren’t like “those” alcoholics. But once we crossed that invisible line, something in us changed. Drinking stopped being a choice — it became a job. We weren’t chasing the buzz anymore; We were just trying to quiet the noise in our head.

Every morning we’d swear we were was done. Every night we’d find ourselves pouring another one, wondering how the hell we got there again. That’s the insanity of it — thinking we're running the show when the show’s already over.

That invisible line is different for everybody, but once it is crossed, we don’t go back. We don’t drink the same, think the same, or live the same. It’s not punishment — it’s just the truth.

When did I realize the line was already behind me — and how long did I keep pretending it wasn’t?
01-28.title: January 28 – The Invisible Line

01-29.body:
January 29 – Alcohol’s Favorite Game

“You ever get so drunk you make plans for the next day you have no intention of keeping?” — Bill Hicks, Comedian

Unmanageability isn’t just about wrecked cars and court dates. For us, it starts to show up in smaller, uglier ways — dodging people because we couldn’t remember what we said the night before, or who we might’ve insulted trying to be funny. We owed money all over town, and not just the big stuff — sometimes it was as small as saying, “Hey, I’ll get the next round,” and then disappearing out the back door before the tab hit.

Our relationships were just as shaky. We burned bridges we didn’t even remember crossing. We were scared of bumping into someone we’d lied to, ghosted, or promised something we never intended on delivering. Toward the end, for some some us, we didn’t even want to go to the store. We’d scan the aisles like we were being hunted, fearing we'd be recognized as the fool in the bar. For some of us, even a text notification would make our stomach drop.

Looking back, it doesn’t seem like we were afraid of people. What we were afraid of was our own truth—and the fact that we weren’t managing life very well. We isolated to avoid the evidence. That’s alcohol’s favorite game: get us alone, keep us afraid, and make sure we keep drinking. The longer we hid, the smaller our world got, until the only thing that felt safe was the thing killing us.

“It’s a lonely deal until you realize it was never the world pushing you away — it was you closing the door from the inside.” — A New Pair of Glasses, Chuck C.

How much of my isolation was really just hiding — and what was I really afraid of?
01-29.title: January 29 – Alcohol’s Favorite Game

01-30.body:
January 30 – The Excuse Machine

“It’s not a lie if you believe it.” — George Costanza, Seinfeld

Excuses kept us drunk longer than alcohol ever did. We had one for every situation — the bad day, the good day, the breakup, the promotion, the weather, the traffic, the nagging, the silence. We could explain away anything if it meant we got to keep drinking. The truth didn’t matter as long as the story worked.

We built a whole defense system around our drinking. We told ourselves we deserved it. We said we earned it. We said we could quit if we really wanted to. And we believed those lies because they made the hangovers easier to swallow. It’s amazing what an alcoholic can rationalize when they don’t want to be honest.

We used to think we were clever — like we were tricking everyone into believing we were fine. But the only one we were fooling was ourselves. The excuses were our way of avoiding the real question: What would happen if I stopped lying to myself? Because deep down, we already knew the answer — We’d have to change. And change scared us more than drinking ever did.

That’s the trap — the excuses keeps us comfortable, keeps us sick, keeps us drinking. The minute we stopped defending our drinking, we finally had a chance to get honest.

“Here’s how part of the mental side of the deal works: it builds you an Excuse Machine. Picture it like some crooked slot machine game sitting in the corner of your brain. You feed it your pain, your excuses, your alibis—and out comes a shiny little ticket stamped: Go drink.” — The 500-Pound Gorilla

What were some of the excuses you had that gave you the right to drink?
01-30.title: January 30 – The Excuse Machine

01-31.body:
January 31 – Not My Fault

“There are such unfortunates. They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way.” — Big Book, p. 58

Some alcoholics unfortunately can’t admit they’ve been wrong. Every bad break, every lost job, every fight — somehow it’s always someone else’s fault. They can’t give a straight apology because, in their story, it’s always the big old scary world did this to me again. It seems like they were born saying, “Not my fault.” And they never truly recover.

We used to avoid people like that because we knew if we got too close, we’d probably be blamed. But the truth is, we weren’t any better. We blamed everyone and everything for the way we felt saying something like "If you had my life, knew the pressure I was under, went through what I went through — you’d drink too." We had a whole list of reasons ready to go. We weren’t lying — We honestly believed our own stories. That’s the part that’s terrifying — We really did believe it.

Blame feels like armor, but it’s really a trap. It keeps us from seeing our mistakes, keeps us sick, and keeps us stuck in a protective, self-willed bubble of delusion. Saying not my fault made us feel safe, but it also kept us powerless. The moment we started considering owning our mistakes, something shifted. The truth didn’t destroy us — it gave us a way out.

It’s easy to spot people who won’t take accountability, but harder to admit when that person is us. The world got smaller when we hid behind blame, and it opened up the moment we started getting honest. Hasn't it turned out the more honest we have been getting, the more free we feel? And freedom feels good.

What’s a mistake you finally owned in sobriety that ended up being a relief instead of a punishment—and what surprised you about how good it felt to stop defending yourself?
01-31.title: January 31 – Not My Fault

02-01.body:
February 1 – In Case of Fire, Break Glass

“When it comes to God, I only have one rule: keep an open mind — but not so open that your brain falls out.” — George Carlin

A lot of us grew up learning to treat God like an emergency service. When things were bad, we prayed. When the crisis passed, we moved on. God wasn’t part of daily life — God was something you called when the house was already on fire.

Many of us watched the adults in our lives do this. Trouble hits, suddenly we’re praying again. Things smooth out, and God goes back on the shelf. Over time, we absorbed the self-destructive idea that prayer doesn’t really work — except maybe in a pinch. So we carried that same thinking into adulthood.

Most of us kept using those same 911 prayers. In trouble, pray. Out of trouble, stop. We didn’t think of it as misguided — it was just the God of our understanding at that point in our lives. When life hurt, we reached out. When it didn’t, we hung up.

Then we got to AA and started hearing people say things like, “God removed the desire to drink from me.” And a lot of us thought, How does that make any sense at all? But by the time we got here, we were out of options. Somewhere under the Steps on the wall, many of us started picturing God in one of those little red boxes that says In Case of Fire, Break Glass.

And then one day it hit us — we were sitting in an AA meeting because our lives were on fire.

We stared at that imaginary box longer than we’d like to admit. Because breaking it open felt permanent. If we did that, things would change. We worried we’d have to become someone else — maybe someone we didn’t recognize. A lot of us weren’t trying to get religious. We just wanted the drinking to stop. That tension was real, and it was confusing. Then it came to us, we already broke the glass and AA is the little red box.

Somewhere along the way, many of us had a moment like this: someone pulled us aside and said, “Do you know the only rule of AA?”
We didn’t.
They smiled and said, “Start praying — and don’t stop.”

What if the trick isn’t learning how to pray — but learning how not to stop?
02-01.title: February 1 – In Case of Fire, Break Glass

02-02.body:
“I think it’s better to have ideas. You can change an idea. Changing a belief is trickier.” — Dogma (1999)
When we first saw Step Two and read “restore us to sanity,” we didn’t feel insane. Who does? We sat around way too long asking ourselves, Am I crazy? Do people think I’m crazy? That line of thinking gave us more anxiety than answers.

Then we started hearing that it wasn’t about padded-room insanity — at least not yet. It was about the sanity of our drinking. We knew there was a solid chance we’d do something stupid if we drank. We might end up locked up, hurt, or worse… and we drank anyway. That’s the insanity of the first drink — running a dead theory again and hoping this time it would work.

We’re powerless against that. If we don’t use this current window of clarity to get some help, the odds are we’ll try to drink safely again. Maybe we make it back to AA. Maybe we don’t. So we admitted there was a crack in the system of our drinking.

At that point, we had a choice. We could exploit that crack — stay sober long enough to see what might actually happen — or we could seal it up and go back to the life we already knew. The one we hated.
So we stuck around to see what these AA folks were talking about. And it turned out we’d been making this way bigger than it needed to be. They told us: act yourself into right thinking. Pray in the morning and ask a Higher Power to keep you sober. Try to stay out of God’s way during the day. If you make it to bedtime sober, say thank you. Do it long enough, and the belief will catch up.

What if sanity isn’t about becoming “normal” — but just not taking that first drink today?
02-02.title: February 2 – The Crack in the System

02-03.body:
“Your a black sheep — not because you were mistaken, but because you chose to be different in a world that often fears what it can’t understand.” — found on Facebook

Some of us grew up feeling like square pegs in round holes. Odd ducks. Black sheep. Always a little out of step and uncomfortable in our own skin. We don’t always know why — it just is what it is. Our default setting has usually been: you don’t know me, followed closely by go away.

When we first got to AA and started hearing other people talk about that same feeling, it stopped us cold. For too long we thought we were the only ones wired like this. Then it hit us — what if all the black sheep ended up in the same room? We might not be the biggest herd, but at least we’re together. And for a lot of us, that was the first real peace we’d felt in a long time.

At some point, one of us finally said out loud what we’d been thinking: “I just want to be normal.”
A woman at the meeting shot back, “Normal? That’s a setting on a washing machine. You’re on the other setting — agitate and spin!”
Then she laughed. Hard. And we laughed too — because it was true.

Before we walked away, she said something that stuck: “I hope you find a God of your own understanding that solves your problem.”
We nodded and said, “Yeah… me too.”

That’s how it started for a lot of us. Not with lightning bolts or certainty — but with a scavenger hunt. Little pieces of Powerful moments here and there that made sense to us. Bits of truth picked up along the way. It wasn’t perfect. It wasn’t polished. But it was enough to keep seeking.

What if the point of a Higher Power isn’t getting it figured out — but staying willing to keep looking, even when we don't like what we find?
02-03.title: February 3 – Higher Power Scavenger Hunt

02-04.body:
“Deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God. It may be obscured by calamity, by pomp, by worship of other things, but in some form or other it is there.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 55

“If one of us is a child of God, then all of us are.” — Chuck C., A New Pair of Glasses

A woman at a meeting once asked one of us a question we didn’t see coming:
“Do you think there’s anyone on earth exactly equal to you?”

He said, “No.”

She smiled and said, “Well then, that makes you a pompous ass.”

For a long time, we believed other people had life more figured out than we did — parents, teachers, even the Pope. And at the same time, we quietly compared ourselves to the people next to us and came out "better than" more often than we’d like to admit.

We’d run the list in our heads: our bank account’s bigger, we’re better looking, we’re more educated, "at least we didn't do that" — the kind of math that never shows up on paper but always shows up in our attitude.

That’s when it becomes clear: the moment we decide we’re either above or below anyone else, something gets blocked. If one of us is a child of God, then all of us are — struggles included. And doesn't this quiet idea of superiority, even when it feels harmless, create distance from a Higher Power?

Maybe the question isn’t about being equal at all. Maybe it’s about finally discovering what is blocking us off from us off from relating to other people in the first place.

Can we measure our distance from God by measuring the distance we put between ourselves and everyone else?
02-04.title: February 4 – Pomp

02-05.body:
“Deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God. It may be obscured by calamity, by pomp, by worship of other things, but in some form or other it is there.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 55

For some of us in AA, the initial instinct was still to claw our way back on top. Our lives stayed loud and messy. Money problems. Family tension. Phones lighting up late at night with reminders of the life we wanted out of.

As we were healing in AA, sometimes out of nowhere the noise would come rushing back. Worry, fear, replaying the same disasters. AA members suggested prayer, not as a demand, just an option. Do it or don’t. It worked for them. Our life, our call.

Looking back, didn't the calamity suit us?

Not because it felt good — but because it fed our own preoccupation with our problems. The chaos kept everything about us. It gave us something to talk about, something to explain, something to carry around like proof that we deserved attention. Drama became a full-time job. The wreckage gave us permission to obsess about our lives, rehearse our stories, and retell the same scenes until everyone around us was worn out.

We claimed we wanted peace, but the truth is we didn’t know how to live without the turbulence. Without the focus on problems, we couldn’t figure out how to keep ourselves at the center. Calm felt unfamiliar. Stability felt empty. Without a crisis, we didn’t know who we were supposed to be.

For those of us running and gunning for a spiritual awakening, learning to deal with calamity is where the real work begins to show up. Not in the big moments, but in how we respond when life gets loud again. Moment by moment, we can pause, get quiet, and take it to a Higher Power or another closed-mouth member who might understand — so we don't go looking for the spotlight again. Many of us found progressing towards this attitude is how the shift starts — enough times that our reaction to life changes, and alcohol slowly loses one of its pulls.

What's blocking you from feeding the drama, trusting God, and letting the calm feel uncomfortable for a while?
02-05.title: February 5 – Calamity

02-06.body:
“Deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God. It may be obscured by calamity, by pomp, by worship of other things, but in some form or other it is there.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 55

For a lot of us, in the beginning, we thought we just needed a new start. A new relationship, a new car, big money — then we’d be fine.

So we’d scroll dating sites like we were picking out ice cream at the grocery store. We’d look at our ride and despise it, wanting something that could take us far, far away. We’d turn our noses up at job offers because the fast money wasn't there.

When we were in meetings, we felt like we had purpose — get sober and help out. But when we left the meeting, we’d occasionally think, “who am I?” — and our inflated self-image had an answer waiting. The ego relentlessly drags us all over our own lives grabbing whatever identity it can find. We’d reach back and pull out some old version of ourselves — who we used to be when we were the big-shot, or when life felt impressive. Or we’d latch onto a future version — who we were going to be once everything finally lined up. Then we’d act from that place instead of where we were actually standing.

Looking back, wasn't it all the same thing? A roundabout, dressed-up version of being way too preoccupied with ourselves. A slick excuse to stop thinking about other people and obsess over ourselves. Using other things to climb an imaginary ladder above everyone else. In the end, wasn’t it really about worshipping anything that made us feel good — and smashing the subtle start to humility we picked up by walking into an AA meeting?

The Big Book has a chapter called Into Action. We were writing our own called Into Distraction.

At some point, with determination to live a new way of life, a lot of us gave up and thought, what if we just take this not-drinking thing seriously for once, and stop worrying about all the other stuff? Goals are good — they keep us moving — but our first goal has to be learning a way of life that keeps us sober. Nothing else matters. Just show up, show up sober, and see what happens.

What direction is your pride trying to pull you right now — and where are you still not satisfied with your life as is?
02-06.title: February 6 – Worship Of Other Things

02-07.body:
“No battery is stronger longer.”— Duracell battery commercial, early 90s

Ever stand in a room flipping a light switch over and over, thinking this time it’ll work? Click. Nothing. Click again. Still nothing. So you flip it harder, faster, like effort alone might suddenly create electricity.

When it came to solving our drink problem hadn't we flipped the switch on relationships? — this one will fix me. Flipped it on the gym? — if I just get healthy enough. Desperately, didn't we sometimes flip it on going dry? — I’m done drinking, problem solved. We flipped it on routines, diets, jobs, promises, fresh starts. Sometimes we even talked ourselves into seeing the light flicker.

We believed somewhere in exhausting our own effort we'd find the power. So we hit the switch harder and harder, not noticing we’d neglected the power company long enough for the lights to get shut off. Towards the end, we ended up exhausted.

Lack of power had become obvious. But what kept us stuck other than the quiet pride of I’ve got this, I’ll figure it out? Asking for help meant admitting that our problem drinking didn’t respond to the same willpower and intelligence we’d used to solve so many other problems.

When we finally stopped flipping the switch and said, “Maybe I need to call on the Power Company,” that’s when recovery started picking up speed — and the Light came on. That pause — that surrender — that’s where the real power showed up.

Where do you notice yourself still flipping the switch in life — trying to figure it out on your own instead of reaching out?
02-07.title: February 7 — Lack of Power

02-08.body:
“Houston, we have a problem.”— Apollo 13

By the time we got here, we already knew the lights were off. Flipping the switch harder wasn’t working, and deep down we knew it never had. The real question wasn’t whether we needed power. It was whether we’d call the power company—or learn to live in the dark with this problem.

Doesn't calling on a Power company greater than ourselves means admitting we’d have to let go of our way?

Some alcoholics stall. They think about flipping the switch again. They try workarounds. They tell themselves they'll figure it out, that they don't need help, they're different, and there's a different way. That they'll handle it on their own. Is this confidence or is it more of the same will-power that failed in the first place?

We needed power greater than our own, hijacked, self-will.

That was our dilemma. Many asked, how do I find that connection, and at what cost to my image?

Well, that’s exactly what the Big Book is about. Its main object is to enable us to find a Power greater than ourselves that will solve our problem.

“That means we have written a book which we believe to be spiritual as well as moral. And it means, of course, that we are going to talk about God.”

What finally convinced you that this problem couldn’t be solved the way you solved other problems?
02-08.title: February 8 — That Was Our Dilemma

02-09.body:
“If a mere code of morals or a better philosophy of life were sufficient to overcome alcoholism, many of us would have recovered long ago.”— Alcoholics Anonymous

That sentence clears up a whole lot of confusion.

This illness is weirdly simple—and wildly misunderstood. Some people can drink and put it down. Some people drink alcoholically and can't put it down. Period. Some of us lack the ability to process alcohol normally. At the liver level, the enzymes that break alcohol down don’t work the same way as in other people. Instead of shutting the craving off, alcohol triggers an allergic reaction that demands more. Once we take a drink, the body keeps asking for another drink. As long as alcohol is in your system, it's asking, begging, pleading, for another.

It’s not a lack of morals. It’s not weak character. It’s chemistry.

That’s it.

Alcoholism is one of the leading causes of death, yet it’s often mistaken for a problem of morals or misguided philosophy on life. It’s a progressive, fatal illness—and when that reality gets minimized, people get hurt.

At some point, many of us quietly realize: this is alcoholism. From there, a choice becomes clear. If we want a different ending, the drinking has to pause. That’s the physical part. For many of us, that meant medical help. Hospitals save lives. Detox saves lives. Alcohol withdrawal isn’t theoretical, and taking it lightly can be dangerous.

Once the body is stabilized, the next real question finally shows up: now what?
That’s where support matters. Alcoholics helping alcoholics works—has for a long time. And somewhere in that process comes the idea of connecting with a power greater than ourselves, because left alone with our own thinking, we already know how this story ends. So isn’t the responsibility on us to walk toward freedom? To dig and uncover something which will help solve our drink problem?

That’s the nutshell version.

Only after the physical problem is addressed does the moral inventory even start to make sense. And the Twelve Suggested Steps are surprisingly effective there, too. But trying to fix behavior while the body is still hijacked by alcohol is like rearranging furniture in a burning house.

And here’s the kicker—we’re not signing up for misery. As the book says, “We absolutely insist on enjoying life.” This isn’t about punishment. It’s about survival first… and freedom to live well after.

When did you first hear alcoholism explained as a physical illness instead of a moral failure—and how did that change (or not change) the way you looked at your own drinking?
02-09.title: February 9 – This Is Physiological (Not Moral—Yet)

02-10.body:
“I was soon to be catapulted into what I like to call the fourth dimension of existence. I was to know happiness, peace, and usefulness, in a way of life that is incredibly more wonderful as time passes.”

As we’ve been trucking along in AA, we kept hearing people talk about this fourth dimension. And like most alcoholics, we wanted a direct route. A shortcut. A way to get there faster and stay there longer.

Obviously the Twelve Steps got us into the ring. They saved our lives. But we wanted to actually live there — to stay in that place Bill was talking about. Happiness. Peace. Usefulness. Not just as an idea, but as something real and daily.

That’s when some of us stumbled onto a simple gratitude inventory Bill talked about in his story.

It’s not complicated. Maybe a spiral notebook. Maybe the Notes app. A dissertation if you want to. Just three questions:

Where have I been happy today?
Where have I been at peace today?
Where have I been useful to other people today?

That’s it.

What surprised us was how grounding it is. Instead of obsessing over what went wrong — or what might go wrong tomorrow — we start noticing what’s already happening. Little moments. Small wins. Ordinary usefulness. Stuff we would’ve blown past before.

It keeps our feet planted in the day we’re actually living. And somehow, over time, that fourth dimension doesn’t feel so far away. Not because we forced our way into it — but because we paid attention long enough for it to surround us.

It works. It really does.

What helps you notice happiness, peace, or usefulness in your day — especially when nothing dramatic or exciting seems to be happening?
02-10.title: February 10 – Gratitude

02-11.body:
February 11 — God Box

Almost everyone has problems. Anxiety. Depression. Frustration. Regret. Life shows up swinging — it happens. And nobody specializes in sitting with that stuff quite like a bunch of bottomed-out alcoholics.

Somewhere along the way, many of us heard about something called a God Box. Some people call it a surrender box. Leave it to alcoholics to make spirituality hands-on and painfully simple.

Here’s how it works. We make a box — any box. Then we write down our problems, worries, resentments, fears, and frustrations. One per piece of paper. This part’s private. Nobody else ever has to see it.

Then we put them in the box.

That’s the surrender part.

Here’s the hard part: once it’s in the box, we don’t get to work on it anymore. We don’t fix it, rehearse it, control it, or mentally reopen it at three in the morning. We let God do His thing.

Then comes the even harder part — paying attention.

Because answers tend to show up quietly. Sometimes the obvious solution is acceptance. Sometimes it’s a conversation we didn’t plan on. Sometimes it’s a person crossing our path at exactly the right time. Sometimes the problem doesn’t change — but we do.

The key is this: don’t touch what’s in the box. The temptation will come. The urge to take it back, rethink it, manage it, or “just check on it” will show up. We let that urge pass.

We trust that we’re doing the next right thing today and let go of the rest. That’s not quitting. That’s trusting. And for alcoholics like us, that can feel unfamiliar — but it works.

What’s something you’ve been tempted to take back after surrendering it — and what helps you let that urge pass?
02-11.title: February 11 – God Box

02-12.body:
“You’ve got to give what you take.”— Freedom! ’90, George Michael

When we first came into AA, many of us were suffering from a hopeless state of mind and body. We didn’t always know it—we just called it life.

It wasn’t like one day things were fine and the next day everything fell apart. Problem drinking can work slowly, like Chinese water torture—one drip at a time—until the problems pile up so high we can’t see a way out.

For a lot of us, the real question showed up just seconds before walking through the door of our first meeting: What’s going to happen to me?
In that moment, we imagined so many possible outcomes. The only thing we knew for sure was this—we were exiting the roller coaster ride of drinking, and that felt like relief.

Even if it wasn’t clearly understood at the time, something deep down inside finally sparked up and said, You’re about to get some help. You’re not alone anymore.”

Looking back, can we admit that it wasn’t just a small spark—but an overwhelming sense of hope, love, and security that had been buried deep inside us, rising up to keep us safe no matter how small we want to remember it?

In the rooms, we found people who had been there. People who understood us. People who cared enough to keep coming back and share their experience with us. As the hope we found in the rooms began to match the courage it took to walk through the door in the first place, we found the strength to say to ourselves, "I can do this too.”

Do you remember the moment you realized, “I can do this too”? What helped that thought finally stick?
02-12.title: February 12 — Hope

02-13.body:
“Take what you need and leave the rest.” — AA meeting wisdom

AA didn’t get its spiritual language from saints sitting quietly and agreeing with each other. Some of it came from a troublemaker.

One of the early guys pushed back hard when the book was being written. He wasn’t buying anyone else’s conception of God, and he wasn’t shy about saying so. He made it clear: if this thing looked like a religious program, he was out. That resistance mattered, and at that moment the group cemented in the idea that spirituality is inclusive, not exclusive, and everyone, yes everyone, is entitled to their own understanding and we can all learn a thing or two from each other.

That’s how we ended up with phrases like “a Power greater than ourselves” and “God as we understood Him.” Not to water anything down—but to widen the door.

For some, old ideas about God kept us stuck for way too long. We’ve heard people joke that when they got here they had a “God of their misunderstanding,” and plenty of us nodded along. We kept trying to shove square pegs of alcoholic thinking into the round holes of our old, worn-out ideas about a Higher Power. Nothing fit, and the more we tried, the more frustrated we became.

Then we really noticed the words as we understood Him.

That was the crack in the door.

That freedom—to let go of old ideas instead of arguing with them—saved us from fighting ourselves. Some of us find what we need in the Group of Drunks. Some use the Great Outdoors. Some use Good Orderly Direction. At the end of the day, who cares, as long as it’s working. We are entitled to use whatever power greater than ourselves to help us stay sober and spiritually alive without debate or argument.

Trying to define another person’s Higher Power can sometimes cause more harm than good. Spirituality, as AA figured out, is broad and roomy. And honestly—arguing about the definition of a Higher Power starts to look a lot like closed-mindedness anyway. That same closed-mindedness is what kept many of us spiritually sick in the first place.

What worked for you today that wasn’t working when you were drinking?
02-13.title: February 13 - You ARE entitled

02-14.body:
“I didn’t find God. I just stopped dodging long enough for something to hit me.” (overheard and never forgotten)

Many of us can say we didn’t have a lightning bolt moment. No choir, no burning bush, no sudden spiritual makeover. What happened was quieter than that. At some point, the idea of something bigger just fell on our shoulders from finally being in the right place long enough.

We kept showing up. We stayed sober long enough. We stayed connected to other alcoholics long enough for something to change. We kept coming back even when we didn’t feel spiritual, inspired, or remotely interested.

Then one day, almost without noticing, we did something kind in a moment where we would have normally lashed out. No big decision. No spiritual announcement. Just a different reaction than usual. What surprised us was that it felt good, and seemed to come out of nowhere.

That’s how it starts for a lot of AAs. With small, almost unconscious actions that went against our old nature as we came to believe. At some point, we caught ourselves wondering what had changed in us, how this new attitude had gotten there—and how we might stay connected to it a little more?

Trying to stay honest, open, and willing — has that started to change your peace of mind at all?
02-14.title: February 14 — It Fell

02-15.body:
“It’s not about intensity. It’s about consistency.”

After being in AA for a while, we start hearing a simple idea: there is only one reason alcoholics drink — they didn't spend time maintaining their spiritual condition. We can't blame the boss, or the spouse anymore. Not money. Not stress. There is one reason, and one reason only. It sounds clean and simple. But if we’re honest, how many days have we not felt in fit spiritual condition and still stayed sober?

Plenty have had days full of anger, selfishness, self-pity, fear, and bad attitudes. Days where prayer felt flat. Days where we weren’t exactly shining examples of spiritual health. And we still stayed sober.

So what happened on those days?

Maybe sobriety isn’t held together by how intense we are spiritually. Maybe it’s about consistency. Now, we show up to meetings regularly. We pick up the phone. We take suggestions. We stay connected even if we don’t feel very connected.

When we really look at it, isn’t something being revealed to us? Many of us came to believe even more when we realized we stayed sober through events we used to drink over. The same kinds of arguments, disappointments, fears, and pressures showed up — but the drink didn’t. And when we quietly ask ourselves the big question, “What changed?” the answer brings a quiet sense of inner peace.

What is a situation you used to drink over that you’ve now stayed sober through — and what do you think changed?
02-15.title: February 15 – One Reason, and One Reason Only

02-16.body:
“There is a principle which is a bar against all information, which is proof against all arguments and which cannot fail to keep a man in everlasting ignorance — that principle is contempt prior to investigation.” — Herbert Spencer, quoted in the Big Book, p. 568

A lot of us stumbled across that line in the Big Book and thought, Huh? Everlasting ignorance doesn’t sound like much fun. Up to this point, hadn’t our pride kept us ignorant about the happiness recovery could offer us? We weren’t short on information. We weren’t short on arguments. We simply dismissed anything that didn’t fit the story we had been telling ourselves.

When we heard the phrase in a meeting — contempt prior to investigation — we couldn’t ignore it anymore. Being foolishly self-reliant, we naturally had an attitude about our spiritual condition: “Nah, that ain’t gonna work. Give me something else.” As if we were royalty in our own lives — and didn’t that attitude treat the people trying to help as if they were servants beneath us?

What were we ignorant of in the first place? That question bothered us. By now, we understood our own willpower fails us — completely — and we needed something greater. So what was holding us back? Didn't old ideas make this more complicated than it needed to be?

Some helped us with Herbert Spencer’s more well known quote — "survival of the fittest" and it was the gut check we needed. Recovery offered its true meaning: either we try to become spiritually fit, or we don’t survive. That realization knocked us off the royal pedestal and led us toward believing in something greater than ourselves.

Where has pride kept you from trying something that might actually help your recovery?
02-16.title: February 16 — Contempt

02-17.body:
“I’m taking life one day at a time — sometimes several days at once.” — comedian Steven Wright

When alcoholics are drinking, they rarely live where their feet are. They live in the past, polishing old stories about who they used to be, or in the future, building grand plans about who they are going to become. They feel important in both directions while sitting on a barstool going nowhere.

They tell stories to stay above their reality. They promise big futures to avoid the present. Meanwhile, the people closest to them watch them drift further into delusion, wasting time.

One of the first things we hear in AA is to take it one day at a time. Be where you are. It felt uncomfortable at first. We were used to escaping — backward or forward. Staying in today felt exposed.

But when we stayed in today, the load became bearable. We didn’t have to solve our entire life before noon. Isn’t it when we stop trying to fix everything that we finally notice a bit of peace?

We began starting our mornings by reaching for something greater than ourselves — a simple ask for help staying sober today — we found a strength that wasn’t ours alone, but it was enough.

Living one day at a time still looks small on the outside. But on the inside, it has given us a life we no longer need to escape.

How does starting your day with a moment of connection change the way you move through today?
02-17.title: February 17 — Taking Life One Day at a Time

02-18.body:
"Now when I got to AA, I had that attitude of a 12-year-old boy who had defied God, his parents and his teachers. When I first walked
into AA I was 38 years old with the spiritual knowledge of God of that 12 year old boy. No wonder we have trouble with this God
thing when we get to AA. Anybody else ever have those kinds of feelings about God and people?" - Joe & Charlie Big Book Experience

Some of us had no idea what agnostic meant before AA. We heard it and assumed it meant atheist, anti-God, or someone we couldn’t relate to. If this thing was going to turn into church, we were already halfway to the door.

Many of us carried old ideas about spirituality — some from confusing experiences, some from avoidance, some from thinking we were too smart to need it. Either way, the idea itself felt like a wall.

When Joe & Charlie walked so many of us through it in plain language, it landed differently. No theology. No pressure. Just the possibility that willingness mattered more than certainty.

We didn’t become believers overnight. We just stopped feeding the assumptions long enough to let the door crack open.

What changed when you stopped arguing with the idea of a Higher Power and simply stayed open to the possibility?
02-18.title: February 18 — We Didn’t Even Know

02-19.body:
“And he wrote another Chapter called, We Agnostics, which I think is one of the greatest pieces of spiritual information I’ve ever read in my life. As I read that and studied that I could see where some of my old ideas, old prejudices, about God and religion, were wrong. And when I could see where they were wrong then I could discard them, and then I could accept some new ideas about God and then I could make a decision. Now based on hellfire and brimstone, based on a God of justice, no way could I have ever made the decision about God.”— Joe & Charlie, Big Book Study

There’s something about the heavy metal — the coins, not the music. The yearly ones feel different in our hands. They weigh a little more than the monthlies, and deep down we know they represent more than time. They carry daily grace, and the quiet sense that something in us has changed. A lot of AAs recognize we’ve we never got a yearly coin by aiming at a yearly coin. We got there the same way we got the 24-hour chip — by living today, turning over our thinking, and asking for the next right action even when we didn’t feel like it, and next thing we know someone was handing us a heavy metal coin in a meeting.

Somewhere along the way, this stopped feeling like punishment and started to feel like sunlight. We began letting go of the old habits we learned while drinking — control, avoidance, resentment — and we acted ourselves into better thinking. We made the call, showed up, paused instead of reacting, and helped someone when we would’ve rather isolated. Against our own predictions, it felt good — not fireworks good, just warm-sun-through-the-window good.

Our understanding of God softened too — not a scorekeeper, just a Higher Good we can line up with. We don’t have to believe perfectly; we just stay willing. And if we keep doing that, just for today, the heavy metal comes — not as a finish line, but as a reminder that this way of living works.

What small “next right action” have you taken that didn’t feel like much at the time, but later turned out to be part of the foundation for the sobriety you have today?
02-19.title: February 19 — Heavy Metal

02-20.body:
“I’ve tried everything, man. I’ve tried counseling, acupuncture, hypnosis, therapy, and everything. And then I tried drinking again — and that worked for about a week.”— Jim Carrey, 1990s stand-up

When we first came to AA, some people kept talking about God. We hadn’t yet figured out how drinking and God connected, all though we kept an open mind to what they were talking about. We thought AA was about quitting booze, not sorting out theology.

We tried to handle our drinking problem on our own in the past. We used willpower, promises, and plans. It worked for a while, and then we would eventually pick up again. Each time, it got worse. Never better.

In meetings, we listened to people talk about a “Power greater than ourselves.” We had a hard time connecting those dots, but they said it worked for them — so we started to wonder how it might work for us.

The truth is, we weren’t rejecting God; we were rejecting the version we’d made up in our own heads.

Looking back, a lot of AAs can laugh at how complicated we were making it. We did believe in something — and that turned out to be enough to get started and stay sober. What held us back were old ideas that clouded that belief, and we needed help clearing them out.

What’s some old ideas about God that might still be blocking us from seeing things more clearly?
02-20.title: February 20 — Connect The Dots

02-21.body:
“Alcoholics Anonymous has been called ‘the spiritual movement of the twentieth century.’ Without theology, without clergy, without hierarchy, AA offered a way for ordinary people to experience the spiritual… It returned religion to its root meaning — a relationship — and made that relationship available to anyone who sought it.”— Ernest Kurtz, Not-God: A History of Alcoholics Anonymous

Phones already worked. But when smart phones came out we were amazed at how absolutely useful they could be to us. Same invention, with new ideas, which made our lives easier.

All developers had to do was drop old clunky ideas to get some new ones and we got something wildly more amazing.

Many of us found we had old, clunky ideas about God that felt the same way — rigid, punishing, impossible to please. Those ideas were minimally useful when our drinking took off.

In recovery, we discovered we had to let those ideas go if we wanted and develop new ideas. Not to throw away belief — but to grow that belief into a loving God of our understanding, one that restores us to sanity and helps us live. A Higher Power that isn’t there to scare us, but to guide us.

If we can reinvent phones to make daily living easier, can't we let our understanding of God grow into something that actually makes our whole life make sense?

What old ideas about God did you have to let go of before recovery started to feel possible?
02-21.title: February 21 - New and Improved!

02-22.body:
“We had to stop playing God. It didn’t work.” — Big Book, p. 62

Many of us came in with old ideas about God — punishing, keeping score, watching us in the dark, judging, waiting for us to mess up. When we inspected each idea and asked where it came from, those ideas usually didn’t come from any real spiritual experience. They came from parents, authority figures, movies, or our own sick minds trying to make sense of a world that felt unsafe.

Looking back, when we got upset, didn’t we often act in those same ways? We punished. We kept score. We judged. We gossiped. We decided who was in and who was out. We played the God of our understanding. No wonder our relationships were a mess — we were trying to manage the universe and couldn’t even manage our own lives without punishment.

If some of the ideas we carried were as sick as we were, it’s no surprise they didn’t work. We needed new ideas — not to look like saints, but to live in a way that didn’t make everything harder.

What’s one old idea you let go of that helped you stop burning bridges in moments of stress?
02-22.title: February 22 — The God Inventory

02-23.body:
“Some of us have tried to hold on to our old ideas and the result was nil until we let go absolutely.”— How It Works, Alcoholics Anonymous

A lot of us in the rooms started feeling immediate relief when we let go of old ideas — old dependencies, assumptions, and the conclusions we used to jump to during our most hungover moments. We started hearing How It Works over and over in meetings, and eventually parts of it began to sink in. “The result was nil” hit home for a few. We wanted to stay sober. Nil wasn’t going to cut it.

The first three suggested steps rolled around in our heads. They had been enough to keep us sober to this point. But when we read the word decision, we wondered what that meant. What would we become? Would we have the same friends? The same job? The same life? Is this really going to work for me? Am I too far gone? Overwhelmed, many of us put the decision on the back burner while we gathered more information in meetings. And then, quietly, something shifted.

Whatever happens will be better than the lying and hurting we lived through while drinking. Hadn’t we been making a bigger deal out of it than it needed to be? Our lives were clearly unmanageable. Fully conceding to our innermost selves that when we drink, we don’t quit on our own willpower — something had to be done. And without a proper mental defense, the thought of trying to drink normally again wasn't too far off in the future.

In that moment of desperation, something guided us toward making a decision — not perfectly, and that’s not the point. Because by the time we made the decision, hadn’t we already made up our minds anyway? And as for whether it would work for us, weren't we already living the answer, one sober day at a time?

What held you back from letting go absolutely — and what finally helped you loosen your grip?
02-23.title: February 23 — The Decision We Already Made

02-24.body:
One of the last bits that needed clearing out was prejudice — the conclusions we made before we were willing to look further.

Not hatred. Not politics. Just the quiet “Nope — not for me” we slapped on fresh spiritual ideas.

Hadn't we already decided what God was — and that we didn’t want anything to do with it? Were we rejecting God… or rejecting the version we were handed? Did we think we had to fit into a religious denomination before it would work? Did resentment toward religious people close us off from willingness to believe? Were we afraid that believing meant losing independence? Did we assume AA was trying to sell us something we didn’t want?

Some struggled through the idea that we had to believe perfectly or not at all. We thought willingness meant signing a contract. But willingness wasn’t certainty — it is a broad freedom of choice. It was curiously taking a peek through a cracked door.

We weren’t being asked to define God. We were being asked to stop pretending we already had.

And something surprising happened. Results started showing up before we had the words. A little more patience. A lot less panic. Moments of calm where there used to be chaos. Not because we figured God out — but because we stopped ruling the fresh ideas out.

It turns out we didn’t need a full understanding. We just needed enough willingness to try something different.

Looking back, what ideas about God or spirituality did you rule out too quickly — and what helped you become willing to take another look?
02-24.title: February 24 — Clearing Out the Old Conclusions

02-25.body:
“I don’t have a problem with God — it’s His fan club that scares me.”

We sat around way too long in meetings doing that internal hostage negotiation:

“Okay… so I’ve gotta turn it over to God to keep from drinking. Fine. But what will that make me then?”

Was AA telling us we had to act like the people we’d met in church? Didn’t we, in fact, deem some of those folks hypocrites — checking in on Sunday, then living however they wanted the rest of the week? If staying sober meant becoming a hypocrite, no thanks. At least when we were drinking, we understood ourselves. It felt honest enough. Disgusting and ugly, sure — but honest to ourselves.

Deep down, did we really doubt what the power of God could do for us — or did we doubt the “people of faith” we had known up to that point? Did we confuse the idea of God with some religious folks who rubbed us the wrong way? Did we reject the solution entirely just because we didn’t like the people we thought it came from? Were we turning down help from a Higher Power or were we turning down the packaging we thought it came in?

When we finally settled down — when we stopped arguing in our heads long enough to just relax and take it easy — we couldn’t ignore the fact that we had met some real salt-of-the-earth people in both church and AA. People that did good for the sake of doing good. People who weren’t selling anything. People who showed up, told the truth, tried to live decent, and helped somebody for no applause.

Looking back, were we making this decision way bigger than it needed to be? We sat in meetings think, think, thinking… when the answer was almost embarrassingly simple: we don’t have to like everyone’s style to make this work for ourselves.

A God of our understanding gives us the freedom to start fresh and drop prejudice against anything that was holding us back from contented, long term sobriety. We no longer have to fight to prove how it wouldn’t work. We get to start with a clean slate and see how this could work for us.

What helped you move past old assumptions and become open to something new?
02-25.title: February 25 - Hostage Negotiation

02-26.body:
“Once the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically.”— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 64

Some of us came in thinking way too small. Not because we lacked ambition, but because we were exhausted and managing wreckage. Our goals were simple: get through today, don’t drink, don’t make things worse. Some would say, “It gets better. Then it gets good. Then it gets real good.” Real good sounded like it was meant for someone else.

But sobriety widens the lens. Hadn't we been finally sleeping through the night, laughing again, and finding hope in this new way of living? Now, we can make decisions we don’t have to hide from. Gratitude showed up unexpectedly. Peace is becoming familiar. We are beginning to feel useful, connected, and at comfortable in our own skin — even when life isn’t perfect.

In this new way of living, we come to understand whatever you are imagining for your life right now is too small. Not because we are failing, but because we are just getting started. God isn’t rationing grace — we are the ones living with a thimble next to an ocean.

We don’t have to figure it all out. Our job is simple: show up sober, one day at a time. That’s the ticket through the gate of an abundant life. On the other side isn’t just survival — it’s a life bigger and more peaceful than anything we could have imagined.

Turns out, we aren’t aiming too high. We are aiming too low.
