When you first got sober, what did you think life would look like — and how has it grown beyond that?
02-26.title: February 26 — Thinking Too Small

02-27.body:
“AA has a wrench for every nut that walks through the door.

Some of us came in with no use for the word God. Some were angry. Some were frustrated due to their old ideas. Some of us just didn’t believe in anything we couldn’t see or measure. And a few of us figured if this whole deal required signing a spiritual contract, we were out.

Apparently, we weren’t the first ones to feel this way.

We started hearing people use different acronyms for G.O.D. — Group Of Drunks, Good Orderly Direction, Gift Of Desperation, Grow Or Die. Some said it meant the Great Outdoors. Some said Grace Over Drama. It didn't matter if we all agreed on the definition, that's personal, and somehow… it still works.

Confusing at first, weren’t we all supposed to agree?

But the longer we stayed, the more obvious it becomes: the point isn’t what we name the power. The point is that it gets us out of the center long enough to move us into a higher level of consciousness. The kind of power that can interrupt self-will, and as a result keep us sober.

We had spent years arguing with definitions while our lives fell apart. Now we were watching people with wildly different beliefs stay sober, rebuild relationships, and find some peace. Not because they solved the mystery of God — but because they tried to use the power behind the definition one day at a time.

What if the point isn’t defining God, but getting out of our own way? What if willingness matters more than terminology? What if the results are the only proof we need?

What did you use as a Higher Power when you first came in — and how did you know it was working?
02-27.title: February 27 — No God, No Problem

02-28.body:
“We found that as soon as we lay aside prejudice and expressed even a willingness to believe in a power greater than ourselves, we commenced to get results…”
— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 46
Something’s been changing, hasn’t it? The constant mental static — the what-ifs and shame loops — aren’t running the whole show every minute of the day anymore. We’ve had moments where we caught ourselves feeling okay. We've found ourselves sitting in meetings relating to stories instead of comparing.
We’ve started to notice people and remember names. As we’ve gotten active, been friendly, found a home group, stacked chairs, made coffee, showed up early and stayed late — we’ve noticed we're a part of instead of apart from.
If we’re honest, we’ve already seen results. Real results. Comfort showing up in unexpected moments. Hope sneaking in when we weren’t looking. The idea that maybe our lives aren’t over — maybe they’re beginning.
Where are you seeing this program start to work in your life?

“We found that as soon as we lay aside prejudice and expressed even a willingness to believe in a power greater than ourselves, we commenced to get results…”
— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 46

Something’s been changing, hasn’t it? The constant mental static — the what-ifs and shame loops — aren’t running the whole show every minute of the day anymore. We’ve had moments where we caught ourselves feeling okay. We've found ourselves sitting in meetings relating to stories instead of comparing.

We’ve started to notice people and remember names. As we’ve gotten active, been friendly, found a home group, stacked chairs, made coffee, showed up early and stayed late — we’ve noticed we're a part of instead of apart from.

If we’re honest, we’ve already seen results. Real results. Comfort showing up in unexpected moments. Hope sneaking in when we weren’t looking. The idea that maybe our lives aren’t over — maybe they’re beginning.

Where are you seeing this program start to work in your life?
02-28.title: February 28 - Getting Results

03-01.body:
“If you don’t go for it, you’ll never know.” — Zack Morris, Saved by the Bell

A few have heard in the rooms: three frogs are sitting on a log. One decides to jump off. How many frogs are left? Three. We know that answer because we’ve lived it. We’ve made decisions our whole lives — no drinking tomorrow, to drink differently, to really mean it this time — and somehow we were still sitting on the same log. Decision alone never moved us. If we want off the log of alcoholism for today, a decision has to be followed by action.

Step One broke through the delusion and handed us honesty. At this point, we realize willpower fails us utterly. We try to outthink our drinking, outrun our drinking, and control our drinking — and we keep losing. Sitting in meetings, we have found hope and came to believe there is something bigger than willpower, something that works when we can’t.

Now we’re standing at the turning point. We know what happens when we drink. We’ve come to believe being sober is possible. We’ve loosened our grip on old spiritual ideas and found hope that this works. Step Three doesn’t ask us to have it all figured out right now — just to take one small step toward acting with honesty, open-mindedness, and willingness, and see what happens today.

Are you jumping for today? — or what’s keeping you sitting on the log?
03-01.title: March 1 — Three Frogs

03-02.body:
“Being convinced, we were at Step Three…” — Alcoholics Anonymous

Some of us noticed that line lands right after How It Works, and the thought comes in: what do they mean? Turning our will and our lives over to the God of our understanding sounds like a tall order. But is it?

Our life is our actions. Our will is our thoughts. Does a court sentence you on your thoughts or on your actions? So we get sponsors and lean on the groups to help us sort out thoughts and actions that are blown out of proportion by alcoholism.

Somehow, some way, drinking cut us off from the real world and we lived in a world of our own making. And when we were asked to step out of our dream world, we collided with reality and fought — hard. Not intentionally. It just happens.

After making the decision — yes, this is going to work for me; yes, I can do this; yes, I have felt like these people in AA; yes, I am ready to move forward — peeking our heads out of the dark shadows of alcoholism, we see a crack of light that is recovery. And we step toward it today.

Our biggest asset is the help in the rooms — connection over isolation — and it starts to feel good. Our own self-will has thrashed our lives, and now that we have taken the smallest of steps toward something bigger, the payoff is already there.

What’s one action today you can take toward the light instead of back into isolation?
03-02.title: March 2 — Being Convinced

03-03.body:
“It’s my way or the highway.” — King Alcohol

There’s something about active alcoholism that separates us from the herd. Maybe we were born this way, maybe it evolved over time, but by the end a lot of us became the wannabe directors of the world, when in reality King Alcohol was calling the shots. We lived in secret, drifting away from family, jobs, and anything resembling healthy living, all while living in our heads and running the world. If they would only do this. If you would only do that. You should have done this. We thought we had life figured out while we strolled down Easy Street, bottle in hand — right up until we hit a dead end and found ourselves detouring into AA. When we weren’t spouting opinions like they were facts, we were mentally rehearsing old stories, replaying hurt, pain, and grudges on a loop, each time a little worse, each time a little more justified. We said drinking took the edge off, but somewhere along the line we drank away the filter of grace we once had. It was our world and everyone else was just in the way — if they would only listen to us, everything would be great. Our own self-will grew so loud we forgot other people had free will, not corrupted by alcohol, and they could live and do as they pleased. Then something strange happened in AA: things got quieter. Maybe relationships aren’t repaired yet, maybe the wreckage still sits where we left it, but we haven’t made anything worse in a while — and for people like us, that’s progress.

Where are you trying to direct a scene in your life today?
03-03.title: March 3 — In the Way

03-04.body:
“What are a couple of nice guys like us doing sitting in AA?”

On the surface, we were nice guys. We held doors, picked up tabs, said “no problem” when it absolutely was a problem. We told people, “it’s all good,” while in the back of our minds we were expecting appreciation, a thank you, attention — maybe even a little admiration. We weren’t just being kind; we were investing. And we expected a return.

Looking back, can we see how transactional our motives were? I do for you, you do for me. I help you out, you give me prestige. I fix it, you give me security. I act generous, you boost my self-esteem. It looked loving on the outside, but underneath was a quiet contract nobody else agreed to.

After a while, didn’t our self-willed motives become obvious to everyone else except us? When people didn’t respond how we pictured, the “nice guy” could turn sharp — resentful, demanding, cold. Our kindness had conditions. The generosity had fine print.

We replayed the scenes in our heads and found that nothing pairs with self-imposed disappointment quite like oblivion. Over time, we cut people out faster than we let them in. The circle shrank. We started deeming them “toxic.” Weren’t we blind to our own toxic behavior in the first place? The isolation grew, along with the fear of running into someone we resented. We avoided rooms, conversations, entire places — just to escape the tension we created for ourselves. Our world got smaller, not safer.

Where do I still have expectations for people to act as I wish — and how do I respond when they don’t?
03-04.title: March 4 — Nice Guy Syndrome

03-05.body:
“The road to hell is paved with good intentions.”— Saint Bernard of Clairvaux

“They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way.”— Alcoholics Anonymous, How It Works

What did psychiatrists notice about alcoholics that made King Baby seem like the right label for us?

His Majesty… the Baby.

Underneath the charm, the helping, the smiling, and the pretending to be reasonable, there’s often a childish demand to run the show: THEY DO AS I WANT OR OFF WITH THEIR HEADS! The problem wasn’t that life didn’t go our way—the problem was we thought it should. Haven’t some of our deepest motives secretly revolved around power, attention, and pleasure? Sometimes we chased those things by being charming, helpful, and overly friendly. Other times we blatantly tried to control the room, steer the outcome, or quietly manipulate things so the story ended the way we wanted it to. Either way, a lot of what we did came with strings attached. We did favors but expected loyalty. We gave things but expected gratitude. We showed up smiling but were already keeping score. Underneath it all was fear—fear that if people saw the real us, they might walk away. So we created a version of ourselves we thought the world would accept and played that part hard.

Eventually the plan falls apart—because the world never agreed to the script we wrote in our head. When that happens, the King Baby doesn’t look inward; he looks outward for someone to blame. If they had just listened. If they had just done their part. If they had just acted right. Blaming other people for the collapse of our plans is like throwing napalm on relationships—rarely anything survives it. Then the familiar resentment sets in and starts running the delusional “not my fault” loop in our heads. We replay the scene over and over, each time polishing the story a little more—making them more guilty and us a little more innocent. Before long they’re the villain and we’re practically saints, because after all we're the King, the judge, jury, and executioner.

Where is the King Baby costing you something in your life today?
03-05.title: March 5 — King Baby

03-06.body:
“Oh, you like tattoos? Then get pages 60–63 tattooed on the inside of your eyelids.” — Sponsor
Active alcoholism has a way of sidestepping purity of heart, magnifying our egocentric, self-centered core. Call it self-preservation, call it fear management, dress it up however. There is no self-seeker greater than an alcoholic whose life has been abducted by King Alcohol. They can be in Florida in the middle of winter and still find something to complain about. The sky is blue, the sun is shining, and somehow they’re irritated about the chair, the coffee, the noise, or the people around. All the while the illness is quietly doing what it does best—pushing people away and steering them back toward isolation.
Isn’t it when they throw back a couple drinks that the embarrassment multiplies? Barstools can turn into a State of the Union podium and suddenly they’re the self-elected Dictator of the room, explaining to everyone how great the world would be if people would just listen to them. Coming to after a bender, aren’t they left confused and embarrassed by the humiliation they brought on themselves? Their natural, yet neglected, sense of gratitude for simply living is now suffocated by self-pity. In its place grows a brilliantly egotistical commentary about what they deserved, what they wanted, and how right they were right along.
These opinions revolve around themselves—what they want, how they feel, and why most everyone seems to be doing it wrong. Opinions so delusionally based on self they can rarely find anyone willing to agree with them. And when conflict ultimately shows up, they throw their hands in the air and wonder why most everyone is so rude. The lenses in their glasses are backwards, constantly looking outward at the world for someone to blame. Comfortably they retreat into resentment, into self-pity, and ultimately back into themselves.Where is judgment costing you something in your life right now?

03-06.title: March 6 — Florida Sunshine

03-07.body:
“The first step toward change is awareness.”— Nathaniel Branden

For some of us, it’s easy to think there’s a special group of alcoholics the book is talking about — guys in trench coats under bridges grasping a bottle. The real train wrecks. Or we read these pages like they’re describing a potential worst-case scenario of what could happen if someone kept drinking long enough.

Doing so, at this point something subtle is happening. We're quietly grading our own report card, giving ourselves a passing grade, and at the same time flunking others to make the curve go in our favor.

While we’re busy scratching out our own D and trying to turn it into a B, hoping it’ll get King Alcohol off our back, the book interrupts our familiar song and dance with an observation that’s about as comfortable as a dentist appointment without novocaine. Not about alcohol — about us.

This line lands differently when we stop reading it like fiction and start reading it like a mirror:

"Selfishness, self-centeredness! That, I think, is the root of my troubles. Driven by a hundred forms of fear, self-delusion, self-seeking, and self-pity, I step on the toes of my fellows and they retaliate…"

Driven by fear. Self-delusion. Self-seeking. Self-pity. It’s not saying we were absolute monsters. It’s saying something simpler — and harder to admit.

We were the center of our own damn universe, and we usually don’t think so, but... everybody else can see it.

A lot of our decisions ran through the same filter: How does this affect me? What do I get out of this? Why are people doing this to me? And when life pushed back — when people retaliated or things fell apart — we started the blame game again...

They did this to me, so I did that.

Where do you catch yourself grading other people’s report cards instead of looking at your own?
03-07.title: March 7 — I Wasn’t That Bad!

03-08.body:
“You know the difference between you and God? God doesn’t think he’s you.”— old AA wisdom

“Selfish? Who, me? I’m the most caring guy I know.”

That’s the tricky part about self-centeredness — it’s blinding. We rarely see it in ourselves. Everyone else can see it just fine, but to us it looks like concern, responsibility, or just trying to make things work out the right way. This is one reason sponsors are so necessary. They can help us slow things down and put a pause between a thought and an action. That little pause alone can save us from a lot of trouble.

We put ourselves at the center of the universe and tried to manage everything around us. At first it might have looked small — wiggling out of responsibilities or sidestepping things so we could relax and kick back with a cold one. But that “kick back time” started taking up more and more space.

Before long, many of us were either drinking or thinking about drinking most of the time.

And behind the scenes we were managing everything we could to protect it. Manipulating people. Manipulating situations. Lying. Sometimes stealing — being hungover at work, not working up to our full potential, wasting parts of our paychecks the family trusted us to bring home, stealing time away from our kids who wondered where we were — whatever it took to feed the secret nature of our drinking.

For us, it’s just like that.

Through grace we finally stumbled our way into AA and heard about a new way of living. We start hearing about faith, spiritual growth, and a power greater than ourselves. And somewhere along the way we bump into a hard truth: our old ways just aren’t going to work anymore.

If we want anything close to a spiritual life, the first thing that has to go is the job we were never qualified for in the first place — playing God. Why? Because it didn’t work. Obviously.

If we truly want rid of this selfishness, we’re going to need God’s help. Left to ourselves, we end up doing what we’ve always done — taking a deep dive into self and trying to fix self with more self. It just magnifies the problem.

What situation in your life right now would probably improve if you stopped trying to run it?
03-08.title: March 8 — Who me?

03-09.body:
“Every time I find myself playing God, I end up with all the stress and none of the power.”

Our old ways didn’t work.

Playing God shows up in invasive ways: offering advice when nobody asked, helping others the way we deem they need help, doubting people, judging them, acting like we know all the answers. Not having faith that everything is fundamentally good, looking for problems instead of what is already going well. Tearing down confidence in other people. Discounting other people’s good intentions.

And maybe most of all, forgetting there is a Divine core in everyone.

For after all, if one of us is a child of God, then all of us are children of God. And the ones that seem to act up the most probably just haven’t figured out what that means yet.

Where in your life are you trying to use your old ways to change something?
03-09.title: March 9 — Playing God

03-10.body:
“Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate.”
— Carl Jung

Along the way, a lot of us can look back and realize we did live by principles. Not exactly spiritual in nature — but principles nonetheless. Work hard, play hard. Never trust a man who doesn’t drink. Don’t take no crap from anybody. Never take no for an answer. You can sleep when you’re dead. Don’t get mad, get even. And other total liabilities...

While drinking, a life of indulgence, conformity, pride, and control seemed almost natural. For a time we thought we had it figured out. Then King Alcohol pulled the rug out from under us and showed us who was the real undercover boss. At the final moment we stumbled our way into AA, defeated.

Has it become obvious yet that we need to wake up spiritually? That our old ways will likely get us locked up?

Have we considered making the decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of a God of our understanding? Could this idea mean we make a handshake deal to start questioning our old instincts and lean on the spiritual principles we seek in the Twelve Steps?

What old “principle” from your drinking days still tries to sneak into your thinking today?
03-10.title: March 10 — Wake Up!

03-11.body:
“There is no use crying over spilt milk.” — Somebody’s Grandpa

We spilled the milk. It happens. As soon as we walk through the doors of AA, we're asking for help with the mess. It’s a shift in momentum. We accept the mess, but we don’t stare at it any longer.

Step Three finally allows us to throw the mess onto a Higher Power, like a father, and say, Hey, I made a mess of my life. Please forgive me for it all. Can you help me clean it up? I know you have the power to change my life and turn me into a winner. We become willing to ask for help and stop slopping the mess all over our lives.

When we make the decision in Step Three, something begins to change. A sense of strength begins.

Building on that idea, we’re promised something powerful—a pass through the arch to freedom. FREEDOM! And over time a lot of us who stuck around begin to see how massive AA really is. We start realizing there are freed people, not just in the microcosm of our own towns, but all over the world.

People who have turned their mess over, passed through the arch to freedom into God’s plan, and are living remarkable lives as examples that this program works—if you work it.

Do I realize today that my experience might help a lot of people?
03-11.title: March 11 — We Spilled the Milk

03-12.body:
“You can’t always get what you want, but if you try sometimes, you just might find, you get what you need.”— The Rolling Stones

When we sincerely take Step Three, we’re promised something pretty radical — we now have a new Employer. Being all-powerful, He provides what we need, if we stay close to Him and perform His work well.

Looking back, can we see our old employer was drunk on the job? Taking too many “three-martini lunches,” then clocking out at “beer-thirty” and leaving a pretty good mess behind for everyone else to deal with.

The old boss is talented. Hard working. Capable of getting a lot done. Consumed by the obsession to drink, he has no mental defense once the idea takes hold.

Humiliated by King Alcohol, did we finally admit something we didn’t want to admit? We needed some friendly direction in our lives. At that point many of us finally tossed aside a little pride and asked the new Boss for help.

As we learned how to slow down a little, we started realizing something. We were being provided with exactly what we needed on a daily basis. We started to notice something — our plans, usually selfish to the core, kept getting quietly sidestepped, and somehow God’s plan kept showing up instead.

Where in your life has God offered you a better plan?
03-12.title: March 12 — Who’s the Boss?

03-13.body:
“Once you pop, you can’t stop.” — 80s Pringles commercial

A doctor who helped the early AA guys used a fancy Latin phrase: spiritus contra spiritum. It sounds like something a wizard would say, but the idea is simple. We alcoholics are people born with an extraordinarily deep thirst for spiritual connection.

Confused, we tried to quench that thirst with spirits of King Alcohol. That obviously didn’t work. In fact it doubled down on us and eventually we became more disconnected than ever before. It became all about us, our little plans and designs revolving around the thing we worshipped. Alcoholism took everything, and there was no room to think about anybody else other than ourselves.

If we're sincere about our decision to restore our connection to God in Step Three, something strange begins to happen with no effort on our part. We become less and less interested in ourselves. That’s good news. Isn’t it proof we finally found what we were looking for all along? We’re taking a step forward to get connected spiritually, and building a solid foundation for connection to the world.

And once this spiritual thirst is quenched even a little, we naturally desire more. Step Three strengthens the connection with God, and the rest of the Steps help us live in it so it doesn’t slowly fade away.

Where have you noticed yourself being more others-centered?
03-13.title: March 13 — Once You Pop

03-14.body:
“And life has a funny way of helping you out.”

— “Ironic,” Alanis Morissette

Once we grabbed our seat in AA and even started to consider turning our self-will over, many of us started to notice strange things happening in our lives. It often feels like God shows Himself through chance and coincidence. That’s when the picture starts getting clearer. Are you finally noticing?

When we become wholehearted about this decision in Step Three, we’re promised that our interests begin to shift. We become less concerned with what we can take from life and more interested in what we can contribute to it. Somehow, some way our destructive nature is getting sidestepped.

Have we realized we’ve been given time freely to do what we ought to be doing? A chance for today. We’re now living in the space between our last drink and the next one, and that space can be broad and roomy as we decide to make it.

What’s been getting your attention lately?
03-14.title: March 14 — Stranger Things

03-15.body:
“All we are saying… is give peace a chance.”— John Lennon, from the song Give Peace a Chance

Some people call AA an “Attitude Adjustment.” A lot of the early guys used something called the Four Absolutes, Honesty, Purity, Unselfishness, and Love, as a kind of yardstick to measure how much self-will might be showing up in their attitude.

When they felt themselves getting worked up again, they would pause and ask themselves a few simple questions to measure the amount of self-will they currently have: Is it true or false? What’s the next right thing to do? How does it affect the other guy? Is my action ugly or beautiful? And then maybe talk it over with each other. A lot of AAs still do this.

Later on in the steps AA promises our whole attitude and outlook on life will change, provided we keep making progress toward removing our self-willed attitude from the picture. While considering the decision in Step Three, we see we are promised a trade, self-will for the enjoyment of peace of mind.

Are you ready to give peace a chance?
03-15.title: March 15 — Yardstick

03-16.body:
"Free your mind and your ass will follow." — Parliament Funkadelic

That’s a good line for ordinary folks, but for alcoholics it might be wise to say: free your ass, and your mind will follow. A drinking life is a selfish life. In AA we learn we act ourselves into right thinking. Our thoughts and actions had been hijacked by serving what King Alcohol ordered us to do. Haven’t we wasted enough time sitting around giving ourselves excuses to chug while the rest of the world goes on?

As we approach Step Three, we’re standing in the doorway of something new. Regularly attending AA meetings, seeing other people disregard their old ways and have beautiful lives as a result, we want that good life. Have we dedicated ourselves to keep trying in AA? The door is wide open if we want to walk through it.

Which direction are you going today?
03-16.title: March 16 — Free Your Mind

03-17.body:
“What a long, strange trip it’s been.” — Grateful Dead, song Truckin'

Many of us said to our Maker, as we understood Him:
"God, I offer myself to Thee-to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt. Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will. Take away my difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness to those I would help of Thy Power, Thy Love, and Thy Way of life. May I do Thy will always!"

Realizing the power in this simple prayer, a lot of us took quiet time to think about what it meant for our lives, making sure we were ready. Like in game of tag-you're-it on the playground, there are NO TAP BACKS once you've offered yourself back to God. God's it.

How good is it to finally be on God's time again?
03-17.title: March 17 — Lucky Day

03-18.body:
“It’s a new dawn, it’s a new day, it’s a new life for me… and I’m feeling good.” — Nina SimoneTaking the chance to be reborn, having turned the whole mess we created over to a Higher Power after taking Step Three, we’re feeling good enough already. We’re feeling connected in AA and making progress to have our lives restored. We can’t thank AA enough for helping us out of a dark spot.“Good enough” is what we said when we were still avoiding responsibility, carving out time to go drink. Having been reborn, we’re now carving out a life worth living. A new way of life which provides the very best for us. We now have the Power to be better than just good enough.
Are you avoiding the trap of the “Step 1-2-3 waltz”? Are you confusing feeling good enough with feeling cured?

“It’s a new dawn, it’s a new day, it’s a new life for me… and I’m feeling good.” — Nina Simone

Taking the chance to be reborn, having turned the whole mess we created over to a Higher Power after taking Step Three, we’re feeling good enough already. We’re feeling connected in AA and making progress to have our lives restored. We can’t thank AA enough for helping us out of a dark spot.

“Good enough” is what we said when we were still avoiding responsibility, carving out time to go drink. Having been reborn, we’re now carving out a life worth living. A new way of life which provides the very best for us. We now have the Power to be better than just good enough.

Are you avoiding the trap of the “Step 1-2-3 waltz”? Are you confusing feeling good enough with feeling cured?
03-18.title: March 18 – Good enough, dude...

03-19.body:
Bondage of self sucks. It’s like living in a pressure cooker. A self-centered life is a fearful life. And what sucks worse is being self-centered and not knowing it. Sure, we see the consequences, relationships ending, avoiding people we genuinely care about, our contact lists shrinking. We worry about what people are thinking about us, wondering if we’re really welcome in certain spots anymore.

Many of us avoid places so we don’t run into people we have a problem with. We skip events we’re invited to, making excuses, rarely telling the truth about why we’re not going.

Sometimes, clinging to a self-diagnosis of social anxiety, aren't we really just telling ourselves stories to ourselves, about ourselves. Stories that are usually built around some kind of resentment with another person? We replay the story over and over, each time getting a little worse, until we, unfortunately, might finally act on it. A lot of the time we end up alone. Taking Step 3, having a new footing in life, are we ready to face facts about these old ways?

Who are you avoiding right now, and what story are you telling yourself?
03-19.title: March 19 - Bondage of Self

03-20.body:
“Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.” — Mike Tyson
A lot of us come in still "fighting to" stay sober, trying to run strategy like we’re the five-star general of our own life. We’re exhausted… but still convinced we’re in charge.
Thankfully, when we have taken Step Three, we stand on a new footing with God. And for maybe the first time, we can honestly say, “I’m done fighting.” Not my plan from here on out. Not my control. Not my war to run.
I’m accepting the thing I cannot change, I’m alcoholic.
We used to think surrender meant giving up, like losing, like laying down and quitting. But that’s only half the story. Surrender isn’t just giving up the fight. It’s walking off the battlefield where we kept getting beat up. Not looking back, we let the winning side honor the terms of surrender and guide us to safety, without getting in their way.
Where in your life does it still feel like a fight?

“Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.” — Mike Tyson

It’s walking off the battlefield where we kept getting beat up. Not looking back, we let the winning side honor the terms of surrender and guide us to safety, without getting in their way.

Where in your life does it still feel like a fight?
03-20.title: March 20 — Surrender

03-21.body:
“God helps those who help themselves.” — Benjamin Franklin
Themselves? What?
A lot of us grew up hearing that. Some people use it like it’s gospel. For alcoholics, nope. Sometimes, confused by the idea, we don’t ask for help. Or think we’re bothering people. We judge ourselves as weak. We even punish ourselves for wanting help. And in some sense, we were. Has it gotten easier to ask for help?
Having taken Step Three, we’ve tapped into an immense power that enables us to have victory over alcohol one day at a time and we want to go further in the program. We’ve gained an understanding that letting people help us helps them stay sober too. So we’ve gotten better at asking for help.
So in fact, it might be better to say God helps those who help others. In AA, we’re losing our selfish ways, and one of the most selfish things we can do is not ask for help. We’re finally in the stream of life. Sometimes we find ourselves helping just to be useful for the day without seeking approval from anyone, and it feels good.

“God helps those who help themselves.” — Benjamin Franklin

A lot of us grew up hearing that. Some people use it like it’s gospel. For alcoholics, nope. Sometimes, confused by the idea, we don’t ask for help. Or think we’re bothering people. We judge ourselves as weak. We even punish ourselves for wanting help. And in some sense, we were. Has it gotten easier to ask for help?

Having taken Step Three, we’ve tapped into an immense power that enables us to have victory over alcohol one day at a time and we want to go further in the program. We’ve gained an understanding that letting people help us helps them stay sober too. So we’ve gotten better at asking for help.

So in fact, it might be better to say God helps those who help others. In AA, we’re losing our selfish ways, and one of the most selfish things we can do is not ask for help. We’re finally in the stream of life. Sometimes we find ourselves helping just to be useful for the day without seeking approval from anyone, and it feels good.

Where in your life are you still trying to handle everything yourself?
03-21.title: March 21 — God Helps Who?

03-22.body:
“I’ve never grown up, and I don’t plan to.” — Hugh Hefner

At this point, we’ve been given a free gift, the chance to grow up the way we always imagined was possible. We’re starting to realize it’s not all about us anymore. We’re taking a look at our self-centered ways and willing to let them go.

We’ve noticed something too. Our relationships have gotten better when we stop trying to run everything. When we stop dominating conversations, when we actually listen instead of interrupting others, when we stop taking more than we give, when we stop acting entitled and demanding our own way.

Growing up in AA, we’ve noticed that when we start taking responsibility, we don’t have to be so defensive. We don’t go though life feeling under mental attack anymore. We start to settle down and exercise the serenity we’ve been praying for. Having taken Step Three, a lot of us agree we still have a long way to go.

It’s not about becoming perfect. It’s about looking at our old ways so we can change.

Do you want to be right, or do you want to be happy?
03-22.title: March 22 — Growing Up (Finally)

03-23.body:
“Why so serious?” — Joker

Since taking Step Three, we’ve been feeling more connected, and we want to go further in the program, so we’re willing to take a real look in the mirror and inspect our old ways. Now realizing that our own self-centeredness blocks us off from God, where have we been rigid and controlling, taking ourselves way too seriously, quick to blame others and avoid responsibility, demanding things be done our way, needing to control conversations or one-up people, having a hard time celebrating someone else’s success, and taking more than we give? Not exactly a highlight reel for successful long-term relationships.

In Step Three, we traded our self-will, which is our power, for something bigger, a Higher Power. We’re ready to take a look at all the resentments we’ve collected, the ones that have been rotting us from the inside out. This isn’t about beating ourselves up, it’s about getting honest so we can get free.

One day at a time, we’ve started trying to be more others-centered instead of self-centered, and it’s actually working. Thinking about other people gets a little easier, and the world doesn’t feel like it’s closing in on us as much. Now we’re ready to take it a step further, not just noticing our self-centeredness, but really seeing how it’s shaped our lives, our relationships, and the messes we’ve found ourselves in. No shame, no more drama, just an honest look.

Where in your life are you still taking yourself too seriously?
03-23.title: March 23 — Too Serious for Our Own Good

03-24.body:
“Everybody’s got a story, and they’re sticking to it.” — “People Hating” by The Red Clay Strays

There seems to be two types of alcoholics. Happy alcoholics who use the tools to work through resentments, and unhappy alcoholics who can't help but to find things to get worked up over again.

Resentment is poison in a spiritual life. It blocks connection with anything bigger than us. Not just God, but people too. It keeps us locked inside our own version of events, replaying the story until we feel justified all over again.

Unhappy alcoholics don't truly let go of resentful thinking. The stories feel like a personal attacks, self-pitying reasons to distract themselves in the mental battlefield they created. Eventually they advance the war, usually through character assassination, and it gets worse. Instead of putting in the work to let it go, they try to recruit people to their side. They tell the story just right until they can get someone to agree. Now they're’re not just hurt, they’re right.

Not being willing to look at a resentment is one of the most self-centered things we can do. We play the victim. We sit in self-pity. And while we’re doing that, we’re cut off. Obvious to everyone else around us, we’re cut off from truth, from connection, from peace.

Resentment makes it all about us. For people trying to stay sober through connection, it quietly infects the whole thing. We can end up isolated, even in a room full of people.

We keep hurting people. Mostly ourselves.

Step Three gives us access to something different. Not instant freedom, but the power to start letting go in a genuine way, if we’re willing to do the work.

People have told us to “drop it.” And a lot of us got really good at pretending to. We say the words, we nod along… but we carry it with us anyway.

Which type of alcoholic are you?
03-24.title: March 24 – Two Types of Alcoholics

03-25.body:
Having taken Step Three, we’re finally open for business.

We’ve lived fear-based lives, collecting resentments like they were worth gold. Turns out they’re fool’s gold. Now we’re ready to take stock and look at our lives, to see where our self-centered ways have been running the show. Not to beat ourselves up, just to see the truth. People make mistakes. We’re people. We need an inventory of what’s useful and what’s not, what helps us grow and what keeps dragging us backward.

We’ve made a decision not to be held back anymore. So if we’re confused about what to do next, we do something different. We ask someone in AA for help. And that connection feels right. We’re not doing this alone anymore. We find an old timer and get to work. We don’t sit on this. We set aside time and get honest, willing to look at the truth.

And something shifts. We start to feel better already. Like we’re finally moving, finally growing. A lot of us were born with the same birth defect, a head that is just entirely too hard for our own good. Left to ourselves, our hard-headed nature can’t see straight. But now we’ve got help to help us see another angle. The relief that comes with that is so wonderful, so powerful, it shows up in our entire being.

This is where Step Three starts to come alive. Not just a decision we made, but something we’re actually doing.

Are you still trying to do this on your own?
03-25.title: March 25 – Open for Business

03-26.body:
“You can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs.” — Fight Club

When we step back and look at the bigger picture, it’s kind of undeniable… life’s been good. Not perfect, but good in a real, steady way since we started hanging around AA. We’re not getting everything we want, but we’re starting to be okay with that—and that’s new.

Somewhere in there, we took Step Three. We asked God to build with us, not really knowing what that meant. And things started moving. People came and went. Situations ended. Doors closed. At first it felt random. Now it feels like something’s actually being built.

If we slow down, we can see it—less reacting, more acceptance, better timing, a little more peace. Our new motto is life on life’s terms, and it turns out living that way hasn’t crushed us. It’s actually made life lighter. More manageable. More real.

And now we want more of that.

All over AA, we see people living lives better than anything they planned for themselves. Not perfect—just real and full. And for the first time, it feels possible for us too.

So we’re getting ready to do our part.

Because if something new is going up, something old has to come down. We’re not trying to be held back by our self-centeredness anymore. We’ve seen where that leads.

So we’re willing to take an honest look. On paper. No spin.

Not to punish ourselves—just to clear the ground so something better can be built.

What in your life are you still protecting that might actually need to be torn down?
03-26.title: March 26 – Buildings

03-27.body:
“Life moves pretty fast. If you don’t stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.” – Ferris Bueller

We’re finding out that living one day at a time ain’t so bad. Sure, problems still come up, and sometimes they feel overwhelming, but deep down we know something’s different now. We have a power today that can lead us in the right direction.

We thank God we found AA. We thank God we get to live one day at a time. And we thank God we’re staying sober.

Mornings have gotten easier. No more hangovers, no more waking up with that heavy feeling of letting ourselves down again. There’s a little more peace when we open our eyes. We’re learning to stay out of our own self-willed ways, and somehow problems don’t hit as hard. Sometimes they even seem to work themselves out when we’re not forcing everything.

We’ve found real friends in the fellowship, people who understand us, and that takes some of the pressure off life. We’re starting to disconnect from our self-centered nature and lean into thinking about others, and weirdly that takes even more pressure off.

In quiet moments, we can actually feel connected to something bigger than our old lives, and for once the future feels hopeful, and were ready to take it a step further. We can do anything, anything, as long as we stay sober today.

What’s one thing in your life that’s gotten easier since you started living one day at a time?
03-27.title: March 27 – One Day at a Time (Ain’t So Bad)

03-28.body:
“I don't wanna grow up, I'm a Toys R Us kid.” — Toys “R” Us jingle

If Alcoholics Anonymous has been simply put as trust God, clean house, help others, then the question becomes, what’s getting in the way of that? A lot of us, before we got here, were pretty selfish, still holding onto ways from childhood. Some say we never grew up. Maybe we did, maybe we didn’t. Maybe we just avoided the whole conversation. Avoided responsibility, avoided looking at ourselves, avoided anything that might slow us down.

Then we get into AA and start hearing people open up about their lives, things they never thought they’d say out loud, and what’s happening for them is so big it’s impossible to deny that something greater is at work. We hear those stories and can feel we’re on the cusp of something bigger now. At the same time, we know something else too. We’ve sabotaged our own growth in the past. We’ve stalled out, distracted ourselves, gone back to what’s comfortable. So when it’s time to move forward, there’s that pull to hesitate again.

Are we stalling on cleaning house because we still want to play with the toys of distraction? That stuff still calls our name. But now we’ve got something we didn’t have before. We’ve got directions, support, and a fellowship that’s actually showing us how to do this thing, showing us a new way of life that is working.

So maybe today isn’t about overthinking it. Maybe it’s just about taking the next step without hesitation, because we finally have a real shot at this.

Where am I still stalling, and what’s one step I can take today instead of reaching for distraction?
03-28.title: March 28 – Trust God, Clean House, Help Others

03-29.body:
“You never know how strong you are until being strong is your only choice.” — Bob Marley

A lot of people recognize Bob Marley the second his music comes on. Hell, a lot of those songs became anthems in the bars we used to hang around. At some point, some really smart people decided to take all his popular songs and put them in one collection for the people. That way nobody gets bogged down listening to stuff they don’t want to hear. They called it a greatest hits album, and it ended up becoming his best-selling record of all time.

That’s kind of what we’re doing when we take the Fourth Step. We’re not writing a novel. We’re not trying to sound good. We’re just being honest, searching, and fearless. What pops out is the greatest hits of our character. The patterns, the fears, the resentments, the things that keep showing up whether we like it or not. The rest of it that bogs us down, we leave behind.

And we become the best version of ourselves moving forward. Not perfect, just better. It works. It really does.

If we’re confused on how to do this process, we grab someone from AA and ask for help. There’s plenty of help out there. The only person standing in our way is ourselves.

Are you ready for your greatest hits album to drop?
03-29.title: March 29 – Greatest Hits

03-30.body:
“Resentment is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die.”

The Big Book tells us resentment is the number one offender. It takes more alcoholics out than anything else. And it doesn’t take much. We can feel judged and be fighting back in our heads in a matter of seconds.

Fact is, some people judge. That’s not going away. So we’re at a fork in the road—we either forgive them, or we carry it for the rest of our lives. What’s your choice?

Something’s been changing though. Since making that decision to stop running the show in Step Three, things have shifted. Not forced like before. Not fake. Just happening. The smiles are real now, not at someone else’s expense. Feeling more connected. Less judged. Or maybe just less concerned about it.

We’ve been taking care of our alcoholism instead of feeding it. Acting more in line with who we actually are. That constant paranoia, that self-centered noise, it’s been easing up. Slowly, but it’s real.

We’ve had mornings where we wake up and don’t immediately run through everything we said or did the night before. That right there is a break. And things just seem to be working out a little more.

Now we’re looking at the Fourth Step and wondering if it is really necessary. But we already know what it offers—a clean slate.

So is it really necessary… or are we going to carry that load the rest of our lives?
03-30.title: March 30 – The Number One Offender

03-31.body:
“Where is the love?” — The Black Eyed Peas

Having been attending AA meetings, we’re starting to feel good. The sober life is a real life, and the old drunken ways of excess are fading away. We’re learning to use the language of the heart instead of the language of the gutter. That old thinking, all get and no give, is slowly losing its grip, and it feels different… better.

Something is shifting. We’re not just thinking our way through life anymore, we’re starting to navigate our way through it given a new moral compass. We’ve been given the gift of thinking with our hearts, and people notice. They’re drawn to it. Not because we’re trying to impress anyone, but because something honest is finally showing up.

The language of the heart is built on honesty. Real honesty. The kind that lets you lay your head down at night without replaying the day like a kid trying to get out of trouble. No spinning, no fixing, no performing. Just truth. And that truth brings a kind of peace we didn’t know we were missing.

Deep down, there’s gratitude now. For being sober. For finding AA. For the people in the rooms who sharpen us without breaking us. By the end of the day, the heart feels full. Not perfect, not problem-free, just… full. And we sleep. Unbothered by the noise that used to run the show.

Now we’re getting ready to take it further. Pen to paper. Looking at what’s been holding us back. Not because we have to, but because we want more of this. More peace. More honesty. More freedom.

We said we’d go to any lengths.

So the question is simple.

Are you still ready to go to any length to stay sober?
03-31.title: March 31 – Think With Your Heart

04-01.body:
“Inventory? I love taking inventory. I take my wife's inventory all the time!” — Heard in a meeting

A personal house cleaning is in order at this point. We’ve finally made a connection with something bigger than us. Life feels different. Not perfect, but real. We’re starting to live that good life again, and we don’t want the old ways creeping back in and taking us out like they always did.

We’ve heard about this Fourth Step in the meetings. Contented members seem to talk about it like it’s some kind of rite of passage in AA. And we notice that. We want what they have. We want to grow in this new community, and yeah, we want that quiet respect that comes from actually doing the work.

Looking back at the lonely life we came from, it’s not hard to see why something has to change. We can’t keep carrying the same thinking and expect a different life. That math never worked. So instead of overthinking it, or waiting until we “feel ready,” we start making a little space for it.

Nothing dramatic. Just a decision.

We set aside some time, sit down, and begin. Not perfectly. Sometimes all at once. Just honest enough to get moving forward.

Because deep down, we know… this is how we move along on our life.

So are we ready to look at our side of the street, or are we still busy managing everyone else’s?
04-01.title: April 1 – Personal House Cleaning

04-02.body:
“Let’s make a list of all the things the world has put you through” — (Lyric) Things Happen, Dawes

So we make some time for ourselves. We sit down, pen and paper in hand… and we start the Fourth Step. We’ve gotten the instructions from the Big Book, and if we're confused, like so many of us are, we ask someone in AA to help us understand what to do. We don’t have to figure this thing out alone anymore.

We’ve told our life’s story plenty of times before. Usually on a barstool, to people who weren’t really listening, or who were just as lost as we were. But the way they have us do it here is different. This isn’t storytelling for laughs or free beers anymore. The same stories, with this new method is going to be useful to us now. So we start.

And the truth is, the hardest part is writing down that first name. Once the pen hits the paper, it gets real. No more running it through our heads, no more editing the story to make ourselves look better. Just honest, simple truth.

And somewhere in the middle of it, we remember we’re not doing this alone.We remember God is right there with us. Not shaking His head, not keeping score… just a proud Father, quietly rooting on his kid as we try to get free of resentment.

So we keep going. One name, one line, one truth at a time. Because this isn’t about beating ourselves up. This is about finally getting free.

So are you willing to put it on paper… or are you still trying to outrun your own story in your head?
04-02.title: April 2 – Our Life’s Story

04-03.body:
So we’re knee deep in our Fourth Step now. We’ve got a list of names, and yeah, the resentments are still spinning around in our heads. But we start to notice something… the list is done. That alone feels like a win. This whole thing is already working, and somehow it’s starting to feel smaller than it did before we ever walked into our first meeting.

Now we move to the second column: the cause.

So… what happened?

Keep it brief. This isn’t where we go relive the whole story and get ourselves all spun up again. We’re not here to get spiritually sick. Just a few bullet points. What actually went down. Enough to remind us what this is about when we come back to it later.

If we need an example, we can always look at Mr. Brown. Seems that flirty bastard messed with the wrong guy’s wife. But even then, we try to keep it clean. Keep it simple. Keep a lid on the emotion and just write what happened.

Facts. Just the facts.

Because this isn’t about proving anything. It’s about seeing it clearly.

So are we writing the truth… or are we still telling the story the way we want it remembered?
04-03.title: April 3 – Tell Me What Happened?

04-04.body:
So one by one, we’ve been making our way down the list, pairing the name with the cause. Not trying to turn this Fourth Step into some abstract finger painting project. We’re just doing the work in front of us.

And something’s happening. The process is finally organizing our thoughts. Giving us a way to start unraveling that alcoholic thinking. Turning the destructive thinking of resentment, into constructive thinking about some deep underlying issues we have. This process was written for us, by people who knew exactly how we think, because they thought like that too. People who knew how twisted it can get in our own alcoholic heads, and how to help us peel away the useless parts and get down to the meat of the situation.

So we keep moving. One name at a time. One cause at a time. And the facts start piling up.

And yeah… this is where it can get a little emotional. No surprise there. We’re finally looking at stuff we’ve been carrying around for a long time. That’s why so many of us keep another AA member close by during this part. Someone we can check in with. Someone who gets it.

It makes sense.

So are we willing to keep going, one name at a time… or are we already looking for a way to skip ahead?
04-04.title: April 4 – One by One

04-05.body:
Still out on our fact-finding mission in the Fourth Step, we start taking a closer look at what’s really going on here. We all have instincts in life, things we try to keep in balance as we move through the world. And when those get threatened or hurt, we don’t usually just sit there… we react.

So now we take a look.

Did they threaten my money?
My security?
My relationships?
Did they mess with my sex life or sense of connection with anyone?
Did they hit my self-esteem… make me feel less than, or have me questioning if I’m even a decent person?
Did it embarrass me?
Did they get in the way of what I thought I was supposed to become?

In this third column, we’re answering a simple question:

What did it really affect in me? Where did they hit that need?

We’re not spinning stories, and we’re not jumping ahead. We’re just looking at it clean. Keeping it professional. Just the facts.

Because we’re in the business of living now, and if something keeps throwing us off from being spiritually grounded decent people, it’s worth knowing exactly where and how its coming from.

So what’s actually being affected here… and can we write it down without exaggerating?
04-05.title: April 5 – What’s This Really Doing to Me?

04-06.body:
At this point, for a lot of us, it feels like the pen has taken on a life of its own during the Fourth Step. We’ve spent some real time here, and we’ve completed the first part of the Fourth Step. Name, cause, and how it affected us… it’s all down on paper.

It’s natural to be a little emotional here. Change is happening. We’re finally looking at things we’ve carried around for a long time. So we stay close to AA. Maybe we hit a few more meetings, make a few more phone calls, and stay connected, because something is shifting.

We did it. We paired the names with the causes, and we saw how it affects us. And if we’re paying attention, patterns might already be starting to show up. But we’re not done yet.

This is where a lot of people stop, and when they do, they can end up more twisted up than when they first walked into AA. Half measures don’t clear anything up, they just stir it around. So we keep going. We’re not here to sit in this stuff. We’re here to move through it, to follow the directions all the way through and finally get free from the mess we’ve been carrying once and for all.

So are we willing to keep going… or are we about to stop right before this thing starts working?
04-06.title: April 6 – Straightening Out

04-07.body:
Stopping the Fourth step at this point is like taking only half of the prescribed medication, and the infection is likely to return. We’ve played that game before, and it rarely works out. There’s no turning back now.

Next, we take that list of names again, sometimes using a new piece of paper. We forget about all that stuff we wrote down in the second and third columns for now, and we start looking at our own behavior.

What did we do? Did we yell? Did we scare or threaten the person? Where did we act out of character? Did we lay hands on them, steal, or lie? Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking, or frightened, and where did we act on it in this relationship?

The mind will want to jump in and say, “yeah, but they started it…” and go right back to the old story. But that’s not what we’re doing here. Who cares who started it.

Where did we go against who we are deep down, our own natural sense of right and wrong, and act out? We all make mistakes. We’re just looking for where ours were in how we handled these situations.

So are you willing to see your mistakes clearly… or are you still trying to prove you were right?
04-07.title: April 7 – But, But, But They Started It!

04-08.body:
“Resentment is the number one offender.” Yeah… turns out they weren’t being dramatic. Resentment takes out a lot of us, and not always with some big explosion—sometimes it’s just a slow burn sitting in the background, messing with everything. You can be having a decent day, then one thought pops up—something someone said or did—and now the whole mood shifts. It starts coloring everything. And if we’re honest, a good resentment can feel justified, like we’ve got a case, like we’re right. But somewhere along the line, we start to see the truth: it’s not hurting them nearly as much as it’s hurting us. It warps things. Our sense of what’s good, what’s fair, what’s real—it all gets filtered through whatever story we’re telling ourselves. We end up as the victim, the prosecuting attorney, and the judge all at once. That’s exhausting.

What’s been showing up in this Fourth Step is something different. Not blame, not beating ourselves up—just clarity. We start to see where our resentful thinking has boxed us in, how it’s cut us off from people, from peace, from any real sense of freedom. Resentment sucks. But there’s also something freeing when you identify it. Because if it’s been our thinking that’s been tying us up, then maybe it doesn’t have to stay that way. There’s a lot of spiritual sickness out there—always has been, probably always will be—but for once, we’re not trying to fix the whole world. We’re just trying to stay spiritually alive ourselves. And this process… it’s like finding a ticket out. We don’t have to live trapped in resentment anymore. We don’t have to carry every slight, every wound, every story like it defines us. We can start putting it down. And man… that feels better than being right.

Have you found freedom in this process, yet?
04-08.title: April 8 – Resentment is the Number One Offender

04-09.body:
Alcoholics tend to read from left to right. We’ve got these resentments so ingrained in our minds that it’s hard to see them any other way. It feels automatic—name, story, how it hurt us, and then how we reacted. That’s just how it goes. Or at least, that’s how it always has gone.

But here in this work, we’re being asked to try something a little crazy… read it from right to left.

And yeah, that’s not always easy. Sometimes it’s easier with another member of AA.

And somewhere in that process, something starts to shift.

Because maybe—just maybe—if we could have kept a handle on the lashing out, we wouldn’t have hurt ourselves the way we did. And if we didn’t hurt ourselves, maybe the story wouldn’t have taken on a life of its own. And if there’s no story… maybe there’s no resentment sitting there, growing legs.

Maybe.

It’s not about ignoring anything. It’s about looking at it in black and white.

And that kind of perspective… can change everything.

Are you prepared to look at one resentment from a completely different angle—and what happens when you do?
04-09.title: April 9 – A Different Angle

04-10.body:
The whole Fourth Step process can be a real mind bender, or it might be more accurate to call it a heart bender. At this point we have our list, we are finally seeing things more clearly, and now it is time to take it a step further into forgiveness. The people who hurt us were potentially spiritually sick, just like us. The whole thing can start to look like spiritually sick people doing sick things, and we ended up hurt and good and drunk over it.

So we realize that these people were spiritually sick, and we begin to shift. Instead of holding onto it the same way, we try to move it onto a spiritual plane and give our hearts a chance to step in. The mind wants to figure it out, keep score, and make things right. The heart just wants freedom.

And maybe that is what this line of action is getting at. When we loosen our grip on it, when we stop trying to collect on it, when we stop needing it to be different, there is a kind of freedom in that. Not because it did not matter, but because we are not carrying it the same way anymore.

And it works. It really does. Not perfectly, but enough. Enough to breathe, enough to feel a little lighter, enough to move forward.

So here is the question. Which is bigger, your heart or your mind?
04-10.title: April 10 — Sick People Doing Sick Things

04-11.body:
“Fear is the instrument of the ego to see if it can spook me.”
Knee-deep in the Fourth Step, we don’t get to skip this part. We start looking at fear—not the surface-level stuff we talk about, but the stuff running underneath everything. So we take one down, pass it around, and yeah… maybe there’s one less bottle of fear on the wall.
A lot of us have had to slow down and actually write it out: when did this fear first show up? How did we act selfish because of it? What do we honestly think will happen if it comes true? And what’s sitting underneath it? Because if we’re being real, fear doesn’t usually walk in and introduce itself. It hides. It shows up as control, avoidance, anger, “I don’t care,” or trying to look right, sound right, be right. A lot of us called it personality, or instincts, or just “how we are.” And a lot of the time, what we thought was resentment had fear sitting underneath it the whole time.
That’s why this matters. We don’t get free from something we’re still protecting. If we’re still explaining it, justifying it, or pretending it makes sense, it’s probably still running the show. So we drag it out, name it, and look at what it’s cost us—missed chances, shut-down relationships, things we never even tried. Not to beat ourselves up, just to finally see it straight. Some of these fears have been hanging around so long they feel normal, like part of the furniture. But they’re not. They’re just bottles, and we don’t have to keep stacking them up.
What’s one fear you’ve seen hiding underneath something else—like anger, control, or avoidance—and what has it actually been costing us?

04-11.title: April 11 – 100 Bottles of Fear on the Wall

04-12.body:
We hear a lot of clever little acronyms in AA. They stick because they’re true—or at least true enough to get our attention. S.L.I.P. means Sobriety Loses Its Importance. S.O.B.E.R. means Son of a Bitch, Everything’s Real. And right about now, knee-deep in the Fourth Step, we run into F.E.A.R. Sometimes it looks like F@*k Everything And Run, and if we’re being honest, that one fits real good. That’s been a lifelong move for a lot of us. Things get uncomfortable, uncertain, or a little too real, and we’re halfway out the door before our brain even finishes the sentence.

But there’s another version: Face Everything And Recover. That one doesn’t come as natural. Because now we’re not just listing fears—we’re looking at them. Where they started, what they’ve been costing us, and the weird ways they’ve been quietly running the show behind the scenes. We start to see how fear shows up dressed like control, avoidance, anger, people-pleasing, and isolation—all the old familiar outfits. And here’s the twist—we’re not doing this to become fearless superheroes. We’re doing it so fear stops being the boss.

Alcoholics are clever folks. And the only thing more cunning, baffling, and powerful than alcohol is the program of Alcoholics Anonymous. So the question is simple—are we running, or are we facing our fears right now?

Are you running from your fears right now, or actually facing them?
04-12.title: April 12 — F.E.A.R.

04-13.body:
Wearing fear is like putting on of those turtleneck sweaters one size too small. It's hot, itchy, hugging our throats, and the more we pull at it the more we think about how much we want out of it. It tells us stories. Most of them about our lives, and a lot of them are about uncomfortable, sudden change. Sit with the story long enough and it starts to feel real.

The Big Book’s answer is almost too simple. Look at the fear, ask God to remove it, then ask what He would have us be. That’s it.

Somewhere in this process, we’ve tapped into a power bigger than our stinking thinking. The same power that got us sober didn’t disappear just because fear showed up. What’s really happening most of the time is self-centeredness—our minds running a game play about you, for you, scaring you.

In a God-centered life, ywe’re not stuck in that loop alone. There’s a steady voice available—quiet, sane, not dramatic. Ask it: What should I do here? The answer is usually simple, honest, and a lot less extreme than the fear.

Simple doesn’t mean natural. Going against that old pull takes practice.

Above all we take it easy. Notice the fear, hand it over, and move anyway. And give ourselves the same grace God already has.

Are you giving yourself the same grace God already has?
04-13.title: April 13 — The Story Fear Tells

04-14.body:
“Those with the most tools do the work.”
The whole point of the Fourth Step is not to rehash old issues and get even more justified in being pissed off at people. It’s to change. If our thinking has not changed, and we're still doing the same things as we did before, then it is time to take another look. Sometimes it takes a little bit. The word is thorough, and this is not about other people anymore. It is about us, how we have behaved, and how we want to set up our future dealings with others.
These alcoholics figured out a pathway out of our stinking thinking that nobody had been able to figure out before, and if we can position our thinking through grace, stop pointing fingers, and inspect our own minds in times of stress, we can live wonderful, happy lives. We have been given the grace to find AA, and we have been given tools to relax, accept, and take it easy.
Sure, the world seems like an insane place, and we have contributed our share of insane choices to it, but resentment, anger, and rage are no longer options. We have tools. This is not about what we can get out of life anymore—it is about what we bring into it. We are in the business of giving grace, not walking around expecting it for every cornball reaction we make. We are trusted by God to help instead of harm. It is a free gift we have been given, and it is time to practice using it so we can get better at it.
Have you changed?
