04-14.title: April 14 — Change

04-15.body:
“Let’s talk about sex, baby…” – Salt-N-Pepa

Having made it this far in our Fourth Step, we’re trusted to be able to work out our resentful thinking,and set aside our fears. This is a big responsibility. Almost everyone who does a thorough job ends up with a deep sense of gratitude for the pathway out of resentment and fear that AA has provided. It has changed our lives, and we can’t thank AA enough.

Now, using these new tools, we’re able to look back on our intimate relationships and take an honest look.

There isn’t a ton of sex talk in AA. It can be touchy, and it can bring up judgment. I heard a guy say once, “Two things we don’t care about in AA: one, what your Higher Power is, and two, how you get your rocks off.” And it makes sense. We listen, and we don’t judge—and in the Fourth Step, we don’t judge ourselves either. We’re here to make things right with our lives and start shaping future relationships in a way that doesn’t harm anyone.

So we start. We make a list of our intimate relationships and take a look at where we might have been selfish, dishonest, or inconsiderate. We’re not doing this to beat ourselves up—we’re looking for the nature of our wrongs, the patterns of behavior that keep us sick.

So we grab a pen… and we continue.

How do you want your future relationships to go?
04-15.title: April 15 – Let’s Talk About Sex, Baby!

04-16.body:
“Sex education in school mostly consisted of watching a VHS from 1987 and hoping for the best.” - Jim Gaffigan

A lot of us took sex education in school and concluded sex is fun, try to stay away from anything that can hurt us, and get as much of it as possible. That was the lesson. And like most things we touched, we didn’t just participate, we used it. We used sex to build our egos up, to feel wanted, important, powerful. For some of us, it turned into a transactional mindset, I do for you, so you do for me. Sex can be a touchy subject. Sometimes we felt like we didn’t have enough, some of us might think we had too much, and most of us, if we’re being honest, weren’t operating on any kind of spiritual principles in this area of our lives. We’re here to get honest about our sexual nature. So now we slow down and take a look, not at the acts, but at the thinking behind them. Did we get used to lying to get sex? Did we stir up fear or jealousy to get what we wanted? Did we make promises of relationships we had no intention of following through on? Did we lead people on just to get something from them? And did our chosen sex lives eventually double down on us in chaos? We’re not here to beat ourselves up. We’re here to tell the truth. Because the same way alcohol twisted our thinking, a lot of us let this area run wild too, and called it sane. And it wasn’t. Sex is a beautiful thing. And now we’re trying to shape our future sex ideals in a way that won’t keep us up at night, well, keep us up worrying about it anyway.

What would it look like for us to bring honesty and respect into this part of our lives today?
04-16.title: April 16 – Sex Education

04-17.body:
“Acceptance is the answer to all my problems today.” — p. 417, Alcoholics Anonymous

The Big Book might be worth the ten bucks just for that one line. Acceptance. The answer to all my problems today. And yeah… that sounds a little extreme until you start actually trying to live it. Because “all” means all. Some of us have gotten fired in sobriety. Acceptance says, “Alright… now I’m the guy without a job. What are we gonna do about it, God?” Some of us have had our hearts broken in sobriety. Acceptance says, “Alright… now I’m the guy with a broken heart. What are we gonna do about it, God?” Some of us have buried people we love in sobriety. Acceptance says, “Alright… that chapter is over. What are we gonna do about it, God?”

It’s not soft, and it’s definitely not passive. It’s just telling the truth about where you actually are instead of fighting reality like it owes you a different outcome. Because the truth is, most of the pain we’re in isn’t just from what happened—it’s from arguing with the fact that it happened at all. And that fight? We lose it every time.

Acceptance doesn’t fix everything overnight. It doesn’t hand you a new job, or heal your heart, or bring people back. But it does something real—it takes you out of the fight with reality and puts you back in a position to move. It turns “Why is this happening to me?” into “Alright… now what?” And that’s usually where God starts doing something we couldn’t see before. Not in the resistance. Not in the replay. But right there in the middle of what is.

What’s something in your life right now that you already know you need to accept—but you’re still quietly fighting it?
04-17.title: 417, bro

04-18.body:
Having done our Fourth Step, we’re on a new footing with a Higher Power. We’ve been given the gift of time. Just a sliver. A few extra seconds between what we feel and what we do.

In the first part, we saw how resentment warped our thinking. In the second part, we saw how fear stole time from us. In the third part, we saw how unchecked thinking can make us manipulative. There is no way we could have concluded these things without the Fourth Step. And now we’re left with something new: the ability to pause. To stop in the middle of stress and ask for guidance instead of reacting the way we always have.

Our personal channel with a Higher Power has been unblocked. Whether we use it or not… that’s on us.

Its use is a practice, not a mastery—and as we go along we remember progress, not perfection.

At this point we desire to talk to someone about this to gain perspective. We've had a small awakening and we need to bring all these dark parts of our lives into light.

Have you done a thorough job to open up your gift?
04-18.title: April 18 — Sliver

04-19.body:
Every morning is an opportunity to treat untreated alcoholism. A lot can happen while we’re sleeping—pathways snapping back, drunk dreams, anxieties creeping back in, old desires reconnecting in the mind. Resentments sneaking back in. And when we wake up, we’ve got a choice: get right for the day, or just truck along ignoring our condition. The Big Book says the alcoholic is a very sick person. We’re not cured. What we have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. A lot of us have taken responsibility for that and tackle alcoholism first thing in the morning. Regular prayer is suggested. Maybe it’s a meeting to get right. Maybe it’s some quiet time to organize the day and make sure we’re close to God. Maybe it’s spiritual reading. One thing we start to realize is resentment isn’t real—it’s our alcoholic mind hijacking us, trying to edge God out. So we bring ourselves back, we get close again, and we gather up another day sober.

Are you edging God out right now?
04-19.title: April 19 — Untreated Alcoholism

04-20.body:
As we’re making a life for ourselves in AA, meeting new friends, finding a place we finally belong in meetings, and learning how to handle our resentments, we might hear, “No dating in the first year!” and think, huh? Alcoholics have a hard time being told what to do. We just don’t listen. Obviously. The Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book doesn’t specifically say no dating, but what it does say is that the alcoholic tends to find themselves drunk at exactly the wrong time, usually when some important decision needs to be made or some commitment needs to be kept. That’s a clue. Because things like dating, new career paths, and moving are all important decisions, and those are the exact moments where our alcoholism likes to wake up. So maybe we just relax a little, take it easy, and try to lean on the experience in the rooms, not as rules, but as people who’ve already stepped in the holes we’re about to step in. Getting sober is hard enough without piling on a bunch of new responsibilities all at once.

Are you relaxing and taking it easy on this journey?
04-20.title: April 20 — Big Decision

04-21.body:
So far in this step process we’ve taken some of the garbage out of our lives and cleaned house, or at least piled it up so we can deal with it later. Some of this old stuff has been sitting around a long time, but now it’s bagged up and not scattered everywhere. We can take it out when the time comes.

The first thing they helped us with is getting alcohol out of the picture. That’s huge. We’re not alone anymore, and we’re cleaning this house together. Next, they helped us remove all our old ideas about a Higher Power so we could feel some new Power flow in to help us live this life one day at a time. Next, we’ve been given a pathway out of resentment, fear, and manipulation.

As a result, we’re naturally changing into wonderful people. People who are helping without the thought of return. It’s what we’ve always wanted for ourselves, and the process is happening so naturally it almost feels like our old lives are just slipping away without much effort on our part. A sober life feels lighter, and the laughs are more abundant.

Are you able to laugh a little easier now that life is becoming more manageable with AA on your side?
04-21.title: April 21 — Trash Day

04-22.body:
Sitting in AA, we might’ve heard the saying, a problem shared is a problem cut in half. The Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book says it plain. The grouch and the brainstorm, those moments when we bottle it up and get so mad we can’t even talk, that’s not for us. That might work for other people. It doesn’t work for the alcoholic, obviously. We have to let it out. So here we are. Fourth step done. It’s all on paper now. Not floating around in our head like a tornado, but written out where we can actually see it. Patterns started to show up. The stuff that sets us off. The thinking that quietly kicks our alcoholic minds into high gear. It’s not as mysterious as it used to be. Now comes the part where we don’t keep it. We take the biggest problem in our lives, our own thinking, and we bring it to another human being. Not to impress them. Not to perform. Just to tell the truth. And something happens when we do that. It loses weight. The pressure comes down. It gets cut in half. A sponsor is ideal. Someone who’s been there, who won’t flinch, who won’t try to fix us or judge us. Just someone who listens while we bring this stuff into the light. Because the goal isn’t to bottle it up better. The goal is to pour it out once and for all and make room for something refreshing and new.

Do you have someone you can talk to in AA?
04-22.title: April 22 — Cut in Half

04-23.body:
A guy who’d been sitting around Alcoholics Anonymous a long time said to me once, “You can’t save your face and your ass at the same time.” That one sticks. As alcoholics, we spend a lot of time saving face. Hell, who wouldn’t? Life’s hard enough, and doing it drunk makes it even harder. By the time we get here, most of our lives don’t look like a greatest hits album. It’s more like greatest misses. It’s not like any of us walked into the rooms on a winning streak. Most of us got kicked out of here, there, and everywhere before we stumbled into a meeting and found something that actually works. Now we’ve written it all down, the misses, the patterns, the stuff we don’t exactly want printed on a billboard, and here comes the part where we stop saving face and start telling the truth. This is where that saying comes alive, because we don’t get to protect how we look and get free at the same time. So yeah, it’s time to qualify. Time to go back through the greatest misses and lay them out with another person. No polishing it up. No excuses. No long speeches about why it made sense at the time. Things happened. Of course they did, especially when King Alcohol had us by the throat. But this isn’t about what happened as much as it’s about what we’re doing right now to deal with it. That’s what matters. That’s what people are actually looking at. And the truth is, most people don’t care nearly as much about our past as we think they do.

Are you trying to save face or your ass?
04-23.title: April 23 – Save Your Ass

04-24.body:
“…so you have swallowed and digested some big chunks of truth about yourself…” — Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book, p. 71

Having fearlessly and thoroughly finished that Fourth Step, we’re sitting there with a pile of stuff that can make us twitch if we start replaying it too hard, so we don’t. We’ve been given the ability to face facts about ourselves and see, quite literally, what they’re talking about when they say “unmanageable.” It’s more like a full-blown mess. We were acting out of character, the people around us reacting out of character, and our drinking turned the whole thing into a drunk life. Everything felt chaotic. Looking back now, it wasn’t just bad luck or circumstances, it was nuts. And now we’ve got some real, undeniable chunks of evidence as to why we need help. We need to be in these meetings.

We’re sitting on these chunks and now it’s time to puke them all out with someone who understands. So we seek out a close-mouthed individual and get to it. It’s time to get it out so it’s not swirling around in our lives anymore giving us the spins. Nobody likes the spins.

Have you found a closed-mouth individual to help you?
04-24.title: April 24 — Blowing Chunks

04-25.body:
Today was a good day.

That might not sound like much to a nonalcoholic, but for us, that’s a miracle in plain clothes. Not a fireworks show, not some big spiritual moment… just a day where nothing owned us. No resentment chewing on us from the inside out. No replaying old conversations like a broken tape. Just a little space to breathe.

Now that the weight of resentment has been lifted off us, we can actually say that more often… today was a good day. We start stacking them. A series of good days in AA. Nothing flashy, just real. And sometimes we catch ourselves wondering why we didn’t start this process sooner.

Somehow resentment blocks us off from the spirit. It keeps us so wrapped up in ourselves that we miss the beauty of life completely. We’re too busy thinking, replaying, reacting. Meanwhile life is happening all around us. The green grass. The bright flowers. A quiet moment that used to go unnoticed. The simple truth that deep down, people are children of God, doing the best they can with what they have.

Have you woken up to this beautiful thing called life now that your resentments are set aside?
04-25.title: April 25 — Today Was a Good Day

04-26.body:
Alcoholics are relief junkies. We’ve chased relief from our own lives like it was some hidden treasure. Bought the books, tried the miracle fixes, looked for anything to take the edge off. And for a while, nothing did it quite like booze. It gave us escape… but everything we pushed away came back the next day two-fold. That’s the cycle. Relief, crash, repeat.

But through this fourth step process, something different starts to happen. We’re not escaping anymore, we’re facing things. Writing them down, seeing them clearly. And that’s where real relief shows up. Not the quick hit. Not the temporary numb-out. Real relief. The kind that doesn’t wear off.

It starts to feel like a new foundation for life, and a big part of this new way of living is to stop fighting things we can't change with resentment. If we can finally face facts, and accept the things we cannot change, life gets a whole lot lighter. Might not like it, but we can certainly accept it.

Have you been getting better at accepting the things you cannot change?
04-26.title: April 26 — Relief

04-27.body:
“Instinct run wild in themselves is the underlying cause of their destructive drinking.” — Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, p. 44

Instincts gone wild. It happens. And more than likely, they come back around and bite us in the ass. Pressuring other people to make us feel comfortable and connected. Unreasonable demands for sex, security, money, and esteem. It happens. That’s not new. What’s new is this: we’ve got options now.

We can pause. We can pray. We can ask for guidance. We can hit a meeting, call someone in AA, write it out, or do something for somebody else until the fog lifts and our thinking untangles a bit. Or… we can go back to the old “seek and destroy” plan—chasing relief, controlling everything, and lighting our lives on fire just to feel okay for five minutes. That road still works… it just works exactly how it always did.

God’s not asking us to wrestle life into submission. He’s not asking us to win the game of instincts. He’s offering something different, something lighter. A way to live where we’re not twisted up in every want, fear, and demand. More like care free kids again. Less managing, more trusting.

So when the instincts start revving, we don’t have to follow them into the ditch. We can lean on God, stay close to the people who get it, and let the storm pass without turning it into a disaster.

Are your instincts running the show today… or are you letting something bigger take the wheel?
04-27.title: April 27 – Seek & Destroy

04-28.body:
“Get honest or get drunk.”

As we’ve been hanging around AA, we’ve probably heard that one tossed around. Not exactly a warm hug. Truth is, neither option sounds great at first. We just came out of a drunk, and yeah… that one was a doozie. Odds are we’re trying to make it our last one.

Now here comes the other option, honesty. Real honesty. The kind where we sit down with another person and with God and start letting out the stuff we’ve been carrying around for years. Not the polished version. Not the “I’ll tell you just enough to look good” version. The real deal. And yeah, that can feel just as scary as picking up again.

But here’s the thing we start to hear from people who’ve actually done it. There’s something on the other side of that honesty. Freedom. It might not make sense yet. It might not even sound believable. But it’s there.

So now we’re standing here with two things in our pockets. In one pocket, our Fourth Step, everything we’ve written down, ready to be shared. In the other pocket, our pride, telling us to hold back, stay safe, keep control.

Which pocket are you reaching into this time?
04-28.title: April 28 – Get Honest or Get Drunk

04-29.body:
“Show me your friends and I’ll show you your future.”

It doesn’t take long for anyone sober to hear that and say, yeah… I get that now. As we look back over this fourth step, a lot of us are asking, why the hell did we even know half of these people? Without the fourth step, we’d still be asking that question and blaming everybody else.

Before AA, we were headed nowhere, down the road of misery, dragging everyone we loved along for the ride. It wasn’t just us falling apart, it was a tornado ripping through everything around us. Hanging around people we had no business being around, except to get drunk. Now we’re here, in AA, doing the deal, cleaning house, trusting God, trying to help somebody else. We’re hanging around a fellowship built on honesty, unselfishness, purity, and love, and if we stick around long enough and do what they did, that stuff can start to show up in our lives too.

It’s not about being better or worse than anyone out there. The million dollar question is, who do I want to become?

Am I surrounding myself with people who help me grow, or people who help me stay the same?
04-29.title: April 29 – Show Me Yours, I’ll Show You Mine

04-30.body:
A guy walks into a priest’s office and says he’s done. Not dramatic, just tired in a way sleep doesn’t fix. He tells the priest he’s thinking about ending it. The priest doesn’t argue. He just says, “Alright. But before you do anything, give me two weeks. For the next two weeks, live like everything that happens comes from God, not as punishment, just like it’s meant for you somehow. And every time something happens, ask, ‘What’s this here to show me?’” The guy shrugs and tries it. Coffee spills, traffic cuts him off, small good moments show up. Nothing changes, but something loosens. Two weeks later he comes back. The priest asks, “You ready?” The guy laughs. Not forced, the kind that catches you off guard. “No. Not even close.” He starts talking about little things that don’t hit the same anymore, stuff he would’ve missed. By the end of it, he’s not just okay, he’s lit up. Not because life got perfect, but because he finally stepped into it instead of fighting it. The same life. Different eyes. And now he’s kind of amazed by it.

What would happen if you stopped resisting everything for the next two weeks and just asked, “What’s this here to show me?”
04-30.title: April 30 – Two Weeks

05-01.body:
We’re ready to put an end to the hiding from ourselves. Having made the personal inventory, there might be some glaring problems with ourselves popping out. Well, it ought to be that way.

So we have the list, and we’re ready to talk to another person, to God, and get it all out on the table. The Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book says if we skip this vital step we may not overcome drinking. Makes sense.

We have a decision to make. Hide our heads in the sand in shame, or own it, seek to learn from it, make it right again and move on.

Are you hiding or are you seeking?
05-01.title: May 1 – Hide & Seek

05-02.body:
“Okay, okay, I’m confessing! I cheated on my history exam… I stole my uncle Max’s toupee and glued it to my face… I pushed my sister down the stairs and blamed it on the dog…”

— Chunk, The Goonies

Chunk just unloads. No filter, no order, just years of stuff flying out. A Fifth Step can feel like that. We’ve been carrying it, and now it’s coming out fast. But we’re going deeper than Chunk.

In Alcoholics Anonymous it says we admit the exact nature of our wrongs. Not just the list, the nature. That word matters. “Nature” comes from natura—birth, character—from nasci, to be born. It’s not just the action, it’s what keeps getting born inside us. Our default wiring. The instinct that shows up before we even think. The part of us that reaches for control, approval, or escape without asking permission. Same situation or different one, it reacts the same way. That’s the nature.

Yeah, we lied, hurt people, manipulated. But why? Approval? Fear? Control? Avoiding feelings? Not wanting to be alone? Same actions, different roots.

This is where it shifts. We stop replaying scenes and start seeing patterns, how we protect our self-centeredness at all costs. Where did we twist the truth, stay in control, avoid being wrong, or not feel uncomfortable? Different situations, same move underneath. And most of us don’t see it alone. We need someone who’s been there, who can hear it, call it what it is, and still sit with us.

Because if we only dump the list, we might feel relief. Alcoholics love relief. If we’re only chasing relief, we may drink again. But if we see the nature, something can change.

So the question isn’t just what did I do? It’s what keeps showing up, what was I trying to get or avoid, what part of me keeps getting born in this?

Have you been chasing relief or change?
05-02.title: May 2 – What’s Under It

05-03.body:
We hear the word surrender a lot in AA. Like a lot. It gets thrown around in meetings, readings, conversations. “You’ve got to surrender.” “I finally surrendered.” “He hasn’t surrendered yet.” But what are we actually surrendering? Most of the time the answer is “our will.” That sounds right, but what does that even mean?

The word surrender comes from the Old French surrendre, meaning to give up or hand over. Break it down further, sur means over, and rendre means to give back or return. So surrender literally means to hand something over, to give it back. Not destroy it. Not erase it. Not pretend it doesn’t exist. Give it back. So what have we been holding onto so tightly that needs to be handed over?

Our opinions. Our judgments. The way we’ve been telling the story. We’ve had such a tight grip on the stories from our Fifth Step that they feel like reality, not just something that happened but something that means something about us and everyone else. Those interpretations have been shaping our character long before we ever got to AA.

So now it’s time to loosen the grip and start surrendering our judgment of what happened, becoming willing to see it another way. Not rewriting history, but letting go of the meaning we’ve been attaching to it. Doing that on our own is damn near impossible, which is why it helps to get an outside, non-biased view. Someone in AA who’s been there, who can hear it and see what we can’t.

And then we get to work. One story at a time. One judgment at a time. We start handing them over, looking for what’s underneath, so something real can actually change.

What am I still holding onto that I need to hand over?
05-03.title: May 3 – Surrender

05-04.body:
On our quest for a spiritual awakening, a psychic change that keeps us safe from alcohol, we uncovered some hard facts about ourselves in the Fourth Step. One of them is this, we tend to run on emotion. Not just feel things, but run on them. And not only that, we built monuments to our feelings. We took anger, resentment, hurt, fear, and turned them into something solid, something we lived inside of and kept feeding. It got so overwhelming that we acted on it, and when that didn’t work, we covered it up with booze. That was the cycle.

Moving forward, we’re still going to get angry, still going to get hurt. Stuff is going to happen. That’s life on life’s terms, it’s unavoidable. But for us, something changes. We lost our card to stay upset. We don’t get to hang onto it like we used to. Sure, we’re going to feel it, but we can’t afford to live there anymore. We can be upset for like an hour. An hour to feel it, an hour to process it, and then we move. We don’t stretch it into a day, a week, a resentment that sits there and grows. We lost that card.

Same thing with getting bummed out. It shows up, we feel it, but we don’t camp out there. Cap it. An hour. Then we get up and move forward, whether we feel like it or not.

For us, it’s just like that. We’re not in the monument-building business anymore, we’re in the acceptance business. And acceptance keeps our character in check and, ultimately, keeps us sober. Might not like it, but we have to accept it.

Are you still building a monument to your feelings, or practicing acceptance?
05-04.title: May 4 – No More Monuments

05-05.body:
“Pride goeth before destruction…”

We admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs… more like the exact nature of being exactly wrong.

Alcoholics hate to be wrong. Our egos rarely allow it. With a whole stack of “yeah buts” and “my part vs their part,” we can still build a case that this whole alcoholism thing is somebody else’s fault. It is not.

The ego likes to fix, sort, place blame, wiggle out of responsibility, talk about other people and why they are so bad, compare, and set us apart from the world, usually on top. It keeps us busy defending instead of getting free.

As Chuck C. said, uncover, discover, discard. There is great freedom in being wrong. We can see it, own it, learn from it, and finally drop it to make room for better things in our lives.

Where am I still trying to be right instead of free?
05-05.title: May 5 – Our Egos

05-06.body:
“I’ve got big balls, you’ve got big balls… but we’ve got the biggest balls of them all.” — Big Balls by AC/DC

Well, there you have it. A lot of us get to this point in Step Five and say to ourselves, “Hold on… you mean to tell me I have to go sit down with another person and tell them the stuff that’s been going on with me for years? And this is somehow part of not drinking?”

Yes.

It takes an awfully big pair to get to this point. But a lot of us also remember being on our knees, beat down by alcohol, saying we were willing to go to any lengths. Well, this is one of those lengths.

And what are we really scared of?

Is it the judgment? Is it not trusting that this person will keep their mouth shut? Or is it the deeper fear that they’ll hear the whole thing and say, “Whoa… yeah, you’re not one of us. You’re too far gone. Get out of here.”

Again, it takes an awfully big pair to walk through this step with absolute honesty. But this is where we stop trying to manage two lives: the one everybody sees, and the one eating us alive inside.

This is trust the process territory.

Are you still willing to go to any lengths?
05-06.title: May 6 – Trust the Process

05-07.body:
“There is One who has all power. May you find Him now.” — Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous

If there is One who has all power, we’re sorry to say there ain’t any left for us to have. And there is only one place to find a God of your understanding: right here, right now. Like, now.

What’s your biggest problem in the world right now? What’s really eating your lunch? What’s scaring you? Kid problems? Money problems? Alone problems? Legal stuff? Fear of drinking again? Most of that stuff exists in two places: the wreckage of our past, or obsessively thinking about the wreckage of our future.

It don’t have to be like that.

In the Fifth Step, we’re looking for some understanding of our reckless natures so we can finally set it aside. Once it’s set aside, we have room for one thought, and one thought only: there is a God, and we are forgiven. Like, truly forgiven. Not ignored. Not shamed into doing something we don’t want to do. Not that conditional love where it’s “if you do this, then I’ll love you.” Absolute love. The kind that has been there the entire time whether we were looking at it or not. A God, that is our champion, moving us along, giving us opportunity to shine.

A lot of us spent years trying to outrun guilt, fear, shame, and our own heads. Then we get here and find out the answer might just be sitting still long enough to realize we are already loved by something bigger than us. Not someday. Not after we become perfect. Not after we clean ourselves up enough to deserve it. Now.

Can you turn off the past and the future and just sit in “right now” for five minutes?
05-07.title: May 7 – Now

05-08.body:
“We stood at the turning point.” — Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous

So we’re sitting here on our Fourth Steps. We’ve pulled the curtain back and seen what happens in our drinking natures. It didn’t start out that way. After all, this is a progressive illness. It developed over time. The lying got more hideous. The stealing went from small-time to big-time. The anger increased, sometimes into violence. Stuff we swore we’d never do somehow got added to the list.

And now we’re at a crossroads.

We can either get this stuff out and honestly talk with another person about it, or not. The Big Book gives all kinds of promises about doing this. Or don’t. But how exactly are we planning to stop these things on our own? How many times have we told ourselves “I learned my lesson this time!” before we’re right back in the same insanity again, wondering what happened?

This is what the bitter end looks like. Not usually one giant explosion all at once, but a slow march further into isolation, fear, and destruction. So where’s the stopping point? Jail? Locked up in some mental ward? Doing something desperate and ending our lives? Alcoholism doesn’t tend to tap us on the shoulder politely and say, “That’s probably far enough.”

The Fifth Step is where we stop dragging this thing deeper into the dark. We stop negotiating with it. We stop pretending we’re somehow going to outthink it this time.

We said we were willing to go to any lengths.

Are we still willing?
05-08.title: May 8 – The Bitter End

05-09.body:
“But we invariably find that at some time in the past we have made decisions based on self which later placed us in a position to be hurt.”— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 62

Some of this Fourth Step stuff takes a crowbar to get off us. Hard-nosed sponsors seem to help with that. When we were living that drinking life, we were vulnerable, and it sure felt like people took advantage of us. Hard to see anything different on our own. We had all the explanations ready. If that guy would’ve just done what he was supposed to do. If that other guy would’ve kept his mouth shut and not ratted us out. If she would’ve just loved us more. If the boss had treated us fairly. If the world would’ve stopped picking on us for five damn minutes.

And some people really did hurt us. That part is true. But we keep this line in the back of our minds: “we invariably find…” Invariably. Not sometimes. Not once in a while. Invariably. Somewhere back there were decisions based on self that put us in places we never should’ve been. We chased approval, control, comfort, attention, security, escape, or ego, and then acted shocked when life blew up in our faces. We kept trying to manage everything and everyone around us while our own lives were slowly catching on fire.

The good news is we hopefully found somebody who can help us see this clearly without crushing us. Somebody who’s been there before. Because once we can finally see our mistakes honestly, we don’t have to keep living like this anymore.

What’s one resentment where, after really looking at it, you finally saw your own mistake in it?
05-09.title: May 9 – But They Did It On Purpose!

05-10.body:
One of the biggest misunderstandings going on today is people constantly talking about “looking for my part.” during the Fifth Step process. First off, the book doesn’t actually say that. And after all, when we start looking for “our part” in problems, subconsciously that means the other person must have a part too. Then once we get rolling on these stories, whose part do you think we’re going to make bigger? Yeah. Theirs.

The book says we “resolutely looked for our own mistakes.” It says, “Where were we to blame?” That’s a different deal entirely. This ain’t about playing judge and jury on a situation while trying to talk our sponsor into feeling sorry for us. Most of us can already build a pretty convincing case against the entire world. We were professionals at it.

This inventory is about us. Where did we compromise our morals? Where did we go against our own good nature? Where did we play God? Where did we force outcomes, manage people, or try to arrange life so we could feel okay? Somewhere along the line, most of us got exhausted from fighting everything and everybody all the time.

The goal here isn’t to become a doormat. It’s to finally get honest enough that we can live in the world without constantly being at war with it.

Where did we play God trying to keep everything manageable?
05-10.title: May 10 – Looking For My Part

05-11.body:
In the beginning, when Bill Wilson finally found a solution to his alcohol problem, he was carrying around six little steps he had pulled from a spiritual group. They were simple, direct, and apparently effective as hell: admit we were licked, take a moral inventory, confess our defects to another person, make restitution, help others without thought of reward, and pray for the power to live this way.

That’s interesting, because right after figuring out what the problem actually is, and finally seeing what the solution might be, the move wasn’t to sit around and think about it for six months. The move was to inspect ourselves, then immediately go talk to somebody. Bill found that when the deep dark stuff got dragged into the light, it got smaller. Manageable. Less powerful. The things that looked like monsters in the dark started looking more like what they actually were: defects, fears, ego, shame, old survival tactics. And when that stuff became manageable, people stopped needing to drink over it.

That brings us here. A lot of us have done the inventory. We’ve looked at the wreckage. We’ve seen patterns we probably wish we hadn’t. And now comes the part our alcoholic ego absolutely hates: honesty, exposure, and another human being. Because ego loves secrecy. Ego loves isolation. Ego loves whispering, you can fix this yourself, just manage it better, keep this one tucked away. That voice has probably never helped us once.

So this is where we go against our own will. Against our own broken instincts. We find the right closed-mouth human being, and we get honest. Because staying sick in secret has already been tested. How’d that plan work out?

What’s harder for you, admitting you were to blame or letting another person hear it?
05-11.title: May 11 – Drag It Into the Light

05-12.body:
“They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way.” — Big Book

So many of us ran around screaming the same mantra in life: not my fault. It seemed like we were born that way, unable to admit when we screwed something up. Deep down, we usually knew better. But admitting fault meant consequences, and consequences meant discomfort, and alcoholics do not like discomfort. Hell, we were already restless, irritable, and discontented. Add uncomfortable on top of that and we’d do just about anything to avoid it. So we got real good at deflecting, explaining, justifying, and rewriting history until the people around us got too exhausted to argue.

Then the sick part happens: we start believing our own nonsense. Everybody else becomes the problem. The world is unfair. We become the victim in every story we tell.

Step Four started breaking that pattern by asking one hard question: where were we to blame? And now in Step Five, we finally say it out loud.

That’s scary for a lot of us. But if you picked somebody who’s actually done this work, they’ve probably been there too. Maybe not your exact story, but close enough. Shame loses power when it gets dragged into the light. You’re not confessing to a judge. You’re talking to another alcoholic who found a way to get well.

You are not alone anymore.

What’s one “not my fault” story you believed for years that you can finally be honest about now?
05-12.title: May 12 – Consequences

05-13.body:
“We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense.” — Big Book, p. 72

We got the warnings and didn’t listen. We knew help was out there, yet we kept doing what we did anyway. We’re the ones who bottomed out, alone, confused, and wondering what the hell happened, so now it’s time to talk about it honestly. This is our inventory, not theirs.

That takes real courage. Because our natural move is to build a case, explain ourselves, and point at what everyone else did wrong. The alcoholic mind loves a defense attorney.

But this step isn’t about saving face. It’s about getting free.

We don’t get to throw other people under the bus to make ourselves look better. That kind of thinking kept us sick. So the question is simple: where did we go against our own good nature?
This is the beginning of a thought process that will continue day by day for us.

Where am I still defending myself instead of just owning it?
05-13.title: May 13 – Save Your Own Skin

05-14.body:
Alcoholics love to think we’re rational, when in reality we’re usually just rationalizers. Isn’t it funny how our “rational thinking” almost always seems to land in our favor?

One trap we waste a lot of time in is trying to find the reason we became alcoholic. Like there was one tragic event we can point to and say, “That’s it. That’s what made me this way.”

And there we go again, playing victim.

The truth is, who knows exactly why we crossed that line. Sure, life may have handed us reasons we took as great excuses to go drink, but we’re the ones who kept choosing alcohol over the situations in front of us. And somewhere in that process, we picked up habits that blocked us off from a Higher Power. Habits that basically said, leave me alone, I know what I’m doing.

And now that we actually need help, that attitude ain’t gonna cut it.

Am I still looking for reasons, or am I finally ready for solutions?
05-14.title: May 14 – Reasons

05-15.body:
“We pocket our pride and go to it, illuminating every twist of character, every dark cranny of the past.”

At this vital Fifth Step, don’t forget there are three listeners in the room. Sure, there’s us, finally saying this stuff out loud. There’s the person sitting across from us, listening without running for the hills. But there’s also the third listener, the one we’ve actually been trying to get near this whole time: our Creator.

This whole thing is about dragging the stuff that’s been blocking us out into the light. The shame, the secrets, the weird thinking, the old garbage we kept stuffed in the back room because we thought if anyone saw it, they’d be done with us. But imagine God sitting right there saying, Go on. It’s okay. Keep going. You’re still loved. You’re still safe. You’re still connected.

Being human is messy business. Trying to sort out life well enough to have a spiritual awakening can feel like we dumped all the puzzle pieces out of the box onto the table and are just staring at the pile, wondering how this is ever supposed to make sense. But as the pieces start going back together, a beautiful picture begins to show up, as long as we keep searching for the missing pieces.

This process isn’t about being judged. It’s about being freed. Slowly but surely, we start gaining traction in a new understanding, a new way of life that demands rigorous honesty, sure, but also offers something most of us haven’t felt in a long time: relief.

And lo and behold, we start to feel good. Not fake good. Not “everything’s fixed” good. Just lighter. Less alone. A little less full of poison.

Are you starting to feel good yet?
05-15.title: May 15 – Hey, Don’t Forget

05-16.body:
There’s some promises that go along with taking each step, if we take them thoroughly. Not maybes. Not “one guy said this happened to him once.” Actual promises. Real promises. Not fluffy pats on the butt to keep you from drinking. Things we can expect for our lives if we do the work.

And in Step Five, we get one a lot of us probably walked into AA desperately wanting: “The feeling that the drink problem has disappeared will often come strongly.”

That’s good news!

And disappeared is even better.

That’s not fighting. That’s not struggling. That’s not white-knuckling your way through dinner because somebody ordered a cocktail. That’s not gritting your teeth at the beer cave in a gas station.

That’s disappeared.

Like Tuesday, alcohol owned every square inch of your thinking. Wednesday, after this Fifth Step, it didn’t.

Where’d the problem go?
05-16.title: May 16 – Promises

05-17.body:
Another one of these Fifth Step promises is that we begin to feel the nearness of our Creator. Well, that sounds like more good news. A lot of us come into AA and connect the dots pretty quick that a Higher Power seems to be part of this whole staying sober deal, so we start looking all around for something that makes sense to us. Trying to “find God” becomes a regular thought, and sooner or later, some wise-ass at a meeting will probably say, “God’s not lost. You are.” Blunt, but true.

Because most of us weren’t spiritually disconnected because God wandered off. We were the ones doing donuts in the parking lot with the map upside down. But here’s the promise: if we take this Fifth Step business seriously, if we do it with all our might, something shifts. We start to feel the nearness of our Creator. Not because we suddenly became monks. Not because we became perfect people. Not because we finally said the perfect prayer.

It just happens.

Are you still lost?
05-17.title: May 17 – And Another Thing

05-18.body:
Before AA, a lot of us were stuck in the same resentment loop. Get frustrated, replay the story until we were sick, blame the other person, talk crap, occasionally fail at getting even, make the problem worse, alienating ourselves in the meantime, and drink.

Horrible way to live. Simply awful.

This Fifth Step business gives us a new end to that loop: forgiveness. Forgiveness for others, and forgiveness for ourselves. It simply ends this whole resentment business. And if a good one gets stuck on us, we have tools now. We can go back to the drawing board, write it out, talk to someone, and get on with life.

We can look life in the eye now. We can enjoy life on life’s terms like we knew was possible all along.

Are you living life on life’s terms?
05-18.title: May 18 – The Gift of Forgiveness

05-19.body:
A lot of people waste so much time on resentment, gossiping, focusing on other people, trying to come up with the perfect plan somebody else should have followed to avoid problems, and trying to control things they cannot change.

Now that we have a solution to this resentment business, we’re not wasting time foolishly anymore. We can finally focus on what we can contribute to life instead of constantly trying to manage everybody else’s.

Resentment takes up a lot of time and mental energy. It drains us. It keeps us stuck in circles, replaying old stories while life keeps moving without us.

But now we have tools. We can write it out, talk to someone, pray about it, and move forward. We can get on with life and start doing things we never thought were possible. It’s no wonder people in AA become some of the most successful people around.

Are you set up for success?
05-19.title: May 19 – What To Do With All This Time?

05-20.body:
“We feel we are on the Broad Highway…”

The beauty of the birth of AA is that it created a new on-ramp to the broad highway. Written for us, by us, for people who think like we do, react like we do, and lived the same kind of destructive drinking lives we did. That’s what makes this thing different. So much advice in life bounced right off us because it came from people who didn’t understand the wiring. AA came from people who absolutely did.

As we complete the Fifth Step, it’s hard not to feel grateful for a program that finally got us pointed in the right direction. We spent years taking detours, missing exits, driving straight past warning signs, and insisting we knew a better route. Meanwhile, life kept ending in the same ditch.

Now the roadmap is laid out in front of us with precise directions from people who already made the trip. Not theory. Not self-help fluff. A real path that actually works if we stay on it.

For the first time in a long time, maybe we’re not just surviving. Maybe we’re finally headed somewhere.

Are you still looking for the next exit, or are you ready to stay on the highway?
05-20.title: May 20 – Broad Highway

05-21.body:
“We are building an arch through which we shall walk a free person at last.”
Freedom. Free from what? Free from drinking? Yeah, of course. Go to meetings, apply some of these AA techniques, and the drink problem generally shrinks. That alone is a miracle.
But what about this freedom business? What exactly are we being freed from? Freedom from the bondage of self.
And what was that bondage anyway? Self-centered resentment. Replaying old hurts like a greatest hits album nobody asked for. Anger. Fear. Trying to control people, outcomes, and future conversations that haven’t even happened yet. Building expectations, then getting furious when life doesn’t follow our script. Exhausting stuff.
Doing this work starts cutting those chains. That’s the real promise here. Not just putting the bottle down, but getting free from the thinking that kept dragging us back to it in the first place.
Sure, relief from drinking was a wonderful thing. But if we’re honest, most of us came here wanting something bigger than just not drinking. We wanted peace. We wanted relief. We wanted freedom. Step by step, we build the arch, and when the time comes, we simply walk through it.
What baggage are you still carrying that doesn’t fit through the arch?
