05-21.title: May 21 – The Golden Arches

05-22.body:
“These alcoholic types can never safely use alcohol in any form.” — Dr. Silkworth

That may mean beer, whiskey, tequila, or gin. But if we look at this thing with an open mind, a lot of us have gotten drunk on other stuff too. Relationships. The fantasy that if we just act a certain way, say the right things, ignore obvious red flags, or deny devastating facts, this one will finally work out and we’ll live happily ever after. Money. The belief that if we just hit some magic number in the bank, life will finally feel normal and we can finally exhale. Control. Approval. Attention. Security. Same movie, different bottle. The mental obsession side of this illness can put us in places we swore we would never end up, and sometimes the strangest part is landing there completely sober, looking around asking ourselves, how did I get here again?

Because the drink was never the whole story. Something in us is always reaching, always looking to be settled, safe, whole, connected. The human soul still wants to connect to something bigger than itself, and if we ignore that, it has a funny way of coming back wearing a fake mustache.

What are you calling normal that might just be another form of alcohol?
05-22.title: May 22 – Fake Mustache

05-23.body:
AA has been called a lot of things. Group therapy. A self-help program. A place to get your life together. But a more accurate description might be a process of self-abandonment. We’re learning to loosen our grip on self-reliance and move toward God-reliance without tripping over our own feet in the process.

Because if “working on ourselves” was the answer, a lot of us would have nailed this years ago. We already worked on ourselves. We managed. Controlled. Planned. Justified. Rearranged reality. Protected our image. Followed our feelings straight into the ditch.

This process in the book points in a different direction. Less self-will. More thy will be done. Slowly but surely, we begin letting go of the need to run the whole show, even when surrender goes against our deepest nature. Especially then.

Are you trying to recover, or are you still trying to manage yourself into peace?
05-23.title: May 23 – Working on Myself

05-24.body:
No buzz ever felt as good as that buzz on the drive home from our sponsor’s house after uttering the last line of a Fifth Step. We said the hard stuff out loud. The secrets. The cringe. The things that looked a whole lot scarier in the backs of our minds than they did once spoken. And somehow we’re still here. Not struck by lightning. Not disqualified from AA. Just human.

Then comes one of the quieter but powerful suggestions in this process: take an hour alone. Not doom scrolling, not calling six people to explain our spiritual progress, not rewarding ourselves with a cheeseburger victory lap. Just us and the Power we just buddied up to.

We look back over what we’ve done so far. The first five steps. We say thank you from the bottom of our hearts. We get honest about whether we left anything out. And if halfway through that hour our brain goes, “Ohhhh no... I forgot THAT thing…” this is not the moment for good enough, dude. We make the call. We clean it up. We get free.

But do what you want. It’s your life. It’s only a suggestion.

A lot of us get here and immediately think, Okay… what next? That’s actually a pretty good sign. For once, we’re not asking how to escape. We’re asking how to continue.

Have you mistaken relief for freedom?
05-24.title: May 24 — Hour of Power

05-25.body:
“But what about the real alcoholic? ... he gets drunk at exactly the wrong moment. Particularly when some important decision must be made or engagement kept.” — “Real Alcoholic,” Big Book

What?

These guys just handed us the cheat sheet.

If our obvious goal is not to drink, it helps to know when our alcoholism likes to wake up: important decisions and engagements that need kept.

Our alcoholism loves uncertainty. The minute life gets unclear, complicated, or emotionally expensive, that old screw-it mentality starts warming up in the bullpen.

That mindset doesn’t just randomly show up. It flares when life gets real, when there’s pressure, when people are counting on us, and when we have to choose.

No wonder so many of us got drunk in the first week of a new job. That’s a buffet of engagements to keep. No wonder some of us jump into relationships and immediately turn them into chaos. Suddenly it’s: is this my forever person? When do they meet my kids? Did we have sex too soon? How do I make meetings and still date without losing my mind?

That’s a lot of important decisions.

This isn’t permission to panic. That explains a lot.

If we know our disease gets loud when responsibility shows up, maybe we quit acting surprised when life gets serious. That’s when we call somebody, stick close, and stop pretending we’re fine.

Because apparently our alcoholism doesn’t wait for the worst moments.

It waits for the important ones.

When life gets real, do you get sober—or do you get squirrelly?
05-25.title: May 25 - Let’s Get Real

05-26.body:
Sometimes in a quiet moment, we look back after this whole Fifth Step and realize we’re almost halfway through. That’s kind of wild. We hear in meetings all the time that half measures availed us nothing, and it makes sense. It’s not like we ever walked up to a bartender and ordered half a beer. It wouldn't have done the job. When we drank, we usually went all in. No moderation. No careful planning. Full commitment to bad decisions.

So now we’re trying something different. Really doing this thing. Not just collecting slogans, not just telling our story, not just circling recovery like it’s a hobby. We’re applying what we’ve learned so far, and if we’re doing that honestly, life should be getting better. Maybe not easier in every way, but at the very least, easier to not drink at.

Half measures kept us stuck because we wanted relief without surrender. We wanted the promises without the process. But somewhere in this work, something starts shifting. The obsession loosens. The noise gets quieter. We stop negotiating with ourselves quite so much.

Turns out we were never afraid of doing too much. We were afraid this might actually work.

Where are you still trying to stay half in and half out?
05-26.title: May 26 – Half Measures

05-27.body:
Through this process in the Big Book, we’ve tapped into something we probably used to hate the sound of: humility. Some people say humility is just the ability to face facts. For a long time, we drank at problems, hoping somehow they’d change if we tried hard enough. If life didn’t go our way, we treated reality like a challenge to enforce our will.

Now we’re on a different path. Acceptance.

Some belief systems can lean toward seeing the world as a broken place that needs fixing. A lot of us lived that way too, even without religion. Everything was a project. Every person was a problem to solve. Every uncomfortable situation needed our input. But something shifts in this work. We stop trying to control life and start looking inward at what bothers us so much that we’re trying to change it.

Through this process in AA, we finally found a way to do that. Took long enough.

Humility starts to show us there might actually be a plan here. Not always our plan, which is usually where the friction starts. We become a little more okay with the fact that God didn’t stop what He was doing to ask our approval.

Turns out humility isn’t thinking less of ourselves.

It’s thinking less like we’re in charge.

What are you still trying to manage that was never yours to run?
05-27.title: May 27 – Humility

05-28.body:
In our drinking careers, we became experts at humiliation. The stuff done in blackouts. Trying to slap Band-Aids on chaos. The alibis. The blame shifting. The broken promises. Constantly asking ourselves, how the hell did I end up here again?

Most of us didn’t need anyone to humiliate us. We handled that just fine ourselves. In AA, we get an antidote for humiliation: humility. That’s a very different thing. Humiliation gets forced on us. Humility gets chosen.

When life gets confusing, when emotions start climbing, when we’re about three seconds away from popping off and making things worse, there’s a simple prayer: God, please show me how to handle this with humility before I am humiliated. And the answer is usually a shift in focus. Off of us. Off of being right. Off of what we think we deserve. Humility usually points us toward the other person, toward patience, toward asking how we can be useful instead of how we can win.

Then we pause. As long as we need to. Because most of our worst moments happened in the space between feeling something and reacting to it. God provides strength if we ask. Enough to get through the next right moment.

This has been written about through the ages, and AA explained it to us in a way we are coming to believe will work for us too. One day at a time. One moment at a time. One situation at a time, we are finally coming to believe.

When has trying to be right led straight to humiliation?
05-28.title: May 28 – Humiliation

05-29.body:
"We were powerless over alcohol."

We were powerless. Were. Like at this very moment it became a thing of the past. Poof. Gone. Powerless until when? Until now. Until we met a friendly group of AA people going through the same thing we were.

As soon as we walk through the doors of our first meeting, we never have to drink again… unless we want to. There’s something special about this fellowship. The more we put into it, the more we seem to get back. The more honesty, willingness, and effort we bring, the more strength seems to appear out of nowhere.

So finally stumbling our way into an AA group turned out to be a gift of grace. An "adult time out" to figure out a new way of living. An opportunity to take what we finally deserve. Nobody has to live life drunk and alone anymore if they don’t want to.

When did “I have to drink” turn into “I don’t have to drink anymore” for you?
05-29.title: May 29 – We Were

05-30.body:
"You gotta give it away to keep it."

That's one of the most common sayings in AA. Some people say we don't even really start to get it until we start giving it away.

We're in a unique position. We bottomed out, came into AA, and started finding the solution. An AA member who knows how to help another alcoholic through a Fourth and Fifth Step is a uniquely useful person. We know what we're looking for because we found it in ourselves.

Helping another alcoholic's attempt at change is an undeniable gift. And after all, isn't it usually the helper who receives the help?

The more we give away what was freely given to us, the more we seem to keep.

What change in yourself have you noticed since you started helping other alcoholics?
05-30.title: May 30 – Gotta Give It Away

05-31.body:
"Man, that brain loves to snap back and start looking for someone to blame, doesn't it?" — AA member

Having gotten this far in the Steps, we are given a new discipline. A new responsibility.

In times of stress, especially when other people are involved, we start looking for our own mistakes. Where did I get the ball rolling? Where did I react poorly? Where did I act against my own good character and make the situation worse instead of seeing how I could be useful?

We use the old slogan think, think, think to get us into the solution... eventually.

And the solution is usually the same: How can I be of help in this situation?

Our egos don't like that very much. After all, isn't the ego there to solve problems? To figure out who's wrong and who deserves the blame? The problem is that our ego has a long history of making things worse.

Just because we did a Fourth and Fifth Step doesn't automatically keep us from pointing fingers. It simply opens the door to a new way of living where we can practice this new discipline. A way of pausing long enough to ask, "Where did I react poorly?" "What could I have done better?" and "How can I be useful here?"

Daily, we try.

Has there ever been a situation where you were absolutely sure someone else was the problem, only to later realize you could have handled it differently?
05-31.title: May 31 – True Discipline

06-01.body:
“You have admitted certain defects; you have ascertained in a rough way what the trouble is; you have put your finger on the weak items in your personal inventory.” — Alcoholics Anonymous

“Drop the Rock” is one of those catchy AA phrases. But what exactly is the rock?

For us, it was like having a giant boulder chained around our necks. It was packed full of self-willed character defects—the anger, the resentments, the lust, the greed, and the absolute selfishness that shows up whenever life starts changing in ways we don't like. It's all the stuff we use to protect our personal reality—our alcoholic perception of things—while ignoring life on life's terms.

It's our rock.

The problem is, it's been hanging around our necks for so long that we've gotten used to the struggle. We've dragged it through relationships, jobs, meetings, and every other part of life. After enough years, it starts to feel normal. We have a hard time imagining what life would even look like without it.

Step Six starts changing that.

It helps move us from self-centeredness to self-awareness. Self-centeredness says, "I'm going to change you to fit my way." Self-awareness says, "I'm going to change me so I can fit into reality."

We don't have to throw the whole rock away in one afternoon. We just become willing. We loosen our grip. We stop defending every defect like it's part of our personality. Little by little, the weight starts coming off.

Turns out, carrying that thing wasn't strength. It was exhaustion.

Are we starting to drop the rock, or are we still decorating it and calling it part of who we are?
06-01.title: June 1 — Drop the Rock

06-02.body:
Being hungover sucks.

It's as close to the phenomenon of craving as you can get without a drink in your hand. We wake up with alcohol still coursing through our veins and promise everyone around us that last drink was our last drink. We mean it, too.

Until about noon.

And most of us don't even realize what's happening. Call it hair of the dog. Call it curing the hangover. Call it whatever you want. Our loved ones usually called it broken promises and lies.

As this becomes a regular part of our lives, dishonesty starts to feel normal. We lie to other people, then we lie to ourselves. The excuses get bigger. The truth gets smaller. Respect disappears. We sink lower, become more isolated, and eventually we're the only ones left who believe our own bag of bull crap.

Step Six asks us to go in the opposite direction. It asks us to become willing to let go of the things that keep us sick. To stop defending our defects. To stop explaining away our behavior. To stop treating every consequence like it came out of nowhere.

One day at a time, we try to line ourselves up with a Higher Power and become willing to have these defects removed. We learn to face life on life's terms, whether we like the terms or not. No more alibis. No more magic tricks. No more pretending that tomorrow will somehow be different if we keep doing the same things today.

And here's the good news is it gets easier. It really does.

What excuse was hardest for you to let go of in sobriety?
06-02.title: June 2 — Hungover

06-03.body:
You can't work on a character defect that is actively engaged.

If we're hellbent on getting revenge, it's hard to channel God's power to help us get revenge. If we're consumed with lust, it's hard to think about much of anything else. If we're busy defending our pride, protecting our ego, or figuring out how to get even, we're probably not in a great position to hear God's direction.

That's why we need His help.

It can be hard to know God's will in every situation, but it's usually not that complicated. It's probably not His will for us to hurt one of His kids. It's probably not His will for us to take advantage of someone, manipulate them, or use them to get what we want.

The problem is that when a defect is fully engaged, it feels right. Anger feels justified. Resentment feels earned. Selfishness feels reasonable. That's why Step Six ask us to pause long enough to invite God into the situation.

If we can rear back for a minute, take a breath, and ask for help, something interesting usually happens. Our focus shifts from what we can get out of the situation to how we can be useful in it.

Most of the time, God's will looks a lot more like helping than being right.

What character defect causes you the most trouble when it's fully engaged?
06-03.title: June 3 — Engaged

06-04.body:
"Alcoholics are not inferior. They are frequently hypersensitive people trying to live in an insensitive world." — Chuck C.

Step Six asks us to become entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character. That's easier to talk about than it is to do.

We alcoholics are funny. We can be hypersensitive enough to notice every little slight, yet completely insensitive to the damage we're doing while we're acting on a defect. When resentment is engaged, we're lawyers building a case. When lust is engaged, we're salesmen closing a deal. When fear is engaged, we're fortune tellers predicting disaster. The problem isn't that we're sensitive. The problem is what we're connected to in the moment.

When we're plugged into a defect, it becomes hard to imagine life without it. Resentment feels justified. Fear feels necessary. Pride feels protective. We don't see them as defects at all—we see them as solutions. That's why Step Six isn't really about removing defects. It's about becoming willing. Willing to admit that what we've been relying on isn't working. Willing to consider that God's way might be better than our way. Willing to stop defending the very things that keep hurting us.

Most of us don't become willing all at once. We become willing a little at a time. One resentment. One fear. One selfish demand. One defect at a time. The good news is that we don't have to remove them ourselves. We just have to become willing and stay connected to the God that can.

Have you ever mistaken a character defect for a strength? What was it?
06-04.title: June 4 — Connected

06-05.body:
"At some time in the past we have made decisions based on self which later placed us in a position to be hurt." — Big Book

A lot of us read that line and thought, Man, I gotta stop doing that. The problem was we had no idea how. So we got more serious, more careful, and more determined not to make mistakes. Not a bad start. But eventually we had to ask a different question: What are these decisions based on anyway?

Most of the time they're driven by character defects of self that show up naturally in everyday life—fear, pride, resentment, control, self-pity. A guy cuts us off in traffic and makes us swerve out of our lane. The old reaction might have been yelling, chasing him down, or introducing him to our favorite finger. It happens. But now we're starting to see that anger doesn't end when the incident ends. We carry it to work, bring it home, and replay it in our heads. A five-second event turns into a five-hour resentment.

That's where Step Six becomes practical. Instead of trying to control every situation, we start looking at what's driving our reactions. We go to the source. We ask God to help remove the defect instead of trying to manage the whole world. That doesn't mean we become passive or ignore real problems. It means we learn the difference between reacting and responding.

The miracle isn't that life stops cutting us off. The miracle is that every little thing no longer has the power to ruin our day.

Have you ever traced a resentment back to the character defect feeding it? What did you find?
06-05.title: June 5 – At Some Time in the Past

06-06.body:
"Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." — Big Book

The overactive ego loves to create problems to solve, and it almost never solves them by going to a Higher Power. Instead, it reaches for its favorite tools: anger, pride, jealousy, greed, lust, self-pity, and control. They feel natural. They feel protective. They feel like they were put there to defend us.

For a lot of us, these reactions became so automatic that we stopped questioning them. We take something personally? We get angry. We compare ourselves to somebody else? We get jealous. Things don't go our way? We feel sorry for ourselves. We get uncomfortable? We start trying to control people and outcomes.

The problem is these are bad defense mechanisms. They don't work. Anger creates more anger. Pride isolates us. Jealousy steals our peace. Self-pity keeps us stuck. Control usually creates the very problems we're trying to avoid.

And when it comes to alcoholics, these are dangerous propositions. They lead to resentment, and resentment leads to drinking. For us, to drink is to die. That's why Step Six isn't about becoming perfect. It's about becoming willing to let go of the things that keep hurting us.

The ego always wants to solve the problem itself. Recovery teaches us to bring the problem to God instead.

Which character defect has spent the most time pretending to protect you?
06-06.title: June 6 – Bad Defenses

06-07.body:
According to the AA statistics in the Foreword to the Fourth Edition, some people got sober right away. Some got sober after a few slips. Some took a little longer but got better if they kept coming back.

In recovery we hear a lot of discouraging statistics. Only 10% recover. In some recovery circles it's supposedly 2%. Honestly, nobody really knows where a lot of those numbers come from. It's not like there's a polling station set up at meetings.

But these old-timers hung around AA for years. They watched people come in, they watched people leave, and they watched what happened.

What they observed was simple.

About half the people who came to AA and really tried stayed sober. About a quarter of the people who came in slipped, got back on the horse, and eventually stayed sober one day at a time if they kept trying. And the remaining quarter of the people who came in and couldn't quite give themselves to this simple program still picked up enough in those rooms to have a better life if they kept trying.

That's not a scientific study. It's just what they saw.

So this begs the question: How do you stay sober?

The word that jumps out is try.

Try to make the meetings. Try to do the steps. Try to get a connection with a Higher Power. Try to be honest. Try to keep an open mind. Try to be willing. Try to be useful. Try again when you screw it up.

Because we all know what happens when we stop trying and let one of these character defects get between us and our Higher Power, the fellowship, and the simple program that can save our lives.

Meeting Starter: What does "trying" look like for you today?
06-07.title: June 7 — Try

06-08.body:
"Change is a bitch. Not changing is even worse."

Change sucks. Hell, we're practically begging God to help us accept it at the beginning of every meeting when we say the Serenity Prayer. And it seems like we have all kinds of character defects standing by to help us resist it.

A relationship ends? Fear shows up. Am I going to be alone forever? Am I damaged goods? Then anger shows up. Resentment shows up. Prideful pouting shows up. We start replaying all the ways things should have gone if the other person hadn't changed into this or that. It sucks.

The further we go along in recovery, the more it seems like impatience is hiding underneath a lot of our character defects. And alcoholics know impatience better than most. We want answers now. Relief now. Results now.

But recovery keeps asking us to do something different. Wait on God's plan to unfold. Pay attention to the people He puts in our path. Try to do the next right thing. Trust that the door will open when it's supposed to.

That's where a lot of us start to struggle, wiggle, and squirm. The alcoholism flares up, and before long we're reacting to life instead of responding to it.

It doesn't have to be that way. Life on life's terms goes a lot smoother with a little self-awareness, prayer, and meditation. The grass stays greener. The sky stays bluer. The smiles seem to come easier.

We stop trying to discipline the world and let God discipline us.

It works. It really does.

Where does impatience show up most often in your life today?
06-08.title: June 8 — Change Is a Bitch

06-09.body:
"God either is, or He isn't. What was our choice to be?"

— Alcoholics Anonymous, We Agnostics

Man, that's a big choice.

But the beauty of AA is that we get to make that choice for ourselves.

It's a pretty simple concept. If we believe in a God of our understanding, then we can start to see God's work everywhere when we sincerely look for it. The people who show up at the right time. The doors that open. The lessons hidden inside the struggles. The coincidences that don't always feel like coincidences.

Of course, alcoholics have a way of blocking that channel. Resentment, fear, self-pity, anger, and all the character defects that help us justify those things can make it hard to see anything beyond ourselves. The good news is we have tools for that now. We can clear away the debris if that's what we choose.

If we choose no God, then we'll see no God. Life can look like a random series of events with no deeper meaning. Coincidence is just coincidence. We're just here taking up space, dealing with whatever gets thrown at us today and cleaning up whatever mess showed up.

Maybe that's true. Maybe it isn't.

But if we're going to spend the rest of our lives looking at the world through one of those lenses, it seems worth asking the question the Big Book asks:

What was our choice to be?

When life gets difficult, do you tend to look for meaning or look for someone to blame?
06-09.title: June 9 — What Was Our Choice?

06-10.body:
"We had to ask ourselves why we shouldn't apply to our human problems this same readiness to change our point of view."
— Alcoholics Anonymous, We Agnostics

There's something about alcoholics that can turn sudden change into dread. The work schedule changes? Oh, this sucks. Someone's relationship status changes? Something bad must have happened. A plan falls through? Here we go again.

We tend to jump to conclusions, and those conclusions are usually based on fear. The funny thing about fear is that it never seems to bring us any good news. It doesn't tell us things are going to work out. It doesn't tell us to be patient. It doesn't remind us of all the times life surprised us in a good way. Fear specializes in worst-case scenarios.

Recovery teaches us a different way to look at things. Today we have tools. We can pray. We can meditate. We can talk to another alcoholic. We can inventory what's really going on instead of automatically believing every fearful thought that pops into our heads.

Maybe the change we're dreading isn't a disaster. Maybe it's part of something bigger. Maybe it's an opportunity. Maybe it's a lesson. Maybe it's a door opening that we can't see yet.

Sure, change can be uncomfortable. Sure, things can suck sometimes. But some of the best things that ever happened to us started out looking like bad news.

We don't have to live in dread anymore. And we certainly don't have to drink over it.

What situation in your life turned out better than you expected after you stopped fighting it?
06-10.title: June 10 — Dread

06-11.body:
"If we are sorry for what we have done, and have the honest desire to let God take us to better things, we believe we will be forgiven and will have learned our lesson."

— Alcoholics Anonymous, Into Action

A lot of alcoholics carry guilt. For whatever reason, we tend to lace guilt together with shame until we can't tell the difference between the two. Then we isolate, hide, and convince ourselves we're no good to anybody. It happens to the best of us.

By this point in the Steps, we've admitted that selfishness and self-centeredness are at the root of our troubles. The funny thing is, guilt can become another form of self-centeredness. We sit around telling ourselves stories about ourselves, to ourselves. We replay old mistakes, old embarrassments, and old failures until they become the main thing we think about.

A little guilt isn't a bad thing. It's like an internal radar that says, "Hey, you messed up. You might need to make this right." That's useful. But when guilt gets mixed with shame, it turns into a resentment against ourselves. And that's no way to live.

We forget that we've been given a very unique education about alcoholism and recovery. The mistakes, the wreckage, the bad decisions, the embarrassing moments—none of them have to be wasted. The more honestly we share them with other alcoholics, the more they become tools instead of burdens. The story that keeps us awake at night might be the exact thing that keeps somebody else from running out the door of a meeting and never coming back.

Faith without works is dead. One of the ways we put faith into action is by being honest about where we've been. When we do, those old guilty stories stop being evidence against us and start becoming weapons against alcoholic thinking.

What's was a guilty story that kept you stuck?
06-11.title: June 11 — Guilt

06-12.body:
Every year we stay sober, AA gathers another year of proof that this program works. We're all spread out, but we're connected by a common solution. The next suffering alcoholic looking for answers needs us to still be here. That's one reason Founders Day means so much to so many people.

Around this time every year, thousands of alcoholics gather in Akron, Ohio, the birthplace of AA. It's the place where Bill W. met Dr. Bob in 1935. But if they met in May of 1935, why is AA's birthday in June?

Well, Bill already had a little program of action he was practicing. There were only six steps at the time. One of those ideas eventually blossomed into what we know today as Step Nine: making amends. Bob wasn't having it. He refused. And he kept getting drunk.

After a few weeks of not being able to stay sober, Dr. Bob finally threw in the towel and did the amends. On June 10, 1935, he took his last drink and never drank again. That was the day AA was born.

It wasn't the day Bill and Bob met. It was the day AA finally had two members who agreed on the formula for staying sober and were willing to practice it. Since then, millions upon millions of alcoholics have followed that same formula and stayed sober too.

Every Founders Day is another reminder that this thing works. Every year we stay sober adds another year of proof. And the next alcoholic who walks through the doors looking for answers needs us to still be here when they arrive.

Meeting Starter: If it worked for them, why wouldn't it work for you?
06-12.title: June 12 — Founders Day

06-13.body:
"We found that we had to be entirely honest..." — Alcoholics Anonymous

One of the biggest surprises in sobriety is finding out that alcoholism can still show up long after the drink is gone.

Everybody around us can see it except us, which is pretty much how it worked when we were drinking too.

For some, lust has them borrowing Grandma's car and driving hours away chasing the next conquest. For others, greed convinces them to steal something at a gas station even though they've got plenty of money in their pocket. Some become habitual liars, covering their tracks and managing appearances. Some get so wrapped up in sloth that they build an entire lifestyle around avoiding responsibility.

The defect doesn't really matter. What matters is that the obsession, the justification, and the blind spot all feel strangely familiar.

The drink may be gone, but the thinking isn't.

Alcoholism has a way of putting on different clothes and pretending it's something else. It can disguise itself as ambition, romance, self-pity, anger, comfort, or even righteousness. Whatever form it takes, it usually comes with the same old story: This time it's different.

That's why rigorous honesty matters. Not the kind we practice after we're caught. The kind that allows us to recognize what's happening while we're still doing it.

Most of us don't wake up one morning and decide to become selfish, dishonest, fearful, or resentful. We slide into it. Then we defend it. Then we wonder why life feels unmanageable again.

Have you ever caught yourself in full alcoholic mode without taking a drink? What finally made you see it?
06-13.title: June 13 — Full Alcoholic Mode

06-14.body:
"Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character." — Step Six

Sometimes alcoholics skip words when we read. We're taking in information so fast, trying to get the meaning, that we can miss a vital part of what's being said.

One word that often gets skipped in Step Six is God.

Then we're right back to beating ourselves up about lust, anger, fear, selfishness, and the whole gamut of character defects that make up our alcoholic condition. It's common to hear people say, "I'm working on my character defects." And that's a great start. But Step Six doesn't say, "You get angry a lot, so go fix that yourself." It doesn't say, "Work harder on your lust," or "Try harder not to be selfish."

What it says is that we're entirely ready to have God remove these defects of character.

That means accepting the fact that the anger is there. The fear is there. The selfishness is there. Then, in those moments when they show up, we lean on a Higher Power and ask for help instead of trying to wrestle the thing to the ground ourselves.

Please don't try this alone.

Once we recognize what's happening, we act as if God has removed it and go about our day. If we mess it up, we make it right and keep moving. We don't sit around beating ourselves up for three weeks. We clean it up, learn from it, and move forward.

We always keep moving.

It turns out that when we're sober, people are a lot more forgiving of us when they see us trying. And maybe that's because God has been doing the same thing for us all along.

Have you ever spent more time fighting a character defect than asking God to remove it?
06-14.title: June 14 — Please Don't Try This Alone

06-15.body:
"Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions."
— Tradition SevenSure, it's easy to understand this tradition in a meeting. The basket gets passed, we throw a dollar in, and the meeting goes on.But what were they really trying to teach us?Alcoholics have a bad habit of walking around with our hands out and not even knowing it. As deeply afflicted self-seekers, we can convince ourselves that we're there to be helpful when we're really looking to get something from someone else.Maybe we're always looking for someone to bail us out of a problem we created. Maybe we call certain people only when we need something. Maybe we're constantly fishing for reassurance that we're right. Maybe it's attention from dating sites, approval from people who tell us what we want to hear, or turning a trusted friend into someone who validates our bad ideas.There's nothing wrong with needing help. We wouldn't have gotten sober without it. But recovery slowly teaches us to take responsibility for ourselves instead of depending on others to carry us.Self-supporting doesn't mean we never need help. It doesn't mean we become isolated or refuse assistance when we genuinely need it. It means we're no longer making a lifestyle out of asking other people to do things for us that we're neglecting to do for ourselves. We begin carrying our own weight. We pay our way when we can. We become contributors instead of consumers.Over time, we stop looking at every person, meeting, and situation through the lens of what we can get from it. Instead, we start asking what we can contribute.That little shift changes a lot more than our finances. It changes our relationships, our recovery, and the way we move through life.Are you trying to be of help, or help yourself?

"Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions."
— Tradition Seven

Sure, it's easy to understand this tradition in a meeting. The basket gets passed, we throw a dollar in, and the meeting goes on.

But what were they really trying to teach us?

Alcoholics have a bad habit of walking around with our hands out and not even knowing it. As deeply afflicted self-seekers, we can convince ourselves that we're there to be helpful when we're really looking to get something from someone else.

Maybe we're always looking for someone to bail us out of a problem we created. Maybe we call certain people only when we need something. Maybe we're constantly fishing for reassurance that we're right. Maybe it's attention from dating sites, approval from people who tell us what we want to hear, or turning a trusted friend into someone who validates our bad ideas.

There's nothing wrong with needing help. We wouldn't have gotten sober without it. But recovery slowly teaches us to take responsibility for ourselves instead of depending on others to carry us.

Self-supporting doesn't mean we never need help. It doesn't mean we become isolated or refuse assistance when we genuinely need it. It means we're no longer making a lifestyle out of asking other people to do things for us that we're neglecting to do for ourselves. We begin carrying our own weight. We pay our way when we can. We become contributors instead of consumers.

Over time, we stop looking at every person, meeting, and situation through the lens of what we can get from it. Instead, we start asking what we can contribute.

That little shift changes a lot more than our finances. It changes our relationships, our recovery, and the way we move through life.

Are you trying to be of help, or help yourself?
06-15.title: June 15 — Self-Supporting

06-16.body:
"We were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives." — How It Works

There's a strange resentment that pops up for alcoholics sometimes. We know our lives are unmanageable, but every now and then we try to hand that unmanageability to someone else. Sometimes they take it. Sometimes they help. Sometimes they carry us farther than they should. And sometimes they say no.

Sometimes they tell us, "Not my problem." Sometimes they tell us to figure it out ourselves. And when that happens, our alcoholism can start squirming around in our heads. I can't believe they're doing this to me. What am I supposed to do now? If they cared, they would help. I don't have as much as they do. They owe me.

Nothing fuels a good dose of self-seeking quite like self-pity.

As deeply afflicted self-seekers, we can become convinced that other people are responsible for solving problems that belong to us. Then, when they refuse, we resent them for it. The funny thing is that the people we're leaning on usually feel it long before we do. Over time, they start backing away, and we're left wondering what happened.

Recovery offers us a different approach. Bill Wilson suggested a life built on self-examination, prayer, meditation, and a sincere effort to do better. Instead of looking outward for someone to rescue us, we begin looking inward for what needs to change in us. It's not always comfortable, but it's a lot more effective.

After all, if we couldn't manage our own lives before recovery, why would we expect someone else to do it for us now?

Are you using the program's way, or are you still moving from person to person with your hand out?
06-16.title: June 16 — A Strange Resentment

06-17.body:
Being sober for a while, relying on a God of our understanding, and becoming more of a spectator in our own lives takes daily discipline. Sometimes we get proud of ourselves. And that's okay. For a lot of us, it's a strange feeling. We spent years buried in guilt, shame, and low self-esteem. Coming out of that pit and growing into a God-consciousness starts to look a lot like confidence.

We find ourselves doing things we never thought we'd do. We pray before disaster instead of after it. We help others. We stay sober through situations that used to send us running. Sometimes we look back and think, Holy crap, I can't believe prayer worked... again. We're grateful, and maybe even a little proud of what God has done in our lives.

Then something happens. Old friends or family members still treat us like the drunk we used to be. Someone brings up our past. Somebody doesn't notice the changes we've made. That old feeling of not being good enough starts creeping back in. At that moment, our alcoholic ego can jump into the driver's seat. We get hurt. We get angry. We start thinking, After everything I've done, how dare they treat me like this?

That's where pride can turn sick. Not because we were proud of our growth, but because we started needing other people to be proud of it too. The next right thing never needed an audience. It never needed applause. It never needed approval. If we can take that hurt to our Higher Power instead of lashing out, we've learned something valuable about our character defects. We gain a little more humility, a little more freedom, and a little more strength for the road ahead.

Have you ever found yourself doing the right thing, then becoming resentful because nobody seemed to notice?
06-17.title: June 17 - Pride Sick

06-18.body:
"We were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character."— Step Six

Either we're entirely ready to have God remove these defects of character, or we're not. Either we're going to let go of anger, pride, greed, lust, and fear, or we're going to keep carrying them around. Either we're going to act on the love, forgiveness, and spiritual principles we've found in recovery, or we're going to act on one of these defects instead. You can go with this, or you can go with that.

How far are you willing to go for a character defect? Does resentment turn into a mean texting war that wastes hours and leaves two people further apart than before? Does anger show up behind the wheel, convincing you that a stranger on the highway deserves your wrath? Does lust have you chasing attention and excitement while doing the bare minimum for your recovery? Does greed convince you that material things deserve more of your time than helping another alcoholic? Does fear keep you frozen in place when you already know the next right thing to do?

The funny thing about A.A.'s spiritual program is that it works. We start feeling better. Life gets better. Relationships improve. The obsession lifts. And then sometimes the ego sneaks back in and says, "Look what I did." The same ego that got us into trouble in the first place suddenly wants credit for the miracle.

Step Six asks a simple question: now that you know both paths, which one are you choosing today?

Have you ever watched a character defect slowly convince you it was actually helping you?
06-18.title: June 18 – You Can Go With This, or You Can Go With That

06-19.body:
"We don't struggle." — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 88

The struggle is real.

Letting in the light of God ain't always an easy task. Life hits sometimes, and it hits hard. Sometimes we flip out and make things worse. It happens. We have a step to tidy that up if need be. When stress shows up, we can wiggle, squirm, and struggle to keep these character defects at bay. In those moments, we may have to mash that built-in pause button like a ten-cent slot machine on a winning streak just to keep from reacting. The good news is that the more we practice, the easier it gets. Little by little, something in our hearts starts to eclipse that sick part of our minds. We settle down. We pray instead of react. We listen instead of lash out. What once felt impossible starts becoming a moment-by-moment way of living.

Sometimes the most spiritual thing we can do is walk away for a minute and hit pause. After all, nothing—absolutely nothing—needs our immediate attention when we're all fired up. We're allowed to take a break. We're allowed to remove ourselves from the situation until the right thought or action comes. That's the promise behind "We don't struggle." It doesn't mean life stops happening. It means that over time, we stop fighting everything and everyone around us. We learn to pause, pray, and let God do some of the heavy lifting. The struggle is real. But the promise is real too. If we keep practicing this way of life, eventually we find ourselves struggling a little less and trusting a little more.

Have you ever made a situation worse because you couldn't hit pause in time?
06-19.title: June 19 – The Struggle Is Real

06-20.body:
"We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve..."

Recovery can turn into a constant search for the next thing. The next meeting. The next step. The next program. The next answer. Before rushing off to what's next, don't forget what you've done here.

Maybe you've just made it through detox. Maybe you've sat through your first A.A. meeting. Maybe you've said your first meaningful prayer in years. Maybe you've started working the Steps. Maybe you've simply made it through another day sober. Whatever it is, don't overlook it. You're allowed to smile again.

Alcoholics have a habit of focusing on the distance still left to travel while forgetting how far we've already come. We get so busy looking ahead that we fail to recognize the small victories that make the rest of recovery possible. There was a time when many of us couldn't make it through a single day without a drink. Today, we're doing things we once thought were impossible.

None of us got sober all at once. We got sober one decision, one action, and one day at a time. Don't forget what you've done here. The same willingness that brought you this far can carry you farther than you ever imagined.

What is something in your recovery that once seemed impossible but has now become part of your life?
06-20.title: June 20 – Don't Forget

06-21.body:
"We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition."

The problem with A.A. is that it works. Finally beaten into a state of reasonableness, we come in tore up from the floor up and get busy. We take suggestions, hit meetings, read the book, pray, and help other people. Before long, life starts getting better. Then it gets good. Then it gets really good. Jobs come our way, families are reunited, relationships are repaired, and we become contributing citizens again.

And that's where the danger can creep in. With all the responsibilities we have now, recovery can slowly take a back seat. We hit meetings when we feel like it. We let somebody else work with the newcomer. The Big Book becomes more of a souvenir than a tool. Nothing dramatic happens. We just slowly drift.

Then, little by little, that old character-defect life starts slipping back in. Fear returns. Control returns. Irritability returns. Before we know it, we're standing in the middle of the broad highway wondering what happened. The drink may not have returned yet, but we're white-knuckling our sobriety again, trying to manage life on our own power and wondering why everything feels so heavy.

Maybe recovery didn't stop working. Maybe we stopped doing the things that connected us to the solution in the first place. The good news is that the way back is usually the same way we came in. A little honesty. A little prayer. A little service. God will provide the necessary balance if we seek it.

Have you ever found yourself white-knuckling sobriety without picking up a drink?
06-21.title: June 21 – White Knuckle Sobriety

06-22.body:
There are times when our emotions sit so close to the surface that it feels like we're only moments away from making a bad situation worse. The resentment is building. The fear is growing. The feeling that this isn't right starts taking over our thinking. Our A.A. discipline wrestles with our lower nature, and finding an opening into the light can feel like searching for a door in the dark.

Most of us know exactly what that moment feels like. The text is half written. The argument is loaded and ready to fire. The steering wheel is getting squeezed a little too hard. The mind is racing, looking for someone to blame or some way to force the world to cooperate.

Right before the breaking point, in a moment of emotional desperation, a simple prayer can be enough:

"God, please keep one hand on my shoulder and one hand over my mouth."

It sounds funny, but it works. It creates just enough space between the feeling and the action. Just enough room for God to get a word in before our character defects do. Sometimes the greatest spiritual victory of the day isn't what we say or do. Sometimes it's what we don't say and don't do.

When was the last time staying quiet saved you from making a situation worse?
06-22.title: June 22 – One-Handed Prayer

06-23.body:
AA gets misunderstood a lot.

Some people treat it like a religion. Some people act like it's a cult. Some people dismiss it entirely because they had a bad experience.

The reality is a lot less dramatic.

AA was started by two guys who were sick of ending up in detox every time they drank. They got together and talked about what worked and what didn't. They stayed sober. Then they shared those ideas with other alcoholics. Some of those people stayed sober too. Some didn't. So they paid attention to that information as well and eventually threw it all into a book to try and help the next alcoholic who came along.

That's really it.

No parades. No secret handshakes. No perfect leaders. No claims that they had all the answers. Just alcoholics trying to help other alcoholics avoid the misery they knew so well.

Their attitude was pretty straightforward: Take it or leave it.

What have I learned from other alcoholics that I couldn't have learned by myself?
06-23.title: June 23 – It Takes Two to Make a Thing Go Right

06-24.body:
A thing I picked up in meetings is the first 24 minutes of your day can have a lot to do with what the next 24 hours look like. Not as a hard rule, just a rule of thumb.

A lot of alcoholics wake up and rattle off the Third Step and Seventh Step prayers, then get on with their day. Some spend an hour reading, praying, meditating, or trying to get their head pointed in the right direction before they go out and play in the world. Some keep it simple and just take a few quiet minutes before the noise of the day starts. And some don't do any of that.

The beauty is that today we have options. We don't have to do what somebody else does. We can find what helps us stay connected, stay useful, and stay sober, and then make a habit of doing it.

A lot of us have found that when we start the day by feeding our recovery, the day tends to go a little better. Not perfect. Not problem-free. Just better. Our reactions aren't as sharp, our thinking isn't as scattered, and we're a little more prepared for whatever the day brings. It doesn't guarantee a good day, but it often gives us a better chance of showing up for it.

What does your first 24 minutes look like?
06-24.title: June 24 – The 24x24

06-25.body:
"I have been trying to produce some such emotional rearrangement within you."

The interesting part is that the doctor didn't succeed, for after all, "b. No human power could have relieved our alcoholism." None. Not doctors. Not spouses. Not kids. Not the police. None.

The rearrangement doesn't begin until we're willing to find a different way. Before that, our emotions tend to run the show. Pride says it's all about me. Lust says I need what I want. Anger says somebody needs blamed. Fear says protect yourself. Self-pity says why is this happening to me?

Then we pause. We pray. We ask God for help. And maybe for a moment, humility gets a chance to speak. Maybe I don't have all the answers. Maybe I don't need to react right now. Maybe there is another way to look at this situation.

That's a rearrangement of emotions. The situation may not change. The people around us may not change. But what drives us begins to change. And for many of us, that's where recovery begins.

What emotion used to drive your decisions, and what has started taking its place in recovery?
06-25.title: June 25 — Rearrangement of Emotions

06-26.body:
One of the unexpected gifts of recovery is realizing there are a lot of things I simply don't need to do anymore. I don't need to have the last word. I don't need to prove I'm right. I don't need to answer every criticism or fix every problem the moment it shows up. I don't need everyone to understand me, agree with me, or even like me.

For a long time I confused peace with getting my way. Today I've found that peace usually comes from letting go instead. The freedom isn't in controlling every situation. It's in realizing I don't have to.

Every time I choose patience over proving a point, or walk away from an argument that doesn't need to happen, I get a small reminder that recovery is working. Life gets a little lighter when I stop carrying things I was never meant to hold.

What's one thing recovery has taught you that you simply don't need to do anymore?
06-26.title: June 26 – I Don't Need To

06-27.body:
When I was drinking, everything had to be loud. Big emotions. Big plans. Big problems. If there wasn't chaos, I'd usually create some.

Recovery has introduced me to something I didn't appreciate before: quiet. A peaceful morning. A good cup of coffee. An honest conversation. Helping someone without expecting anything back. Going to bed with a clear conscience.

I've found that the best parts of sobriety rarely make a lot of noise. They don't demand attention. They just quietly remind me that this way of life is working.

What's one quiet blessing recovery has brought into your life?
06-27.title: June 27 – The Good Stuff Doesn't Yell

06-28.body:
In the destructive phase of our drinking, we spread the consequences of our alcoholism everywhere we went. Our families felt it. Our friends felt it. Our jobs felt it. Missed games. Broken promises. Calling off work. Wasted hours on the clock. Hangovers. We became so consumed by our drinking that doing the next right thing rarely even crossed our minds. Untreated alcoholism has a way of touching everything around it.

Then, at the final moment, we came to AA looking for a solution. We started doing a few simple things. We stayed sober one day at a time. We prayed. We made amends. We tried to be useful. We didn't set out to change the world—we were just trying to stop destroying our own.

Something strange begins to happen. Without forcing it, recovery starts spreading too. Our families notice we're showing up. Our coworkers see someone they can count on. Friends begin to trust us again. Peace replaces chaos a little at a time. Joy, freedom, and usefulness have a way of rippling outward just like alcoholism once did.

We may never know how far those ripples travel. That's okay. Our job isn't to measure them. It's simply to stay sober today, do the next right thing, and let the rest spread on its own.

What am I spreading today?
06-28.title: June 28 – Spread 'Em

06-29.body:
Having realized that the root of our alcoholic behavior is self-centeredness, we begin to develop a different way of looking at life. We still look at our character defects, the past, the future, the ups, and the downs—but we don't stare. We take an honest look so we can see what needs to be done, then we do the next right thing.

Sometimes we catch ourselves replaying yesterday, rehearsing tomorrow, or sitting with a resentment longer than we need to. Sometimes a character defect shows up again and we'd rather spend the day beating ourselves up than taking the next right action. Recovery gives us another option. We acknowledge it, accept it, make it as right as we can, and move on.

Life gets messy. We're all just trying to do the best we can with what we've got today. We look, but we don't stare.

What have I been staring at lately that only needed an honest look?
06-29.title: June 29 – We Look, But We Don't Stare

06-30.body:
"We have admitted certain defects; we have ascertained in a rough way what the trouble is; we have put our finger on the weak items in our personal inventory."

One of the greatest gifts of recovery is finally hearing something we probably needed to hear our whole lives: we're not perfect, we're never going to be perfect, and that's not the goal. We're human. We have defects. We miss the mark. If we somehow got everything right all the time, it would probably be a little strange.

Recovery isn't asking us to become flawless. It's asking us to become honest. To recognize our biggest defects, ask for help, and try to do a little better today than we did yesterday. That's progress. And for alcoholics, progress is enough to stay sober.

As we keep doing that, something begins to change. We're connected. We find a little more serenity, a little more acceptance of ourselves and the people around us, and before long we discover that life is becoming worth living. Not because we became perfect, but because we finally stopped expecting ourselves to be.

If perfection isn't the goal, what does progress look like for you today?
06-30.title: June 30 – We're Human, After All

07-01.body:
"My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad. I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows. Grant me strength, as I go out from here, to do your bidding. Amen." - Seventh Step Prayer, Alcoholics Anynymous

Step Seven is where all the work we've done up to this point begins to come together. We've admitted we're not perfect, we've come to believe we need help beyond ourselves, we've taken an honest moral inventory, and we've admitted our wrongs. Now comes the humble request to have our defects removed.

Notice the goal isn't to become a perfect person. The prayer asks only that the defects standing in the way of our usefulness be removed. That's an important distinction. Recovery isn't about creating a new personality. It's about becoming less driven by fear, pride, resentment, and selfishness so we can be of greater use to God and the people around us.As we continue to practice these principles, we often discover that usefulness grows as self-centeredness shrinks. That's the quiet work of Step Seven.
What defect of character gets in the way of your usefulness the most today?

Recovery isn't about creating a new personality. It's about becoming less driven by fear, pride, resentment, and selfishness so we can be of greater use to God and the people around us.

As we continue to practice these principles, we often discover that usefulness grows as self-centeredness shrinks. That's the quiet work of Step Seven.

What defect of character gets in the way of your usefulness the most today?
07-01.title: July 1 – All of Me

07-02.body:
"Humbly, on our knees, asked Him to remove our shortcomings—holding nothing back." — Original AA Seventh Step

The original manuscript of AA was a little more hardcore than what many of us are used to today. Those early members had watched friends go back out and die. For a real alcoholic, getting sober wasn't one option among many—it was the only option, or don't waste our time.

Being on our knees wasn't anything new anyway. We'd spent enough nights kneeling over a toilet, sick, broken, and out of answers. We'd been so broken down by alcohol that we could barely stand. When it came time to pray, many of the early members got on their knees.

Then, in true AA fashion, nobody said you had to. They simply passed along what worked. Some people with long-term sobriety still pray that way today. Some don't.

Maybe there's something about physically getting on our knees that helps us remember who we're asking, and who we've finally stopped trying to be.

It's your life. Your recovery. Do what you want. Just don't let laziness make the decision for you.

Have you ever prayed on your knees? If so, what was different about it? If not, what keeps you from trying it?
07-02.title: July 2 – Knees

07-03.body:
As we've gone through the Twelve Steps, a lot of us have settled down. That pause before reacting. The need for everyone's approval. The lying. The one-upping. Getting offended over small stuff. And the sickest of all, resentment. Those things still show up from time to time, but they don't run our lives anymore. And when they do, we have tools now.
Somewhere along the way, we become better friends.
We listen more. We don't have to dominate every conversation or always be right. We can admit we're wrong, laugh at ourselves, and simply be there for another alcoholic.
And if we're lucky, somewhere along the way we meet one of those rare people in AA who has truly given themselves to this simple program. The kind who went to any lengths to stay sober. They don't usually preach. They don't have to. The way they live, the way they treat people, and the peace they carry says enough.
Maybe that's one of the greatest gifts of recovery. Every once in a while, the pressure of "staying sober" disappears, and we're just two drunks doing life together, helping each other through another day.
I have a feeling that's what the first two guys found.
Who has quietly taught you the most about recovery simply by the way they live?

And the sickest of all, resentment. Those things still show up from time to time, but they don't run our lives anymore. And when they do, we have tools now.

I have a feeling that's what the first two guys found.

Who has quietly taught you the most about recovery simply by the way they live?
07-03.title: July 3 – Friends

07-04.body:
Alcoholics love fireworks.

Not the ones in the sky—the ones we create. We had a way of making every argument bigger, every problem louder, and every room revolve around us. Good attention or bad attention didn't matter much, as long as we got it.

Then Step Seven starts doing something strange. We don't need to be the loudest person anymore. We don't have to win every argument or have the last word. Humility has a way of settling us down. It doesn't make much noise, but it changes everything.

Real recovery isn't nearly as flashy as we imagined it would be. Most days it's quiet. And that's probably the point.

When was the last time humility kept you from creating unnecessary fireworks?
07-04.title: July 4 – Fireworks

07-05.body:
"Ideas, emotions, and attitudes which were once the guiding forces of our lives are suddenly cast to one side, and a completely new set of conceptions and motives begin to dominate us." — Alcoholics Anonymous

Change is a bitch.

For most of us, change has always meant loss. We have to give something up, leave something behind, or let go of what feels comfortable. Even when the old way is making us miserable, at least it's familiar.

The Twelve Steps slowly help us to see it differently.

What if change isn't loss at all? What if it's transformation without loss? Every resentment we let go of makes room for peace. Every fear we face makes room for courage. Every selfish decision we stop making leaves room for usefulness. We aren't becoming less. We're becoming more of the person alcohol never let us be.

It doesn't happen overnight. At first, every change feels like a fight. But after enough experience, we begin to trust the process. We stop asking, "What am I going to lose?" and start wondering, "What gift is waiting on the other side of this?"

And when that way of thinking starts coming naturally... that's a hell of a psychic change.

What change in recovery felt like a loss at first but eventually became one of the greatest gifts in your sobriety?
07-05.title: July 5 – Psychic Change

07-06.body:
"The Old Adam in us should, by daily contrition and repentance, be drowned and die..."

Ever hear that little voice that says, "Ah, screw it. Just this once." Or the one that has to be right, has to get even, has to have the last word, or wants everybody to know we got screwed? Ever catch yourself halfway through one of those moments and think, "There I go again." Maybe that's what Martin Luther meant by the Old Adam. Not some demon hiding inside us. Just that old way of thinking that keeps trying to pull us back to self.

Recovery doesn't ask us to pretend he isn't there. It asks us to notice him. To recognize those old patterns before they take over. To ask God for help, and then do the next right thing anyway.

Stick around long enough, and something starts to change. Some of those old reactions don't even sound like us anymore. What used to feel natural starts to feel foreign. And when doing the next right thing starts coming naturally... that's a hell of a psychic change.

What does your Old Adam usually sound like?
07-06.title: July 6 – The Old Adam

07-07.body:
"I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to You and to my fellows."

One of the quiet gifts of Step Seven is that, as God begins removing our character defects, we start recognizing them in everyday life.

Someone interrupts every conversation. Someone always has to be right. Someone is looking for approval. Someone is carrying around a resentment.

Years ago, we probably wouldn't have thought twice about it because we were doing the very same things.

Today, those moments aren't invitations to judge. They're reminders. We remember where we've been, what it felt like to live that way, and what we were really searching for underneath it all. Most of our defects were trying to protect us from fear, insecurity, loneliness, or pain.

Instead of thinking, "What's wrong with them?" we begin asking, "How can I be helpful?"

Then something beautiful starts to happen. The very defects God has been removing from us become a doorway. They allow us to meet people exactly where they are because we've been there ourselves. We understand the fear because we've lived it. We understand the pride because we've hidden behind it. We understand the resentment because we've carried it.

We don't meet people from above them. We meet them from beside them.

That's one more way God makes us useful to Him and to our fellows. He doesn't waste our past. He redeems it. Our old character defects become bridges instead of barriers, giving us the compassion and empathy to reach out a hand instead of pointing a finger.

When was the last time you replaced judgment with the question, "How can I be helpful?"
07-07.title: July 7 – New Eyes

07-08.body:
"Self-righteousness, the very thing that we had contempt for in others, was our own besetting evil." — Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions

One of the more subtle character defects is the need to be right.

After all, if we're right, the story is over. We don't have to change. We don't have to apologize. We don't have to look at ourselves. Everyone else just needs to realize we were right all along and leave us alone.

Most of us spent years building a case for ourselves. We had an explanation for everything. We defended every decision, justified every resentment, and always had one more reason why things weren't really our fault.

Then we got sober and discovered something strange.

We don't have to win every conversation anymore.

There's a freedom that comes from saying, "I was wrong." There's peace in letting someone else have the last word. We don't lose anything by admitting a mistake. In fact, we usually gain something far more valuable than being right—we gain humility.

Step Seven isn't about becoming quiet or weak. It's about no longer needing our ego to be fed every time someone disagrees with us.

The longer we stay sober, the less important it becomes to prove ourselves, and the more important it becomes to be useful. Sometimes the most spiritual thing we can say is, "You know what? I could be wrong."

When was the last time admitting you were wrong brought you more peace than proving you were right?
07-08.title: ly 8 – I Don't Have to Be Right

07-09.body:
"Obviously, a solitary self-appraisal, and the admission of our defects based upon that alone, wouldn't be nearly enough." — Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions

One of the more exhausting character defects is living for other people's approval. We spend years wondering what people think about us. Did they like us? Did we say the right thing? Are they mad at us? Did they notice what we did? Before long, we find ourselves making decisions based on keeping everyone else happy instead of simply doing the next right thing.

The strange part is, no amount of approval is ever enough. Someone can compliment us ten times, but the one criticism is the one we carry around all day. That's because approval can never give us the peace we're looking for. It only leaves us wanting more.

Step Seven begins to loosen that grip. As God removes this defect, we slowly stop asking, "What do they think of me?" and start asking, "Am I doing the next right thing?" Those are two very different ways to live.

The first makes us prisoners of other people's opinions. The second makes us useful. When our worth depends on approval, we're always chasing something we can never quite catch. But when our worth comes from trying to do God's will one day at a time, we're finally free to let people think whatever they're going to think. And that's a freedom no one can take away.

How much of your day is spent seeking approval instead of simply trying to do the next right thing?
07-09.title: July 9 – Prisoners of Opinion

07-10.body:
"I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to You and to my fellows."

One of the easiest character defects to justify is talking about other people. We tell ourselves we're just venting. We're just being honest. They need to know. It's true. Before long, we've convinced ourselves we're helping when all we're really doing is spreading someone else's story.

Step Seven asks a different question: Is what I'm about to say making recovery safer... or making it harder for the next alcoholic?

Think about the newcomer walking into their first meeting. They don't know who to trust. They don't know if they're going to make it. Then they hear us tearing another member apart in the parking lot or over coffee. What have we taught them? That meetings aren't safe. That sponsors gossip. That if they admit something embarrassing, they'll become the next conversation. Then we wonder why nobody asks us for help.

Somewhere along the way, we forgot what it felt like to walk through those doors scared to death. We forgot what it was like to need help, to confess something we thought we'd take to the grave, and to pray that someone would keep it there.

Recovery isn't a place to impress people. It's a place to protect people.

Every word we speak is either building someone's confidence in this program or tearing it down. We can become the reason someone asks for help—or the reason they never do. Let's never forget where we came from.

If a newcomer heard every conversation I had after the meeting, would they feel safer asking me for help—or less likely to?
07-10.title: July 10 – Did I Say That?

07-11.body:
"We humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings."

One of the hardest character defects to recognize is our need to control everything around us. We tell ourselves we're just being responsible. We're planners. We like things done the right way. But underneath all that is often a simple fear: If I don't stay in control, everything will fall apart.

For a lot of us, that's how we lived before recovery. We manipulated situations, managed people, rehearsed conversations, and tried to stay three steps ahead of every problem. Even then, life still managed to surprise us.

Step Seven slowly loosens our grip. Instead of trying to force outcomes—or "helping God" get the outcome we already picked—we begin trusting Him with the results. We still do the next right thing, but we stop believing the whole world depends on us. We discover there's a big difference between taking responsibility and trying to play God.

White-knuckling isn't just for alcohol. We can white-knuckle life, too.

The strange thing is, the tighter we hold on, the more anxious we become. The more we trust God, the freer we become. Turns out, God never asked us to manage the outcome—only our willingness. That's one of the quiet miracles of recovery. We don't have to control everything to have peace. We just have to stay willing, stay useful, and let God be God.

What outcome are you trying so hard to control that you may be leaving no room for God to work?
07-11.title: July 11 – White Knuckles

07-12.body:
"Self-righteous anger can be very enjoyable. In fact, it can give us a feeling of sinful satisfaction." — Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, Step Ten

You can spend a lot of money and come away with a diagnosis that sounds like Persistent Authority-Related Oppositional Defiance with Maladaptive Resistance to Corrective Feedback Syndrome.

Good Lord!

Around here, we usually call it something a whole lot cheaper.

Pride.

Pride doesn't listen because it already knows. Pride shuts out valuable suggestions as criticism. It debates others'wisdom as a personal attack. It makes us argue with our sponsor, the meeting, our spouse, our Higher Power, and eventually reality itself.

The illness of alcoholism loves pride because pride shuts every door. Pretty soon it's just us and the bottle. And for an alcoholic, the bottle always seems to agree with everything we think.

Recovery starts when we stop trying to win every argument and become willing to hear something we don't already know. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself. It's finally admitting that maybe—just maybe—we don't have all the answers.

Am I making this whole thing more complicated than it needs to be?
07-12.title: July 12 – It's Just Pride

07-13.body:
There are all kinds of scoreboards in life. Money. Careers. Houses. Cars. Recognition. Success. The trouble starts when we carry that same scoreboard into our recovery.

How many sponsees do they have? How many years sober? Why do people always go to them? Why did they ask him to speak instead of me? Why does she seem to have it all together while I'm still struggling?

Pride wants us to believe recovery is a competition. We compare our recovery, our knowledge, our service work, and even our suffering. If we're ahead, we quietly pat ourselves on the back. If we're behind, we either get discouraged or start looking for flaws in the other person just to even the score.

Humility reminds us that God never asked us to be better than the next alcoholic. He simply asked us to stay close to Him and help the next person.

The miracle of Alcoholics Anonymous isn't that one person shines brighter than another. It's that broken people help broken people. Every person who stays sober is proof that this thing works. Their victory doesn't take anything away from ours—it reminds us that miracles are still happening.

Humility doesn't ask, "Where do I rank?" It asks, "What can I learn?" Sometimes the person God uses to teach us isn't the old-timer with forty years of sobriety. Sometimes it's the trembling newcomer who just walked through the doors and reminds us exactly why we came.

Can I learn something from someone who just walked through the doors?
07-13.title: July 13 – Keeping Score

07-14.body:
One of the sneakiest forms of pride isn't talking all the time—it's quietly deciding we've already heard everything worth hearing.

After a few years sober, it's easy to sit in a meeting thinking, "Yeah, yeah... I've heard this one before. I know this reading. I know what they're going to say." The funny thing is, the moment we decide we already know it all, we stop listening. We may still be sitting in the chair, but our mind has already left the room.

I've heard people with thirty years sober say something that changed my life. I've also heard someone who just walked through the doors say something that hit me right between the eyes. God has never seemed too concerned about using the person with the longest sobriety date. He just uses whoever is willing.

Pride says, "I've got something to teach everyone else."

Humility says, "I wonder what I can learn today."

The Big Book tells us we have a daily reprieve based on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. Yesterday's insight doesn't keep me sober today. That's why I still need meetings, still need sponsorship, and still need to listen like my life depends on it—because it does.

Can I learn something today from the person I least expect to learn from?
07-14.title: July 14 – Still Taking Notes

07-15.body:
Dr. Bob kept this prayer on a plaque sitting on his desk. We doubt that was because he had already mastered humility. More likely, he needed to be reminded of it every single day, just like we do. Listen to how he describes humility: "Perpetual quietness of heart. It is to have no trouble. It is never to be fretted or vexed, irritable or sore; to wonder at nothing that is done to me, to feel nothing done against me. It is to be at rest when nobody praises me, and when I am blamed or despised..." That's a pretty high bar, isn't it?Now here's the question we have to ask ourselves. If those things aren't true for us today, what's getting in the way? Usually, it isn't our circumstances. It's our pride. Pride tells us we deserve better treatment. Pride wants recognition. Pride wants people to understand our side of the story. Pride keeps score. Pride takes things personally. Pride gets offended because it believes life should go according to our plan.Humility doesn't mean people will always treat us fairly. It means our peace no longer depends on whether they do. That's why this prayer is so powerful. It doesn't ask us to change other people. It asks God to change us. Maybe that's why Dr. Bob kept it where he could see it every day. It wasn't just a beautiful thought to admire. It was a daily reminder that if we lose our peace, become easily offended, or constantly need approval, we probably don't have a circumstance problem—we have a humility problem.Which line of Dr. Bob's Humility Prayer reveals the biggest humility problem in our lives today?
