Which line of Dr. Bob's Humility Prayer reveals the biggest humility problem in our lives today?
07-15.title: July 15 — Humility

07-16.body:
When we hear the word lust, most of us immediately think about sex. That's certainly part of it, but for many alcoholics, lust goes much deeper. It's our mental obsession that just found a new toy.

Before recovery, that toy was alcohol. We couldn't stop thinking about it. We planned around it. We justified it. We chased it, believing it would finally make us feel okay.

Then we got sober.

But if we're not careful, our minds simply find something else to obsess over. Maybe it's money. Maybe it's a new truck. Maybe it's Facebook Marketplace. Maybe it's a relationship, a promotion, golf clubs, a boat, food, respect, politics, or having everyone agree with us. The object changes, but the obsession stays the same.

How many of us have spent weeks researching something, watching YouTube videos, checking prices, and convincing ourselves, "If I can just get this, everything will be different." Then we finally get it... and before long we're already looking for the next thing. Sound familiar?

The problem was never just alcohol. The problem was a mind that always wanted one more thing. Recovery isn't about learning to chase better toys. It's about learning to be content with what God has already given us. That's a freedom no purchase, promotion, relationship, or hobby could ever give us.

What "new toy" has my mental obsession been chasing instead of finding contentment in God today?
07-16.title: July 16 — Lust

07-17.body:
One of the quietest forms of lust isn't always sexual. Sometimes it's the belief that if I could just find the right person, I'd finally be okay.

Recovery doesn't tell us relationships are bad. It reminds us that people make terrible Higher Powers.

When we expect another person to fix our loneliness, give us purpose, or complete us, we place a burden on them they were never meant to carry. Before long we're disappointed, they're overwhelmed, and resentment begins to grow.

The Big Book doesn't promise that another relationship will fill the hole inside us. It points us toward a relationship with God that changes us from the inside out. Healthy relationships become a gift instead of a rescue mission.

Ironically, the more we stop looking for someone to save us, the more capable we become of loving another person well.

Am I looking for a partner, or am I looking for a savior?
07-17.title: July 17 — Relationship Status

07-18.body:
Imagine if, just for today, we could get a handle on our pride and lust. Not get rid of them completely. Not become saints by lunchtime. Just turn them down a few percentage points.

Pride says, “I don’t need help from you.” Lust says, “I need this, that, or the other thing to feel complete.” One pushes people away, while the other keeps us reaching for something to fill the hole.

But what happens if we point both toward God?

Maybe pride becomes less about standing alone and more about realizing we are part of something bigger. Maybe we can stop fighting everything and trust that God has us where we're supposed to be. And maybe lust—that constant desire for more—can be redirected too. We can want more peace. More usefulness. More connection.

And how do we get more of that?

Maybe by becoming more service-minded in all our affairs. By asking where we can help instead of what we can get. By getting out of ourselves and into the lives of the people around us.

We don't have to conquer pride and lust today. Maybe we just need to turn them down a little and redirect our attention toward something greater than ourselves.

What would my day look like if I turned down pride and lust by just a small percentage?
07-18.title: July 18 — The Redirect

07-19.body:
"If you want esteem, you have to do esteem-building things." — Heard in the rooms

By the time we've worked through our Fourth and Fifth Steps, one thing usually becomes obvious: somewhere along the way, our self-esteem disappeared. The fearful life we lived while drinking slowly chipped away at it. In its place grew self-centeredness. We either thought we were better than everyone else, or so far beneath everyone that we didn't even belong. Either way, we ended up isolated.

The program offers us another way to live. Instead of trying to feel better first, we're encouraged to act differently. We shake hands and introduce ourselves at meetings—something we rarely did at the bar. We share honestly about our problem with alcohol—something we would have hidden at all costs. We exchange phone numbers and actually use them, staying connected with people who understand exactly where we've been. Little by little, these simple actions begin rebuilding something we thought was gone.

Our esteem doesn't return because we wish for it. It returns because we practice living differently. AA becomes a small playground where we learn a new way of living. Before long, those same habits begin showing up in the big playground of life. Job interviews become a little easier. Relationships aren't as complicated as they used to be. Family seems to enjoy our new attitude. We stop trying to prove our worth and quietly begin living it.

What is one esteem-building thing you've done in recovery that eventually started showing up in the big playground of life?
07-19.title: July 19 — Esteem

07-20.body:
One of the greatest esteem-building things we've discovered in recovery is learning to hold back gossip and criticism. In AA we hear a lot of sensitive information. We learn about people's lives, their fears, their mistakes, and the things they've never told another soul. If empathy hasn't taken root in us yet, those stories can sound like fuel for tearing someone down.

But after a while in the program, something changes. We begin to realize that the person sharing may have never had a safe place to tell the truth. For some people, that one hour in an AA meeting may be the only place in their entire week where they can finally be honest. They trust us with something precious.

That leaves us with a choice. We can use what we've heard to make ourselves feel a little bigger by making someone else look smaller. Or we can quietly protect their confidence. Nobody applauds us for it. There isn't a trophy waiting. But something inside us strengthens.

Keeping another person's confidence gives us a quiet reward. It builds the kind of self-respect that gossip never could. We become known as people who are safe to talk to. People don't have to wonder what we'll say once they leave the room. They know they'll be met with understanding instead of judgment.

That kind of quiet integrity is one more esteem-building thing. And before long, we find ourselves becoming the kind of friend we always hoped we would have.

Has someone in recovery ever made you feel safe enough to tell the truth? What did they do that made the difference?
07-20.title: June 20 — Quiet Reward

07-21.body:
A guy at a meeting shared something he had heard from a preacher, and it stuck with me.

"What's the most common word people use for God? Jesus? Nope. Buddha? Nope. Higher Power? Nope. The word we hear most often is something. Something changed. Something made this happen. Something did this."

After thinking about that, I realized he had a point. Not everyone comes into AA ready to believe in a God of their own understanding. And that's okay. But it's pretty rare to find someone who doesn't believe in something. Something is keeping me sober. Something brought me to these meetings. Something is putting the right people in my path. Something changed in me. Something is different this time.

For a lot of us, that's where it starts... and maybe that's where it stays. And that's okay. If something is helping you stay sober today, keep following it.

When was the first time you thought, "Something's different this time"?
07-21.title: July 21 – Something

07-22.body:
We're slowly gaining our self-esteem back. Paired with this God-centered way of living, we begin feeling something that has been missing for a long time: confidence. We can actually feel God putting us back on the path of goodness, and we know something bigger than us is working in our lives.

That confidence starts showing up in simple ways. We feel confident that we have the tools to not drink today. We feel confident that we're probably not going to create any new major trouble for ourselves. We feel connected to the world again instead of hiding from it. The isolation begins to fade, replaced by a growing sense that we're right where we're supposed to be.

Our past has been neatly compartmentalized in the previous steps. We're starting to think about the next steps and what they entail. With our Higher Power right beside us, we're gearing up to go and face our wrongs.

Can you feel it?
07-22.title: July 22 — Gearing Up

07-23.body:
"I pray that You now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to You and my fellows."

Alcoholics can be sensitive people. Sometimes alcoholism is called a disease of perception. We've heard people say we have a magic magnifying mind. We can take just about anything and blow it completely out of proportion. Not getting a job. Wondering what people think of us. Feeling left out. Being criticized. And somehow we almost never magnify the good stuff.

Our spiritual illness loves to convince us that we're disconnected, rejected, alone, or somehow not enough. The scary part is how fast it can happen. One thought can change the direction of our whole day.

If we're truly powerless over not getting the job, over someone else's half-cocked opinion of us, or over whatever story our minds are telling us today, maybe we don't have to fight it alone. We can stop, admit that we're powerless over where our thinking is taking us, and humbly ask God to remove the shortcomings that are standing between us and being useful.

Sometimes the situation doesn't change. But our perception of it does. And a lot of times, that's the miracle we needed all along.

What's something your mind tends to magnify that you could turn over today?
07-23.title: July 23 – Shortcomings

07-24.body:
"I pray that You now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to You and my fellows."

Self-pity can be sneaky. It doesn't always sound like, "Poor me." Sometimes it sounds like, "Does this always happen to me?" "Nobody understands." "I just can't catch a break." Before long, we've built a whole story in our minds, and we believe every word of it.

Our alcoholism can take one disappointment and distort it into proof that nothing ever goes our way. Before we know it, we're convinced we're alone, forgotten, or somehow getting a worse deal than everyone else. That's when it's time to stop, ask God to remove our shortcomings, and let Him help us see the situation a little differently.

The problem isn't always the situation. A lot of times it's the way we're seeing it.

When we catch ourselves headed down that road, maybe we don't have to argue with our thinking. We can simply stop, admit that we're powerless over where our minds are taking us, and ask God to remove the shortcomings that are keeping us stuck. Then we can look for one thing to be grateful for, one person we can help, or one small way to be useful today.

It's amazing how quickly our perspective can change when we stop asking, "Why is this happening to me?" and start asking, "How can I be useful today?"

What's one situation where self-pity may be affecting the way you're seeing things today?
07-24.title: July 24 – Self-Pity

07-25.body:
"I pray that You now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to You and my fellows."

Resentment has a way of freezing us in time. We replay what happened, what was said, what should have happened, and what we'll say if we ever get the chance. The event may have lasted five minutes, but our minds can relive it for years.

Our alcoholism can take a real hurt and distort it into proof that people can't be trusted, that the world isn't fair, or that we'll always be the one who gets hurt. Before long, we're not seeing people as they are—we're seeing them through the lens of our resentment.

If we're powerless over where our resentment is taking us, maybe we don't have to fight it alone. We can stop, admit that we're powerless over the situation, and ask God to remove our shortcomings about it. Maybe the other person never changes. Maybe what happened can't be undone. But our perception can change, and that's often where our freedom begins.

As we let go of the resentment, we slowly become willing to trust again—not because people are perfect, but because we trust that God is helping us see things a little more clearly than we could on our own.

Is there a resentment you've been carrying that you could ask God to help you see differently today?
07-25.title: July 25 – Forgiveness

07-26.body:
"Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions." — Seventh Tradition

"Most alcoholics owe money."

Isn't that fitting?

Being a practicing alcoholic is almost like having a second job. We go to work all day earning a paycheck, then spend our evenings figuring out how to drink it away. Along the way, bills pile up, promises get broken, and the people who count on us get whatever is left over. We neglect family responsibilities, skimp on what we could have provided for our children, and become experts at keeping the lights on without actually paying the electric bill. Our stories get longer, our excuses get better, and our debt gets bigger.

Then we land here.

In a program built on rigorous honesty, we're introduced to the Seventh Tradition and asked to become self-supporting through our own contributions. It can feel like a strange request. After all, our first thought when the basket comes around might be, I can't afford it. Someone else will take care of it.

Maybe that's true. Maybe the meeting will be just fine without our dollar.

But the real exercise isn't about the dollar.

It's about trusting God enough to do the next right thing. Sometimes that means putting a dollar in the basket even when our instincts tell us to hold onto it. We stop acting out of fear and start acting out of faith, believing that if we're trying to do God's will, He'll take care of the rest. More often than not, He has a way of giving back far more than we ever imagined.

Looking back, what was your relationship with money really like? Was it something you managed... or something that managed you?
07-26.title: July 26 – The Unhealthiest Relationship

07-27.body:
"Every A.A. group ought to be fully self-supporting, declining outside contributions." — Seventh Tradition

It's easy to think of money as our money.

My paycheck. My savings. My bills.

But what if we've been looking at it backward all along?

Everything we have came from God anyway. We're simply trusted to manage it for a little while. Money isn't the reward—it's a tool. How would you have met that cashier at the grocery store if money hadn't brought you there? How would you have gotten to know the waitress who always asks how you're doing? How would you have met your coworkers if no one ever had to earn a paycheck? How many conversations, friendships, and opportunities to show kindness only happened because money brought your paths together? Maybe money isn't the point at all. Maybe it's just one of the many ways God weaves people's lives together.

In God's economy, the real currency has always been kindness.

When you think about it, what person in your life did money unexpectedly introduce you to?
07-27.title: July 27 – It's All God's Money

07-28.body:
"Helping God's kids do the things that God's kids needed to do." — Chuck C., A New Pair of Glasses

As practicing alcoholics, many of us became expert takers. We took more than we gave. We took people's time, their trust, their peace of mind, and often their money. The funny thing is, we thought we were getting away with something, but takers are usually the real losers in life.

Then sobriety begins to change our perspective.

Maybe we go back to work. A taker's mentality says, "These people have me trapped here for eight hours. I can't wait to get out of this place." But a giver's mentality asks a different question: "God put me here today. How can I help God's kids the best I can?" The job hasn't changed. The people haven't changed. The paycheck hasn't changed. Only our perspective has.

When we stop asking, "What can I get?" and start asking, "Who can I help?" we begin to discover that helping God's kids was never about the job. It was about becoming the kind of person God can trust wherever He puts us.

When you walk into work—or anywhere else—are you thinking about what you can get from the day, or what you can give to it?
07-28.title: July 28 – Helping God's Kids

07-29.body:
"Money is a terrible master but a wonderful servant."We've all served bad masters before.We've served anger and watched it steal our peace. We've served pride and found ourselves alone. We've served lust and carried the regret that followed. We've served fear and let it make our decisions for us. We know what it's like to give something power over our lives.So here's a question.Has money ever quietly taken a seat at the table?Have we ever lost sleep over it, chased it, feared losing it, or let it decide what really mattered? There's nothing wrong with money. We need it. We earn it. We use it every day. But maybe it's worth asking whether we're using money... or whether money is using us.Recovery doesn't ask us to sit around waiting for someone else to take care of us. It asks us to become self-supporting—to do the footwork, earn an honest living, and trust God with the results.Has anything besides alcohol ever quietly become your master without you realizing it?

"Money is a terrible master but a wonderful servant."

We've all served bad masters before.

We've served anger and watched it steal our peace. We've served pride and found ourselves alone. We've served lust and carried the regret that followed. We've served fear and let it make our decisions for us. We know what it's like to give something power over our lives.

So here's a question.

Has money ever quietly taken a seat at the table?

Have we ever lost sleep over it, chased it, feared losing it, or let it decide what really mattered? There's nothing wrong with money. We need it. We earn it. We use it every day. But maybe it's worth asking whether we're using money... or whether money is using us.

Recovery doesn't ask us to sit around waiting for someone else to take care of us. It asks us to become self-supporting—to do the footwork, earn an honest living, and trust God with the results.

Has anything besides alcohol ever quietly become your master without you realizing it?
07-29.title: July 29 – The Almighty Dollar

07-30.body:
"As active alcoholics we were always looking for a handout in one way or another."

— The Twelve Traditions Illustrated, p. 14

A lot of us were always looking for a handout instead of a hand up. A solid drinking habit takes money, and once alcohol became our master, we funneled everything we had into it. There wasn't much left for groceries, rent, or gas, let alone generosity. We got used to showing up empty-handed, expecting someone else to pick up the tab. We borrowed money we had no intention of paying back. We bummed cigarettes. We expected rides, meals, and favors. Somewhere along the way, many of us quietly began believing the world owed us something simply because life had been hard.

The strange thing is that this never brought us closer to people. It pushed them away. Friends grew tired. Family became cautious. Invitations became fewer. Trust slowly disappeared. The more we expected others to carry us, the more disconnected we became. Alcohol had convinced us we were victims, but it also kept us from becoming contributors.

Recovery teaches us a different way to live. Today we ask, "How can I be useful?" We don't want to show up empty-handed anymore. Sometimes that means bringing coffee to a meeting. Sometimes it means helping stack chairs. Sometimes it simply means being a listening ear. We begin to experience the quiet dignity that comes from carrying our own weight and looking for ways to lighten someone else's.

That doesn't mean we never need help. We absolutely do. AA was built on one alcoholic reaching out a hand to another. The difference is that we're no longer demanding the world parent us. We accept help with gratitude, not entitlement. Then, as soon as we're able, we look for someone else to help. That's how the circle keeps moving.

Can you remember a time when someone in recovery gave you a hand up instead of just a handout? How did that change the way you think about helping others today?
07-30.title: July 30 – Can You Spare Some Change?

07-31.body:
"Self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles."
— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 62Alcoholism is sometimes called a disease of perception. Around the rooms you'll hear people talk about having a magic magnifying mind. Others simply call it what it is: self-centeredness. Our disease has a way of turning reality into disappointment without us even realizing it. We don't get the job, we're losers. We get laid off, we weren't good enough. A relationship ends, and we're unlovable. The facts rarely matter as much as the story our minds create.The truth is, our egos love a red carpet. We want to feel noticed, appreciated, and important. When life doesn't roll one out for us, our disease whispers that we don't belong. We can end up angry, hurt, or drowning in self-pity over something that may not even be true.That's our cue. We can keep wrestling with those thoughts, or we can ask God, with humility, to remove the shortcomings behind them. The longer we wait, the more our disappointment turns into resentment, anger, sarcasm, coldness, or self-pity. Before long, the people around us begin paying the price for a battle that was never really about them. It's much easier to surrender a shortcoming than it is to clean up the damage it leaves behind.Can you think of a time when you mistook disappointment for rejection? What happened once you saw the situation more clearly?

"Self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles."
— Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 62

Alcoholism is sometimes called a disease of perception. Around the rooms you'll hear people talk about having a magic magnifying mind. Others simply call it what it is: self-centeredness. Our disease has a way of turning reality into disappointment without us even realizing it. We don't get the job, we're losers. We get laid off, we weren't good enough. A relationship ends, and we're unlovable. The facts rarely matter as much as the story our minds create.

The truth is, our egos love a red carpet. We want to feel noticed, appreciated, and important. When life doesn't roll one out for us, our disease whispers that we don't belong. We can end up angry, hurt, or drowning in self-pity over something that may not even be true.

That's our cue. We can keep wrestling with those thoughts, or we can ask God, with humility, to remove the shortcomings behind them. The longer we wait, the more our disappointment turns into resentment, anger, sarcasm, coldness, or self-pity. Before long, the people around us begin paying the price for a battle that was never really about them. It's much easier to surrender a shortcoming than it is to clean up the damage it leaves behind.

Can you think of a time when you mistook disappointment for rejection? What happened once you saw the situation more clearly?
07-31.title: July 31 – The Red Carpet

08-01.body:
Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all.

The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution are called the Bill of Rights. Over the years, more amendments were added. Not because the Constitution was a failure, but because it needed to grow, improve, and correct its course. Amendments made it stronger.

Step Eight is where we begin writing the amendments to our own lives.

We start making a list of the places where our actions, words, and attitudes caused harm. We're simply becoming honest about the places where our good nature was taken off course by our drinking life. We aren't rewriting history, and we aren't beating ourselves up. We're simply preparing to make the changes that will help us live differently than we used to.

There is no need to rush this step. In fact, we ought not. But we don't sit on it procrastinating either. We simply take the time to be thorough because our sobriety depends on it. Every resentment we clear away, every relationship we become willing to repair, and every wrong we become willing to face removes another obstacle between us and God. Step Eight is careful preparation for the action that follows.

What amends to your life have you become willing to make?
08-01.title: August 1 – Amendments

08-02.body:
Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all.

When we hear the word harmed, most of us immediately think of physical injury. But harm is much broader than that. To harm someone is to cause damage to their well-being. It can be physical, emotional, mental, financial, or even damage to their reputation. Sometimes the bruise heals while the words we spoke are remembered for years. Sometimes the money is paid back while the trust never quite returns. Harm is anything we did that left another person carrying a burden they didn't deserve.

This step asks us to be honest enough to see our part.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: the people we harmed usually didn't get to vote on whether they were harmed. We don't get to say, "I didn't mean it," or, "They should be over it by now." The wound belongs to the person who was cut. Our intentions may explain our actions, but they don't erase their consequences.

If someone still carries pain because we shattered their trust in us, then that belongs on our list. Not because we're bad people, but because good people living a sick drinking life often leave behind damage they never intended to cause. Step Eight is where we become willing to stop arguing with the past and start making it right.

Where have you created harm lately and what are you going to do about it?
08-02.title: August 2 – Harmed

08-03.body:
Step Eight asks us to make a list of all the people we have harmed and become willing to make amends to them all. At first, that can feel overwhelming. It's a little like going to the grocery store when you're starving. Without a list, everything looks important. We throw things into the cart that we don't need, forget the things we do need, and end up spending far more than we planned.

Recovery can be like that too. As we come out of the darkness of alcoholism, we're finally awake. For the first time in years, we begin to see the wreckage we've left behind. Our minds start making a list before we ever put pen to paper, and before long, our mental list feels impossible. That's exactly why we don't rely on our emotions alone. We work with a sponsor to bring honesty, balance, and perspective to the process. They help us separate real harms from imagined ones, healthy responsibility from unhealthy guilt, and keep us focused on making an honest list instead of an endless one.

The goal isn't to create the biggest list—it's to create an honest one. Organized, realistic, and guided by truth instead of emotion. God isn't asking us to carry the weight of our entire past in one day. He's simply asking us to become willing and take the next right step.

Have you ever made your Step Eight list bigger than it really needed to be, or smaller than it should have been? How did another person help you see it more clearly?
08-03.title: August 3 – The List

08-04.body:
The phrase "faith the size of a mustard seed" has been around for thousands of years. The mustard seed was used because it's incredibly small, yet it grows into something far larger than anyone would expect. The lesson isn't about having big faith. It's about discovering that even the smallest amount can grow if we're willing to use it.

Most of us didn't come into recovery overflowing with belief. We came in with doubts, fear, resentment, and maybe just enough hope to walk through the door. That tiny bit of willingness was enough to get started.

Recovery has never required perfect faith. It only asks us to be open enough to take the next right step. So many of us worry about staying sober for the rest of our lives, but we don't need that kind of faith today. We only need enough faith to get through today's events and stay sober, just for today. A mustard seed is plenty.

Looking back, what was your very first mustard seed of faith in recovery?
08-04.title: August 4 – Extra Mustard

08-05.body:
When we begin making amends, it's easy to think we need the perfect speech. The Big Book cautions us against approaching people on a spiritual basis. After years of drunken behavior, showing up acting like a holy roller may only make matters worse. We're not there to preach or even to be forgiven.

We're there to clean up our side of the street.

The spirit of forgiveness begins with us. We've forgiven ourselves enough to honestly admit our wrongs and do our best not to repeat them. We're willing to listen without excuses, arguments, or debate. We show up, stand tall, and stay sober. We put in the footwork and leave the outcome to God.

Our responsibility isn't to earn forgiveness. It's to become the kind of person willing to make things right. In the end, our actions speak louder than any words we could ever say.

Which is harder for you: admitting your wrongs, listening without defending yourself, or letting go of the outcome?
08-05.title: August 5 – The Spirit of Forgiveness

08-06.body:
Alcoholics do some unbelievable things. We've left our families, walked away from jobs, started fights over resentments we invented out of thin air, skipped out on bills, become homeless, and somehow convinced ourselves that was just life. Looking back, it's hard to believe the things we accepted while we were drinking. To say our behavior was shocking is an understatement.

We didn't just leave behind wreckage. We left behind stories. Stories that started with, "Did you hear?" or "Can you believe what they did this time?" While we were drinking, we were held hostage by the endings to those stories, unable to imagine our lives could become anything different.

But Step Eight gives us the chance to rewrite the ending. Now the story simply becomes, "They stopped drinking and turned out to be a really wonderful, helpful person."

The truth is, most people will never hear that ending, and that's okay. What other people think of us is no longer our business. We don't make amends to repair our reputation or convince the world we've changed. We make amends because it's the next right thing to do. Every amend, every act of honesty, and every sober day changes our story. Even if we're the only ones who ever know the complete ending, we'll know we did everything we could to make it a good one. And that's more than enough.
08-06.title: August 6 – Changing the Story

08-07.body:
Alcoholics know resentment well. It can take us back out on a drinking spree faster than just about anything, and most of us have proved that to ourselves more than once.

But resentment isn't just something we carry. We created it too.

Our drinking left people angry, hurt, disappointed, and distrustful. We made promises we didn't keep. We borrowed money we never repaid. We disappeared when people needed us most. While we've spent years nursing our own resentments, others have been carrying resentment toward us.

Step Eight and Nine give us the chance to hand some of that burden back. When we honestly admit what we've done, make restitution where we can, and listen without excuses, arguments, or debate, we give another human being the opportunity to finally say what they've been carrying for years. Sometimes it isn't pretty. Sometimes it hurts to hear. But that's part of cleaning up our side of the street.

Whether they're able to let go of their resentment is up to them. Our job is simply to give them the opportunity. We put in the footwork, return what we owe, listen to the hurt we caused, and do our best to make things right. That's how character is built. Not by talking about change, but by living it.

Have you ever realized someone had every right to resent you? What did making that amend teach you?
08-07.title: August 7 – Resentment

10-01.body:
OCTOBER 1 — Spiritual Maintenance Required

“We have a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 85

Some days we can forget recovery isn’t a trophy we won — it’s a car that still needs gas. We can coast for a while, thinking we’ve got this figured out, then wonder why the whole thing starts sputtering. What we usually find is that we stopped doing the little stuff: the prayers that felt dumb but worked, the calls we didn’t want to make, the quiet check-ins that keep us right-sized.

Maintenance isn’t glamorous. It’s the oil change nobody thanks us for. But that’s where the peace hides — in the work nobody sees. Humility isn’t a posture; it’s knowing the engine only runs because we’re not the ones who built it.

Hasn't the trouble usually started when we confuse progress with graduation — like we’ve somehow earned a break from what keeps us alive?

What does daily maintenance look like to you?
10-01.title: October 1 – Spiritual Maintenance Required

10-02.body:
OCTOBER 2 — Check Engine Light

“We continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear.” — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 84

It’s strange how fast we can forget we’re not bulletproof anymore. Things start going well, and we quietly slip away from the stuff that got us there. Then that old restlessness shows up — the kind that used to send us to the bar or the phone or the fridge. These days it can just send us deeper into ourselves, which somehow feels worse.

Step work taught us to watch for the warning lights — irritation, judgment, exhaustion — the signs that the spiritual oil is running low. When the “check engine” light comes on, we don’t need a mechanic; we need honesty. We can pull over, pop the hood, and tell the truth about what’s really going on inside.

The danger isn’t when the light comes on — it’s when we decide to ignore it.

What’s flashing on our dashboard today that we’ve been pretending not to see?
10-02.title: October 2 – Check Engine Light

10-03.body:
October 3 – The Rewind Button

“We can only change our experience in reality.” — Chuck C., A New Pair of Glasses

Awareness used to feel like punishment. Every time I saw myself clearly, I’d flinch — pride pretending to be purpose, motives dressed up like miracles. But the truth doesn’t hurt — it humbles. Awareness isn’t about shame; it’s about getting another shot at honesty. It’s the rewind button for my soul — not to edit the movie with excuses, just to notice where I started directing again. When I can look back without guilt, I learn instead of hide. What part of my story might look different today if I watched it with humility instead of shame?
10-03.title: October 3 – The Rewind Button

10-04.body:
October 4 – Volume Down
“Don’t let your ego write checks your body can’t cash.” — Top Gun (1986)

Humility doesn’t announce itself. It just turns the volume down on all the noise in my head.

For years, I thought humility meant humiliation — like I had to keep guilt, shame, and remorse front and center to prove I’d changed. But it’s not that. It’s not about thinking less of myself. It’s about thinking about myself less. There’s a difference.

Humility is the quiet moment when I realize I don’t need to be right, admired, or even noticed. It’s freedom from that constant “but what about me?” When I stop auditioning for the world, I can actually show up and be useful. And half the time, that’s the miracle — not that I did something amazing, but that I didn’t make everything about me.

Today, try to do one helpful thing that nobody knows about — and tell no one. Let it stay a little secret between you and God.
10-04.title: October 4 – Volume Down

10-05.body:
October 5 – Say It, Don’t Spray It
“You can’t handle the truth!” — A Few Good Men (1992)

Restraint is brutal when our mouths want to run. We can still confuse volume with power, sarcasm with honesty, and “telling it like it is” with spiritual growth. Step work teaches us something different: truth without love is just another form of harm — and restraint is the quiet version of courage.

We don’t have to win the argument; we just have to stay right-sized in it. The disease in us still wants to hit send, slam the door, or give a speech nobody asked for. But we’ve learned something simple: silence has never made our lives worse. When we can hold the truth long enough to speak it kindly — or not at all — that’s the real power.

When was the last time we didn’t say what we were thinking — and it actually made things better?
10-05.title: October 5 – Say It Don’t Spray It

10-06.body:
October 6 – Clean-Up Aisle 10
“I get knocked down, but I get up again.” — Chumbawamba

Step 10 isn’t about being perfect — it’s about staying honest enough to clean up after ourselves. When we skip that, life starts to feel sticky. We smear our ego all over the new life we have been trying to build for ourselves. A little self-righteousness here, some silent judgment there. The funny thing is, our defects don’t scream anymore — they whisper. We can look calm on the outside and still be running the show on the inside.

The self-reflection of the program has a way of asking, “How are we really doing with this whole new way of life?” and hands us the mop. Most days, humility is simply admitting we left a mess and cleaning it up without needing a round of applause. Discipline is quiet — like a janitor after hours, just doing the work nobody sees.

What’s something we noticed about ourselves recently that needed a little clean-up — even if nobody else saw it?
10-06.title: October 6 – Clean-Up Aisle 10

10-07.body:
October 7 – Pocket Inventory
“I still haven’t found what I’m looking for.” — U2

I used to think “taking inventory” meant locking myself in a mental warehouse with a clipboard, counting defects like expired cans of guilt. But it’s simpler than that. These days, I just carry a small version in my back pocket. When I’m off, I can usually feel it — a little tension, a little ego. So I pause and ask: Was I selfish? Dishonest? Mean?

If the answer’s yes, I don’t have to spiral into self-loathing. I just call it what it is, clean it up if I can, and move on. Secrets rot fast; honesty travels light.

What’s one thing you caught yourself doing recently that made you go, “Yeah… that’s probably something I should clean up”?
10-07.title: October 7 – Pocket Inventory

10-08.body:
October 8 – Sweep, Don’t Shovel

“Every time a person imposes his instincts unreasonably upon others, unhappiness follows. Demands for too much attention, protection, and love can invite only domination or revulsion. When an individual’s desire for prestige becomes uncontrollable, other people suffer and often revolt.”-As Bill Sees It – #282 “Instincts Run Wild”

Step 10 is where I find out my ego still does push-ups in the dark. It doesn’t kick down the door anymore — it sneaks in wearing a volunteer badge. One minute I’m helping someone, the next I’m quietly auditioning for sainthood. Good service work — real service work — is like the perfect crime: you get in, do your thing, and nobody even knows you were there. That’s the sweet spot.

Self-centeredness still flares up when I least expect it, especially when I think I’m doing something “good.” Step 10 gives me a flashlight and a broom. I don’t need to fix everything — I just need to notice where I tracked in a little ego and sweep it up before it starts to stink.

Where have you noticed your ego sneaking in lately — even when you were trying to do something good?
10-08.title: October 8 – Sweep, Don’t Shovel

10-09.body:
October 9 – The Echo in the Room
“Hello, hello, hello, how low?” — Nirvana

I still hear the echo of my old self bouncing around the room — the one who always had to be right, get the last word, and prove I wasn’t weak. Turns out, the quieter I get, the faster I grow. The echo fades when I stop feeding it.

I don’t have to slam doors or win arguments anymore. I just have to keep the floor clean between my ears. The disease still loves noise; humility whispers. Most days, the work is just learning to hear the difference.

Where do you still hear the old version of yourself getting loud, and what helps you quiet it down today?
10-09.title: October 9 – The Echo in the Room

10-10.body:
October 10 – Check-Up from the Neck-Up

“Check yourself before you wreck yourself.” — Ice Cube

Step 10 is the daily check-up from the neck-up — a little spiritual pit stop to see how the engine’s running. Not a guilt trip, just a quick, “Hey, how are you doing with this recovery thing today? There used to be a lot of bad habits going on, and those are hard to shed overnight, any sneak back in lately without you wanting them to?” The road’s rough, and nobody drives it perfect.

Some days I’m cruising; other days I’m leaking attitude all over the pavement. This check-up is pulling over long enough to patch the tire before it blows, tighten a few loose bolts, and get back out there. It’s not punishment — it’s just staying road-worthy, one honest look under the hood at a time.

Which one of your tires usually goes flat first — patience, honesty, or humility — and how does everyone else know before you do?
10-10.title: October 10 – Check-Up from the Neck-Up

10-11.body:
October 11 – Own Your Scene
“I’m not even supposed to be here today!” — Clerks (1994)

Accountability starts when I stop explaining and start cleaning up. It’s that part of recovery where I admit I made the mess and grab the mop before somebody else slips on it. My ego still wants to negotiate, blame, give excuses, justify, or quietly disappear.

But growth looks more like catching myself faster, apologizing sooner, and saying “my bad” without the legal defense. Half the time the most spiritual thing I do all day is admit I was wrong before someone else has to point it out. It’s not weakness — it’s spiritual maintenance. It keeps my side of the street clear enough to walk barefoot if I need to.

What’s the last mess you wanted to explain instead of clean up — and what happened when you finally owned it?
10-11.title: October 11 – Own Your Scene

10-12.body:
October 12 — Garbage Day
“If I don’t look at my mistakes, I start to think I don’t have any.” — Chuck C.

Most of my trouble doesn’t come from one big blow-up. It comes from the slow pileup — a quiet resentment I didn’t say out loud because I couldn’t see where I made a mistake, a truth I kind of rounded off, a feeling I told myself I’d deal with “later.” That stuff stacks up the same way trash does. At first it’s just a bag in the corner. Then it’s the whole kitchen. And one day I wake up wondering why my spirit feels cramped and sour.

God didn’t leave. I just stopped taking anything out.

There’s something oddly gentle about keeping a short spiritual memory. I don’t have to excavate my childhood or write a confession novel — I just have to notice what’s starting to stink and not pretend it’s furniture. A little honesty, a small cleanup, and the air changes again. That’s usually all it takes.

What’s one piece of emotional trash you’ve been stepping over lately instead of picking up?
10-12.title: October 12 — Garbage Day

10-13.body:
October 13 — Bad Reception
“Muddy water is best cleared by leaving it alone.” — Alan Watts

Whenever I start thinking I’m running the show again, the signal gets fuzzy. That calm I had doesn’t disappear — it just gets buried under the static in my head. It isn’t that God goes anywhere. It’s that I get loud.

Pride, control, and judgment crank up the noise until I’m arguing with life instead of listening to it. The channel never shuts off — I just forget how to tune in. Most days, all it takes to hear it again is a little less me and a little more quiet.

Humility isn’t humiliation. It’s not making myself small or swallowing shame. It’s just turning the volume down on the part of me that insists it already knows what’s going on. When that voice softens, something truer gets a chance to speak — guidance, perspective, maybe God. I don’t lose anything by lowering the volume. I finally get to hear what I’ve been missing.

What’s been making the most static in your head lately — and what helps you turn it down?
10-13.title: October 13 — Bad Reception

10-14.body:
October 14 — Honesty

“When we were wrong we probably admitted it.” — a guy mis-reading Step Ten in a meeting

I make this thing way harder than it has to be sometimes. I was sitting in a meeting when a guy was reading the Steps and he got to Step Ten and said, “When we were wrong we probably admitted it.” I chuckled, because… yeah. That’s about how I live some days — halfway honest, halfway hiding, hoping it all just kind of works out.

Then life handed me a tiny pop quiz.

I found a watch sitting on a table that wasn’t mine. A nice one. And my alcoholic brain lit up like a slot machine: You need this. It would look great on you. Nobody’s gonna know. That voice has always been fast, loud, and convincing. But then there was that other voice — the quieter one I’ve learned to trust — saying, Hey, it’s not yours. Even if you never find the owner, it’s still not yours.

Because if I take it, now I have to wear it. And if I wear it, I have to worry about who might see me wearing it. And once I start worrying, there’s no room left for God — just me, fear, and myself. That’s what dishonesty really is for me: living in a little private world I have to keep defending.

So I took it to the office nearby and walked away.

Nothing dramatic happened. No angels sang. But I left with a clear head and a clean chest. That’s honesty — not just telling the truth out loud, but living it quietly when nobody’s watching. These days, I can buy my own watch if I want one. I don’t have to steal peace in small, sneaky ways anymore. Somebody out there was missing that watch. Maybe they’ll get it back, maybe they won’t. But I know this: it was never mine to take.

What’s a small moment — maybe something nobody else even saw — where you chose honesty instead of the old familiar shortcut?
10-14.title: October 14 — Honesty

10-15.body:
October 15 — Do They Even Know?

“What you deny or ignore, you delay.”

It took me about six years before I actually got real with my sponsor. I thought I had, but I was still editing myself — leaving out the parts that made me look small, scared, or uncomfortable. I told myself I was not wanting to waste their time, but really, I was protecting my image.

The truth is, I had this little ball of crazy I was guarding.

Somewhere inside me was a tight, twisted cluster of things I had never told anyone. I tried to keep it buried under Big Book quotes, clever one-liners, and pretending everything was fine while parts of my life were quietly not adding up. I could talk recovery all day long, but inside, things were still unsettled.

One day I finally stopped hiding it.

I sat down with my sponsor and let it all come out — childhood, past relationships, hating drinking while I was still doing it, my kids, the guilt, the fear. I did not try to make it sound spiritual. I just put it on the table.

And there it was, out in the open.
Yes, I struggle.
Yes, there are things I cannot figure out.
And pretending they are not there has not been working.

What came back was not judgment or a lecture.

It was, “Welcome to the club. You are officially human. Now that it is out, we can fill it with something different.”

That was the moment honesty stopped feeling like exposure and started feeling like relief.

Sponsorship does not work if I am still wearing a mask. My sponsor cannot help the version of me I am managing — only the person I actually am. And every time I hide something, denial quietly returns.

What’s one thing that might be holding you back from doing the thing you already know you need to do?
10-15.title: October 15 — Do They Even Know?

10-16.body:
October 16 — Static Days

“We continued to take personal inventory and when we were wrong promptly admitted it.” — Step Ten

Some days I wake up feeling like I am walking on a cloud. Other days I wake up and it is more like, Okay, I am not drinking today — that is the best I have. Then I look back at the spiritual days and start wondering what I did wrong, like I somehow broke the connection.

Maybe I did. Maybe I did not.

The truth is, I am a spiritual being having a human experience, and some days that human side is just very human. Tired. Moody. Foggy. That does not mean I am failing — it means I am alive.

This is where Step Ten lives.

Some days I wake up and feel off. Not bad. Not broken. Just moving through static. Nothing is especially wrong, but nothing feels clear either. I used to think that meant I had lost my connection. Now I see it as something else: this is what continuing feels like.

Most of my growth does not happen on the days when everything clicks. It happens on the days when I keep going anyway. When there is no emotional reward. No spiritual fireworks. Just the quiet choice to stay pointed in the same direction.

That is what the word continued really means — to extend farther in the same direction.

So on the days when self-pity, dishonesty, or self-seeking shows up without warning, I do not stop. I do not spiral. I keep moving. I try to use the training I have been given. I make the calls. I read the pages. I do the things I do not feel like doing.

And I go.

What helps you keep going on the days when you do not feel anything working?
10-16.title: October 16 — Static Days

10-17.body:
October 17 – Big Book Trivia
“Remember: the way you see others is often the way you still need to see yourself with love.” — Louise Hay, You Can Heal Your Life

There’s this guy at my morning meeting who used to make my skin crawl. Every share was like a lightning round of Big Book quotes, and I’d sit there thinking, Man, this dude doesn’t even get it. I’d cross my arms and silently play AA police, ready to write him up for missing the point.

Then I heard my sponsor’s voice in my head: “Maybe that’s how he learned to stay sober — he teaches the way he learns.” Boom. Pride check.

That’s the trick with Step Ten — ego doesn’t announce itself; it slides in through self-righteousness. I didn’t need to correct him. I just needed to admit I was the one off-center. Once I dropped the judgment, something weird happened — I started listening again. He didn’t change. I did.

How do you handle it when someone’s version of recovery rubs you the wrong way — can you let them have their way without making it mean yours is better?
10-17.title: October 17 — Big Book Trivia

10-18.body:
October 18 – Black Ink Days
“Gratitude should go forward, rather than backward. If you carry the message to still others, you will be making the best possible repayment for God’s grace to you.” — As Bill Sees It, p. 29

My inventory isn’t written in red ink every day — and thank God for that. Some days it’s black ink, the good kind, where I actually get to write down what went right. For the longest time I thought inventory was about digging through defects, trying to fix myself like a broken engine. But lately I’ve realized it’s also about gratitude — writing down the grace that showed up uninvited.

If I’m really powerless, then every sober day is proof that something bigger is still working in my life. I didn’t earn this. I just get to carry it forward. When I hear a guy say he’s got ten years, I don’t think, wow, he’s strong. I think, wow, God gave him ten years of grace, one day at a time.

That’s what keeps me steady. When I forget the grace, I start believing I got myself sober — and that lie has taken stronger people than me right back out. These days, my inventory’s got a few thank-yous mixed in with the amends.

What would your day look like if you counted blessings instead of blunders?
10-18.title: October 18 — Black Ink Days

10-19.body:
October 19 – Be Excellent
“Be excellent to each other.” — Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure (1989)

Love and tolerance sound easy — like something you’d see on a bumper sticker next to a peace sign — until you actually try to live it. Some mornings I feel all centered and spiritual, then somebody cuts me off or rambles in a meeting, and there go the horns.

Recovery doesn’t turn me into a saint; it just gives me a few extra seconds before I act like a jerk. That pause — that breath before my sarcasm — is grace in motion. And every time I take it, I’m reminded that everyone’s just trying to win their own battle to get home sober too.

Being excellent isn’t about pretending to be holy — it’s about remembering I’m not in charge of the world and choosing kindness anyway.

When somebody gets under your skin today, can you take that breath and practice grace instead of judgment?
10-19.title: October 19 – Be Excellent

10-20.body:
October 20 – The Lazy Kind of Selfish
“We lean upon people until they fall. Then we blame them for not holding us up.” — The Little Red Book, p. 83

There’s a difference between trying to run someone’s life and just refusing to run your own. Codependence can be about control — but Over-dependence? That’s the lazy kind of selfish. It’s the spiritual version of, “Can you do it for me?”

I’ve caught myself calling three people about the same problem, acting like I’m seeking wisdom when really I just don’t want to move. I wasn’t looking for guidance — I was looking for a shortcut. I wanted to keep talking about my favorite subject: me.

It’s sneaky. It looks humble, sounds spiritual, but it’s really just comfort dressed up as connection. Laziness keeps my ego cozy and my growth on pause. Nobody can do my push-ups for me — not my sponsor, not my friends, not even God.

When you reach for the phone today, ask yourself — do I already know what to do and just not want to do it?
10-20.title: October 20 – The Lazy Kind of Selfish

10-21.body:
October 21 – Old Ideas, Dirty Dishes
“When we stop arguing with life, life stops arguing with us.” — The Little Red Book, p. 102

For years I lived by what I thought was a fair deal — if I cook, you do the dishes. Sounded reasonable, right? I loved the principle of fairness… mostly because I got to define it.

So there I was, on my day off, sitting in my grand idea of balance while my wife came home from a ten-hour shift. I wasn’t trying to be a jerk — I just had an old idea calling the shots. Somewhere in my head, I thought fairness mattered more than kindness.

Then it hit me: nobody said I couldn’t cook and do the dishes. Lightning wouldn’t strike, and the Recovery Police wouldn’t kick in the door. Turns out, I was more attached to being “right” than being useful.

Now, when that old voice says, “That’s not my job,” I just grab the sponge and get quiet. The peace I get from letting go always beats the satisfaction of being fair.

When was the last time you gave a little more than you thought you should — just because you could?
10-21.title: October 21 – Old Ideas, Dirty Dishes

10-22.body:
October 22 – I’ve Got People for That
“Spiritual growth begins the moment we stop expecting someone else to carry our load.” — Father John Doe
Over-dependence isn’t asking for help — it’s outsourcing your life and then getting mad when the staff quits. I’ve done it a hundred times. I’ll ask someone to remind me, pick something up, handle a call — and when they forget, I act like I’ve been betrayed. Like my to-do list was supposed to be a group effort.
Truth is, half the time I wasn’t overwhelmed — I was just avoiding. I once asked a buddy to drop off paperwork because “I was swamped.” Translation: I didn’t feel like doing it. When he forgot, I turned it into a character defect of his instead of a truth about mine.
That’s the lazy kind of selfish again — expecting people to carry what’s clearly mine, then catching resentment when they drop it. These days, when I catch myself trying to hand something off, I stop and ask: Am I asking for help, or am I just trying to skip responsibility again?
What’s one thing you’ve been waiting for someone else to do — that you could just take care of today?
