10-22.title: October 22 – I’ve Got People for That

10-23.body:
October 23 – Just Finish the Damn Thing

“How do you eat an elephant? One bite at a time.”

I’ve got a bad habit of stopping at about 85%. I’ll fix the door but leave my tools laying around for weeks. I’ll clean the kitchen but leave one cup in the sink. Somewhere in my head, I tell myself, good enough, I’ll finish later. But later piles up, and before long, I’m living in a world of half-done projects that quietly eat at my peace.

When I start leaving things unfinished, it’s not because I don’t care — it’s because I’ve let myself get overwhelmed again. My brain starts spinning with all the little things I’ve been avoiding, and suddenly everything feels too big. Then the irritation sets in — not with the world, but with myself — and my self-esteem takes the hit, and I’m back to telling myself I’m never good enough.

One day, I saw that old Nike commercial: JUST DO IT. And weirdly enough, it clicked. I didn’t need to conquer the whole mountain — I just needed to take one bite-sized step at a time. That’s what this program taught me: break it down, keep it simple, and follow through.

So I made a list — every unfinished thing sitting in the back of my mind. Turns out, it wasn’t that bad once I saw it in black and white. And one by one, I started knocking them out: fix the door hinge, pay that old phone bill, take my dad to lunch, make it to a meeting. Each checkmark gave me a little more peace. Turns out, progress feels a lot like relief.

When life feels too big today, ask — what’s the easiest thing on my list that I can take care of today, and make a start?
10-23.title: October 23 – Just Finish the Damn Thing

10-24.body:
October 24 – The Center Shift
“I’m looking for a record that says, ‘I’m okay, you’re okay… but in a cool way.’” — Barry (Jack Black), High Fidelity (2000)

My sponsor once told me, "It’s all either self-centeredness or others-centeredness — the whole thing.” I thought that sounded dramatic, but he was right. Every day I’m shifting between the two — me or we, take or give, control or trust.

Some days I catch myself trying to run the show again, and it doesn’t look like arrogance — it looks like stress, judgment, or the need to be right. Step 10 keeps me honest. When I’m disturbed, it’s a signal that the center has shifted back to me. The fix isn’t more control — it’s surrender, service, and a little humility.

When you feel that tightening today — that I, me, mine vibe — how can you slide the focus back to us instead?
10-24.title: October 24 – The Center Shift

10-25.body:
October 25 – The Fear Factory
“The average alcoholic is the individual who was pampered or neglected in childhood… and through regular alcoholic intake, fear is accentuated beyond control.” — Sobriety and Beyond, 1948

I read that a lot of us grew up one of two ways — we were either spoiled or ignored. Either way, we never learned how to deal with fear. When I found alcohol, it felt like the answer. It made the noise stop for a while. But when the drink was finally out of my life, I was left with all the fear I’d been running from — raw, loud, and looking for a way out.

Through the AA program I have the ability to see fear shows up in me as being too sensitive, too proud, too bossy, or too childish. Yeah… guilty. I used to think I was tough, but really, I was just scared of everything — losing control, being seen, being wrong. The more I hid it, the worse it got.

These days I don’t try to kill fear — I just stop feeding it. I ask God to help me face what’s in front of me, shaky hands and all. I don’t have to be fearless; I just have to keep walking. Every time I do, I grow up a little more.

When something sets you off today, can you take a moment to ask yourself — am I scared right now, or am I pretending not to be?
10-25.title: October 25 – The Fear Factory

10-26.body:
October 26 – The Defiant One
“The typical alcoholic has a narcissistic, egocentric core, dominated by feelings of omnipotence... a defiant individuality and grandiosity. Inwardly, the alcoholic brooks no control from man or God. He will fight to the end to preserve that position.”
— Dr. Harry Tiebout, AA Comes of Age, p. 311

When I first read that, I thought, Dang, that’s rough. Then I did the Steps and realized — yeah, that’s me. I’ve got that streak that says, Nobody tells me what to do. I wanted freedom, but I was really fighting anything that looked like surrender.

Nowadays, you hear “narcissist” all over social media like it means someone’s an uncurable monster. Sometimes it fits. Most of the time it’s just childish name-calling. Truth is, a lot of us are just carrying old wounds — the kind that scream for control when what we really need is connection. Healing that doesn’t mean pretending I’m not self-centered. It means seeing it, owning it, and trying not to let it drive the bus.

That’s where Step 10 saves me. Every day I’ve got to check for that pride, control, or quiet little voice that wants to be the director again. I’m not bad for having it — I’m just human. Some days I catch it quick, some days it catches me. Either way, I get another shot tomorrow.

How fast can you spot that “I’ll do it my way” attitude when it starts running the show?
10-26.title: October 26 – The Defiant One

10-27.body:
October 27 – The Ping Test
“To be the man, you gotta beat the man!” — Ric Flair

Humility is funny. The desire to have it might be a gift, but it’s also something you’ve gotta work at every single day. My mind still wants to be the man. So before I make a move, I try to ping my thoughts through something higher — like, Okay God, you handed me this moment; don’t let me wreck it with my ego.

That little pause changes everything. Doesn’t mean I suddenly turn into a saint — it just means I give God a second to speak before my pride grabs the mic. Most days humility looks like shutting up for half a beat and remembering I’m not the main character. That’s not weakness — that’s peace.

Bill W. left me a tool for this in the Big Book with a daily check in to see where I’m getting in my own way. It’s not about guilt; it’s about growth. It's saying "Hey, how are you doing with trying to practice these principles in your life? Are you finding any weak points? Where's your growth?" Thank God for progress not perfection. Every time I see my mistake and make it right, I build the kind of self-respect that sticks — the kind that says I can stay sober, useful, and free.

When you catch yourself about to charge ahead today, can you ping it first — is this me, or is this God?
10-27.title: October 27 – The Ping Test

10-28.body:
October 28 – We All Need Somebody

“I just might have a problem that you’ll understand / We all need somebody to lean on.” — Bill Withers

Some days the best inventory I can do isn’t neat. It’s not a perfect paragraph or a moral essay. Sometimes it’s a napkin and a pen, sitting in the car, scribbling out what just happened and how I feel about it. The point isn’t to look smart — it’s to get the thoughts out of my head and into the light. Because left alone, my brain can take a small problem and turn it into a whole season of bad television.

When I write it down, I start to see patterns — where I overreacted, where fear crept in, where I might owe an apology. And when I share that stuff with another drunk who’s been there, it’s like taking the pressure off a valve. A sick mind can’t heal a sick mind, but two honest ones can make sense of the mess together.

Sometimes all recovery asks of me is this: pick up a pen, tell the truth, and let someone else read the scribbles. That’s how I get my head clear enough to hear God again.

When was the last time you picked up a pen?
10-28.title: October 28 – We All Need Somebody

10-29.body:
October 29 – The Worst Gift

“Don’t put off ’til tomorrow what you can screw up today.” — Unknown

“Promptly” doesn’t mean “after I cool off,” or “once I’ve justified it a little more.” It means right now. That small window before pride kicks in and starts rewriting the story. When I delay admitting my wrongs, it’s usually because I want to stay the hero in my own head — but that delay has a cost. It lets resentment start brewing, in me or in the other person.

A resentment’s just a wound that never got cleaned out. And when I won’t own my part, I’m basically handing someone the worst gift ever: the gift of potential resentment. Nobody needs that. Least of all me.

People are naturally prone to resentment; I don’t have to feed it with my silence or my ego. A little humility early saves a whole lot of damage later.

When was the last time you made it right promptly?
10-29.title: October 29 – The Worst Gift

10-30.body:
October 30 – Shit Happens, Then Grace

“We’re all just walking each other home.” — Ram Dass

Admitting means confessing — usually with reluctance. I don’t leap into it; I drag my feet. When I’m unwilling to admit my wrong, it starts building pressure inside me. Somebody once said in a meeting, “Anxiety shows up when you’re trapped between doing what you shouldn’t do and not doing what you should do.” Yeah, that’s about right.

I forget all the time how forgiving people can start when I show a little humility and clean up my side of the street. Most of the time, I’m not scared of being wrong — I’m scared of being seen. I don’t want to look weak, or human, or messy. But nobody’s perfect, and shit happens. Lies sneak out as exaggerations, selfish motives take the wheel, anger makes a scene. Sometimes my intentions are good, but my actions still confuse even me.

That’s why I’m grateful for the AA program that gives me a way to reset. I don’t have to stay stuck in guilt or pride. I can admit it, fix it, and go to bed with a clear conscience.

Is there any wrong in your heart right now that you’re still hanging on to?
10-30.title: October 30 – Shit Happens, Then Grace

10-31.body:
October 31 – The Mask Comes Off

“If you don’t deal with your trash, it starts to stink.” — Unknown

Halloween used to feel like my life year-round. I wore a mask every day — the tough guy, the know-it-all, the good-time friend. That old character was my armor, built to hide the fear underneath. I didn’t realize how heavy it was until the steps gave me a chance to take it off. In this process, I finally got to take out the garbage — all the lies, guilt, and junk I’d been hiding behind.

My life used to look like a junkyard of old identities, and I was lucky to have a guide who showed me how to clean it up and start fresh. I don’t ever want to build another one. Today I’m allowed to screw up without putting the mask back on. I can admit my mistakes, make them right, and move forward.

Keeping my channel clear with a Higher Power is like keeping the lights on inside. When I don’t hide behind pride or fear, life just runs smoother. Screwing up is human; pretending I don’t is the real trick.

What part of the old costume are you still holding onto?
10-31.title: October 31 – The Mask Comes Off

11-01.body:
November 1 – The Quiet Voice

“You got to know when to hold ’em, know when to fold ’em.” — Kenny Rogers

I heard in a meeting that prayer is talking to God, and meditation is shutting up long enough to listen. I like that. I’ve spent most of my life trying to negotiate with the universe, like I could bargain my way into peace. Step 11 isn’t about getting what I want — it’s about staying quiet enough to find out what I already have.

There’s this quiet voice that usually kicks in right before I do something stupid. It doesn’t shout, it doesn’t argue — it just drops one calm warning and walks away. I only hear it once. Some days I pray for God to turn up the volume on that voice. God shows up like a gentleman — invited, not forced. Usually I have to pause and not do anything until the answer is very clear to me. It’ll come, as long as my own house is in order.

The trick, for me, is learning to listen before the noise starts again.

When’s the last time that quiet voice showed up for you — and did you listen, or did you argue with it?
11-01.title: November 1 – The Quiet Voice

11-02.body:
November 2 – The Plan

“I love it when a plan comes together.” — Colonel John “Hannibal” Smith, The A-Team

The Big Book says, “On awakening, we think about the twenty-four hours ahead.” I try to do that — consider my plans, ask God to direct my thinking, and move through the day with some sort of purpose. But sometimes, just sometimes, my plans aren’t what’s going to happen. That’s where life on life’s terms shows up and humbles me.

One day I was dead set on finally taking care of my yard. I just wanted to be alone, sweat it out, get it done. Then a few guys called asking if I could take them to a meeting that night. “Ugh, great,” I thought, “don’t they know I’m busy?” But that quiet voice said, go.

So we went. And like every time I actually show up, I didn’t regret it. I heard some stuff that would save my ass down the road. After the meeting, I met a woman who would eventually become my wife a few years later. God works in mysterious ways.

I’m glad I listened to the voice instead of my strict plans — turns out His plan came together a lot better than mine ever could.

What’s one time life interrupted your plan, and you realized later it was exactly how it was supposed to go?
11-02.title: November 2 – The Plan

11-03.body:
November 3 – The Pause

“Never half-ass two things. Whole-ass one thing.” — Ron Swanson, Parks and Recreation

If I had a dollar for every time I doubted God’s plan, I’d be pretty well-off by now. For me, getting past selfishness has never been a breeze—it’s more like needing a crowbar to pry myself loose, especially when there’s more responsibility than feels manageable in the moment.

The Big Book suggests pausing when agitated or doubtful. Sounds simple, but that’s usually when my mind wants to sprint. For me, that’s the hardest time to slow down. Sometimes the best I’ve got is a quick prayer: “God, help me see through my own selfishness so I can see the truth.”

Then comes the pause—the breathing, the waiting, the next right thing, even if it’s small. Protecting that quiet voice inside feels like the most important work I can do today. Without it, I know where I’d end up: right back where I started.

What helps you hit pause before reacting when fear or pride tries to take the wheel?
11-03.title: November 3 – The Pause

11-04.body:
November 4 – The Path In

“It’s not the years, honey, it’s the mileage.” — Indiana Jones, Raiders of the Lost Ark

I had this buddy who got real deep into meditation. He wanted to know how to do it right, so he went to a Buddhist temple for a retreat. He figured, these guys must have the secret. After dinner one night, he found one of the monks sweeping the floor and asked, “How do you meditate?”

The monk shrugged and said, “I don’t know.”

That answer messed with him for a while. But the more I think about it, the more it makes sense. There isn’t one perfect way to reach conscious contact — there’s just the way that works for you. For some people, it’s silence. For others, it’s music, walking, journaling, or just sitting still long enough to hear their own heartbeat.

Meditation isn’t about mastering a method — it’s about finding that quiet inner path where I stop running the show. God speaks the language of peace, and each of us has to learn how to listen in our own way.

What’s something that helps you quiet the noise long enough to feel that connection inside?
11-04.title: November 4 – The Path In

11-05.body:
November 5 – Spiritual Metabolism

“The purpose of prayer and meditation is to tune ourselves in with the rhythm of life, not to rewrite the song.” — Chuck C., A New Pair of Glasses

One day I was sitting around an AA meeting and they asked if there were any prayer requests. I thought, Here we go again… let’s just get into the meeting so I can hopefully hear something good. Selfish. Then it hit me—AA is a group of people praying and meditating for God’s will to come alive. Not necessarily to change the course of events—I don’t even know if that’s possible—but to bring acceptance into the picture is.

Each of us has a kind of spiritual metabolism. We take in the negativity of the world and, through prayer, honesty, and connection, we have the ability to metabolize it into acceptance. That’s power to me. For me it’s easy to magnify negativity—it spreads on its own. It takes real work to turn that negative into something useful.

In AA groups, through connection, we have the ability to take the events of the world and digest them into something purposeful. Like little spiritual bright spots on the map, where chaos becomes harmony. Problems come our way, we break them down through prayer, meditation, sharing and use them as experience to grow. I pray I stay in this stream of life, doing my small part each day to keep the whole body of AA healthy—whether I’m in a meeting or not.

When life throws you something sour, how do you help turn it into something useful?
11-05.title: November 5 – Spiritual Metabolism

11-06.body:
November 6 – Open Mind, Open Heart

“So I got that goin’ for me, which is nice.” — Carl Spackler, Caddyshack

“Be quick to see where religious people are right.” That line has always stuck out. It’s a touchy subject because, for me, church used to mean showing up for all the wrong reasons. When AA introduced the idea of spirituality, I was hesitant. It sounded like another version of what hadn’t worked before. But the program suggested something different—keep an open mind. Spirituality, they said, comes from within. Use a God of your understanding, or not, it's your life. We're just telling you what worked for us.

Over time, that line—be quick to see where religious people are right—kept echoing. It’s not in there by accident. Staying open-minded when talking with people of faith—whether a pastor or just someone who genuinely believes—has become part of conscious contact itself. That kind of awareness can’t really be taught; it grows from the inside out.

Once that little spark got lit, truth started showing up everywhere—a line from a sermon, a verse in a song, a Facebook post. The source didn’t matter; the message just landed differently. That’s how it works for me: a personal understanding of God that builds, one small spark at a time. It’s not my job to bash someone else's way now that I finally found my way. Kind of arrogant when I think about it.

When’s the last time something spiritual came from a place you didn’t expect—and you actually let it in?
11-06.title: November 6 – Open Mind, Open Heart

11-07.body:
November 7 – Feet on the Ground

“I never met a man who relapsed or got drunk who began his day with quiet time with God.” — Dr. Bob Smith, Co-founder of AA

Dr. Bob said it, and it hits hard. I can't forget he was one drink away from destruction, just like me—here because he wanted to stay sober. For me, it’s important not to forget that the same desire brought me into this fellowship. I can’t lose sight of what I am or how much damage I can cause, no matter how spiritual I might start to feel.

Some days the ego polishes up nicely, and it’s easy to stroll into a meeting acting like I’ve been handpicked by God Himself—radiating wisdom, tossing around serenity, talking about all the things that “work for me.” Then that line from the Big Book lands: “Yet we keep our feet on the ground, for that is where our fellow travelers are.”

That one keeps me in check. The minute I start quietly judging what works for you versus what works for me, I’m back on a spiritual high horse that’s headed for a crash. Staying grounded reminds me that I belong right here with everyone else. That sense of belonging is part of the miracle.

The only “how” that ever mattered to me is H.O.W.—honest, open-minded, and willing. After that, the spiritual path is personal. I’ve learned I’m just another bozo on the bus, trying to stay teachable. Nobody told me what to do, and that freedom of choice kept me here. Sometimes saving my ass looks like keeping both feet on the ground.

When’s the last time you looked around and realized the people walking beside you are exactly where you belong?
11-07.title: November 7 – Feet on the Ground

11-08.body:
November 8 – All or Nothing Thinking

"You will respect my authoritah!" — Eric Cartman, South Park

There’s that episode of South Park where Cartman gets appointed as a junior police officer. He’s wearing aviator sunglasses, waving a nightstick, and strutting around town barking orders:

“You will respect my authoritah!”

The funny part is that everyone sees through it — nobody listens — which only makes him yell louder. His motives don’t take x-ray vision to spot. It’s all self-righteousness dressed up as purpose, and every time he doubles down, he just spins himself deeper into his own self-centered panic. It’s all about running the show — trying to force everyone to fall in line so he can feel like he’s on top.

Unfortunately, I used to get like that. For me, anxiety sounds like “Nobody is listening!” Then depression hits, and it turns into “nobody is listening…” Same words, different volume — all my problem. That kind of all-or-nothing thinking has been with me for years, built somewhere along the way of my alcoholism. It can still sneak up before I even notice it’s there. And just like Cartman, everyone else usually spots it before I do — which, of course, frustrates me even more.

AA has given me tools to pause before I react, because my reactions usually knock me backward — two steps back after one step forward. A friend in AA regularly reminds me that a big part of this program is learning how to relax and take it easy — you know, actually surrender instead of waiting for other people to surrender to me. Prayer and meditation don’t have to be some huge holy production where I transcend to another planet. Sometimes it’s just taking a quiet second to seek God before I swing my nightstick.

When was the last time you realized you were trying to run the show—and how did that usually work out?
11-08.title: November 8 – All or Nothing Thinking

11-09.body:
November 9 – Morning Meditation

"If circumstances warrant, we ask our wives or friends to join us in morning meditation." — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 87

When I heard Dr. Bob say he never saw anyone drink again who spent time with God every morning it hit me. The guy worked with thousands of alcoholics, so I figured he knew what he was talking about. It motivated me to get out of bed and get active in my recovery.

Sometimes that means reading a meditation book, sometimes journaling, sometimes just sitting quietly before the day starts. It’s taken on different forms as I’ve gone along in the program. The main thing is—I do it. It seems to make me a better person to handle the events of the day.

A funny thing happened along the way. My wife noticed. She didn’t say much at first—she just saw me doing it and staying sober. Over time, she started joining me when she could. Nothing was forced—it was a beautiful thing the way it happened. No expectations, no plans, just me doing my thing—and somehow, it drew people in without me even trying. Curiosity must’ve gotten the best of a few others, too, because before long some AA friends started asking me to text them the reading of the day. We’d talk when the sun came up about what it meant to each of us. It built a pretty solid foundation for my relationships along the way—turns out we understand each other a little more when we start from the same page.

It built something steady and quiet in my life. AA showed me it was important, and without expectation or even realizing it, I showed the people closest to me that it was important. That’s all it really takes—consistency, not perfection.

What’s one quiet habit in your recovery that’s built more than you expected?
11-09.title: November 9 – Morning Meditation

11-10.body:
November 10 – Burning Up Energy

"We become much more efficient. We do not tire so easily, for we are not burning up energy foolishly as we did when we were trying to arrange life to suit ourselves." — Alcoholics Anonymous, p. 87

In an episode of Seinfeld, Kramer comes crashing through Jerry’s door with a wild new idea: he’s going to renovate his apartment to look like ancient Egypt. He’s totally consumed with the vision of getting rid of his furniture and building floor levels like an Egyptian palace inside his one-bedroom apartment. Nobody can talk him out of it, no matter how goofy it sounds.
Jerry asks, “You drew up plans for this?”
Kramer grins and says, “No, it’s all in my head.”
Then he challenges Jerry, “You don’t think I can, huh?”
And Jerry fires back, “I know that you can’t, and I’m positive that you won’t.”

As absurd as it is, I can relate.

In my own life, I cringe at how much energy I’ve burned up foolishly the same way. Most of it was spent trying to figure out ways to drink like a normal guy. I plotted, schemed, twisted — never figured it out. The problem was that this thinking bled into the rest of my life. I’d make grand plans, sell my friends and family on them, then end up trying to figure out how to escape the mess I’d made. Vacations I couldn’t afford, moves I couldn’t pull off, new “healthy lifestyles” that never made it past Tuesday. The more fried I got on alcohol, the more insane the plans became.

Each time, I swore I’d learned my lesson. Then I’d start another big plan to fix the last one. Eventually I dug myself into a hole of distrust — and it sucked.

These days, when I wake up, I get to consider my plans for the day. Are they realistic, or are they another set of “levels”? I still have a tendency to take on too much, and before I know it, I’m tired, frustrated, and tempted to escape. There is no chance of following through. The beauty of conscious contact is that I get to slow down. Small goals are enough today. And I regularly have to remind myself, staying sober is enough just for today.

Where in my life am I still building “levels” — wasting energy trying to rearrange things instead of accepting them?
11-10.title: November 10 – Burning Up Energy

11-11.body:
November 11 – Small Steps

“You miss 100% of the shots you don’t take.” — Wayne Gretzky (quoted by Michael Scott)

It seems alcoholics are either strong starters or strong finishers—rarely both. We get so perfectionistic about the plan that we never start, or we finally start something and get so hung up on how it’ll end—and how it’ll look to everyone else—that we never finish. Half the time I wasn’t chasing progress; I was chasing approval.

A part of overthinking, I’ve gathered, is really just self-seeking that hasn’t found the right plan yet. I want every project to go perfectly, making my life easier, and to get me that invisible A+ from the world. Deep down, I’m still that kid from A Christmas Story, daydreaming that my teacher’s gonna yell out, “A plus… plus! PLUS!” while the whole class celebrates me.

By the time I got to AA, I had a lifetime’s worth of half-finished projects sitting on the shelf in my head. From the outside, I probably looked lazy. But if you could’ve hooked a computer up to my brain, you’d see I’d burned ten times more energy thinking about doing the thing than the average guy who just rolled up his sleeves and got to work. I was exhausted from imaginary labor.

For me, the real problem wasn’t laziness—it was trying to control an outcome. I spent most of my life trying to script the ending and earn applause I didn’t need. The Steps taught me I can’t. I have to let go and let God, loosen that white-knuckle grip I’ve had on the world, and stop trying to bend it to my own self-centered plans.

Putting in the footwork means starting, not perfecting. It means a small step forward is still a step forward, whether I'm starting a project, or finishing one. And here’s the kicker—I’m allowed to admit I’m overwhelmed. I’m allowed to rest. I'm allowed to rest and ask for help. It turns out nobody’s ever criticized me the way I’ve criticized myself.

So when I feel myself getting jammed up, I try a simple prayer: “God, please let me see if I’ve taken on too much here and steer me back on course.”

Then I pause. Pay attention to who God puts in my path. And move along.

Nothing—nothing—in God’s world happens by mistake.

What has you froze up from overthinking at this moment—and what small step forward could you take?
11-11.title: November 11 – Small Steps

11-12.body:
November 12 – Discipline Isn’t Punishment

“Wax on, wax off.” — Mr. Miyagi, The Karate Kid (1984)

For a long time, I thought “discipline” meant punishment. Growing up, it was what happened when I messed up — not something I’d ever choose for myself. But recovery flipped that whole idea around. I’ve learned that discipline isn’t punishment; it’s freedom.

This is a program — emphasis on program. It works when I do. The daily actions I take — prayer, inventory, meetings, service — aren’t penalties; they’re protection. They keep me from drifting back into the chaos that used to run my life.

The Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, in Step Eleven, suggests that we take the Prayer of Saint Francis and “reread the prayer several times very slowly, savoring every word and trying to take in the deep meaning of each phrase and idea.” That’s not about perfection — it’s about practice. Spiritual discipline means showing up, even when I don’t feel like it, and letting the principles do their quiet work.

When I stop practicing the basics, I start slipping into old habits and old thinking. But when I stay consistent, when I let these spiritual principles work even when I want to get in my own way, something steady happens inside me. I don’t have to fight the same old battles anymore.

Discipline is a beautiful thing. It’s a choice I get to make — one day at a time — to live by a way of life that keeps me sober and sane.

How does my view of discipline change when I see it as a form of spiritual freedom instead of punishment?
11-12.title: November 12 – Discipline Isn’t Punishment

11-13.body:
November 13– Channel of Peace

“Lord, make me a channel of thy peace. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

In AA meetings, there’s never a shortage of problems. The gift is that problems have solutions. Sometimes what feels overwhelmingly real to me might not even seem that big to someone else—and that’s okay.

For me, there are three tools worth keeping close: experience, strength, and hope. It took me a while to realize that doesn’t mean opinion, strength, and hope. My part isn’t to be the solution to peace — it’s to be a channel for it.

If I have experience, I can share it, or point in the direction of someone who's been there. If not, I can help someone find strength and hope instead. Being a member of AA doesn’t give me the right to act like an ad-hoc therapist or doctor. I’m here for my own recovery, not to fix you.

Peace doesn’t come from me; it moves through me. These days, there’s no obligation to fix anyone else’s problems — and that’s its own kind of freedom.

If at the end of the day all I've done is lend a listening ear to members of AA I've done my service. Peace shows up when there’s no need to try and play God and have all the answers. When the effort shifts from fixing to carrying—just doing what’s been given to do—things start to calm down, inside and out.

When’s the last time peace felt more important than being right?
11-13.title: November 13 – Channel of Peace

11-14.body:
November 14 – Bring Love

“That where there is hatred, I may bring love. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

Hatred is such a self-centered emotion to have. It's lazy. Gossip and talking crap about what "they should have done," the mix of disgust and intolerance used to make me feel oddly special—up on a pedestal, looking down on everyone else. It’s a familiar trap, that feeling of being disconnected yet somehow “better.” And ultimately, it only hurts me in the end.

AA reminds us that love and tolerance are our code. We are going to be kind and loving toward all—ALL? Now that takes work. Nobody said it would come easy. These days, it helps to relate more than compare. Somewhere in that connection, peace starts to show up—a little softer, a little more human.

There’s no requirement to join in anger—it spreads on it's own. I've learned to be careful because it can be contagious. Pausing long enough to whisper a quiet prayer for love to surface can be a roadblock for hatred. It can flip the script...sometimes for everyone involved. I heard that Bill's wife, Lois prayed before every meeting to invite God in. That’s become a practice for me too: “God, please let love come before resentment sinks in.”

When’s the last time love guided your response instead of ego leading the charge?
11-14.title: November 14 – Bring Love

11-15.body:
November 15 – The Spirit of Forgiveness

“That where there is wrong, I may bring the spirit of forgiveness. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

The entire prayer of St. Francis would be a whole lot easier to live by if that line weren’t in it. Forgiveness and wrong—those are tricky words, and they’ve always been confusing ones for me.

The first step is figuring out what’s actually wrong, and that’s not simple. These days, the only safe ground is my own behavior. Still, people do hurtful things—lie, manipulate, steal. It’s human. It happens.

Early in sobriety, dating seemed harmless enough—until it wasn’t. The person I was seeing hadn’t fully left their last relationship, and I labeled that “very wrong.” My sponsor listened to my rant, then went quiet. Finally he said, “Forgive her, or hang on to it for the rest of your life. Your choice.” That landed hard. Resentment had already dug in deep.

The only way out was back through the Big Book process. A little willingness cracked open the door, and light started to come in. Forgiveness followed right behind it. I once heard in AA “Those with the most tools do the work.” That line stuck. The inventory, the prayers, the surrender—it all helped move the resentment out and the peace in.

Things still go sideways sometimes. People still disappoint. Life still happens. But for me, staying sober and staying free means forgiving faster, even when I don’t want to. That’s where the spirit of this program really starts working.

What’s something you’ve had to forgive so you could be free?
11-15.title: November 15 – The Spirit of Forgiveness

11-16.body:
November 16 – Bring Harmony

“That where there is discord, I may bring harmony. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

One of the best examples of a band that really nailed this harmony thing was The Beatles—John, Paul, George, and Ringo. The final versions of their songs sound so polished, like everyone just knew their part. Sometimes it was Paul’s turn to lead, sometimes John, sometimes George got a shot, and every now and then Ringo stepped up to the mic. At no point did they seem to compete in the music itself—the finished product was harmony. Beautiful melodies that carry me away while the record spins.

I can’t forget that I can be an extreme example of self-centered behavior. I’d prefer to be the lead singer all the time. In meetings, people bring a lot of problems—and I watch what old experience takes the lead. Sometimes I get to be the bass player, steady and simple, holding the tone of strength. Other times, I keep the beat with the drum of hope.

Nothing knocks me out of harmony with the world faster than my opinion, telling someone else what to do or how they should live their life. It's easy for me to forget that everyone’s got their own instrument, their own rhythm, their own timing. My job is to start bringing a steady beat when things seem chaotic—something soft enough that others can find their way back to the song if they want to. That’s real harmony.

Harmony can be a tricky thing, but practice in the meetings makes me a better player. I don’t always get to sing lead, but I can still be part of the song. When I play my part instead of trying to control the whole band, life sounds a lot more like music and less like noise.

When was the last time you let someone else take the lead so harmony could happen?
11-16.title: November 16 – Bring Harmony

11-17.body:
November 17 – Bring Truth

“That where there is error, I may bring truth. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

“Divided we fall.” Sometimes I used to catch myself with this Super Bowl mindset—like life’s a big game and someone has to win. There can only be one winner, and everybody else loses. Coke vs. Pepsi. McDonald’s vs. Burger King. Me vs. you. Somewhere along the way, I started believing that’s how life works— that’s capitalism, not spiritual life.

Just because the Browns are good doesn’t mean the Steelers have to suck. The truth is, we’re all walking home together on this spiritual path. While sitting in an AA meeting, I try to remember that each of us had one really rough night that connected us here. Loss of hope is a hell of a motivator. Making someone feel disconnected, less than, or like they don’t belong is not going to help anything move forward.

In AA, as soon as you walk through the door, you become a winner. That’s the truth. It takes an immense amount of courage to seek help. For me, truth wasn’t thrown at me—it was developed over time. The first truth was simple: this alcohol problem was kicking my ass. From there, more was revealed.

Old harmful ideas built on opinion start slipping away the longer we stick around. Inventory helps. Meeting with other alcoholics becomes a top priority. And patience—with myself and others—starts growing, in the meetings and out in the world.

It’s life. Welcome to the Winner's Circle. As long as the drink isn’t in my hand, I get to participate. There’s a barstool somewhere with my name carved into it, waiting for me to come back—but today, that thought hits like a nightmare instead of a fantasy.

What’s one truth that keeps you grounded when your ego wants to compete?
11-17.title: November 17 – Bring Truth

11-18.body:
November 18 – Bring Faith

“That where there is doubt, I may bring faith. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

When people talk about Star Wars, they usually jump straight to Luke and Vader — the Force, the family drama, all that. But the guy I relate to most is Han Solo — the doubter.

Luke found a power greater than himself in the Force and just rolled with it. Han, on the other hand, was grounded in material things.

“Hokey religions and ancient weapons are no match for a good blaster at your side, kid.” — Han Solo, A New Hope

Luke was on a spiritual journey, and Han wasn’t having it. After voicing his reservations, Luke didn’t lecture or argue. He didn’t try to convince anyone. He just lived his truth and kept doing what he believed in. His actions spoke louder than words — and that’s the quiet beauty of real faith.

Han watched it all happen — the miracles, the mistakes, the courage — and something in him started to shift. He softened to the idea that maybe there was something bigger out there. By Return of the Jedi, the same guy who once mocked the Force was risking his life for his friends and a cause greater than himself.

Han didn’t find faith through argument or explanation. He found it through experience — one act of loyalty, one step of courage, one day at a time. That’s how it works for a lot of us. Nobody can really give us faith; we seem to grow into it by living around people who already have it.

Faith isn’t taught. It’s caught — through action, through showing up, through doing the next right thing even when you don’t believe yet.

What’s something you’ve come to believe in — not because someone told you to, but because life showed you?
11-18.title: November 18 – Bring Faith

11-19.body:
November 19 – Bring Hope

“That where there is despair, I may bring hope. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

There’s a line in the Big Book I hope I’ll never forget — “the Four Horsemen: Terror, Bewilderment, Frustration, and Despair.” They say if we want to get a handle on our drinking problem, we have to learn to live by the spiritual principles of the Steps. There are principles in those Four Horsemen too — the principles of untreated alcoholism.

Terror — extreme fear.
Bewilderment — confusion.
Frustration — the inability to manage.
Despair — loss of hope.

Having alcoholism means those Four Horsemen are still out there, polishing the one-way ticket back to booze with my name on it. Purpose doesn’t mean perfection—it just means showing up and letting recovery do the talking.

Peace of mind speaks louder than any words I could ever speak. I try to remember the newcomer who’s walking through that door, probably carrying those Four Horsemen on his back, grinding him into the ground. A simple handshake or a hug might be the first spark of hope he’s felt in years.

What simple thing has someone done for you that reminded you hope still exists?
11-19.title: November 19 – Bring Hope

11-20.body:
November 20 – Bring Light

“That where there is darkness, I may bring light. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

In Pulp Fiction, Jules has a spiritual awakening right in front of everyone. His heart softens, and one moment changes his course — going from hitman to shepherd, from taking lives to trying to lead them. “I’m trying, Ringo. I’m trying real hard to be the shepherd.” It’s not perfect, but it’s real.

Just walking into an AA meeting changes my course too. It says, “Hey, I found the solution here — and you might too, if we both do what they did. I’m curious to find out more.” And just like Jules, I don’t have to get it all at once — I just have to try. Try to walk through that door, try to keep an open mind, and see what happens without forcing it. In that simple action of trying, We have the ability to be an example that brings light to darkness.

A guy once said in a meeting, “There’s usually someone here in their first 30 days of sobriety and someone in their last 30 days.” You never know who you’re setting an example for. My purpose now is to show up — show up sober — and see what happens. That light shines brighter than any words I could ever say.

When was the last time you realized just trying was enough to let the light back in?
11-20.title: November 20 – Bring Light

11-21.body:
November 21 – Bring Joy

“That where there is sadness, I may bring joy. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

At the end of E.T., the little alien is getting ready to leave, and Elliott’s crushed. He doesn’t want to say goodbye. But E.T. touches his finger to Elliott’s forehead and says, “I’ll be right here.” That line hits me every time. It’s not a promise that things won’t hurt — it’s a reminder that love and connection don’t vanish just because life changes shape.

Sadness is part of the deal. People move on, relationships end, plans fall apart. But I’ve learned in recovery that joy doesn’t depend on the outcome — it grows out of presence. Sometimes joy is just sitting with someone who’s hurting, not fixing a thing, and letting them know they’re not alone.

AA taught me that laughter is sacred. It’s medicine. In meetings I’ve cried, and five minutes later, I’ve laughed harder than I ever thought possible. Tears are a one-way street, and I’m glad it’s built that way — it would be strange if tears could go back inside of me. So let them out into the world, and don’t try to hold on to them. Getting the tears out of the way helps me remember there is still purpose in my life, no matter how confusing that may look to me at the time. That’s what joy looks like to me now — a strange mix of tears, truth, and lightness.

When trying to bring joy where there’s sadness, it’s not about cheering anyone up. It’s about showing up. Maybe with a cup of coffee. Maybe with a quiet nod across the room. Maybe just with my presence — saying, without words, “You’re not alone. I’m right here.”

When was the last time someone’s simple presence brought you a little light when things felt heavy?
11-21.title: November 21 – Bring Joy

11-22.body:
November 22 – Seek to Comfort

“Lord, grant that I may seek rather to comfort than to be comforted. (Today)” — Prayer of Saint Francis

When I was a kid, I’d get so caught up playing on the playground that I wouldn’t hear the recess bell. Before I knew it, I was the only one still going down the slide, and the teacher was yelling at me for not paying attention. It sucked — I’m not even going to pretend otherwise. It felt like I’d missed the memo on life. I took it hard, like something was wrong with me.

Fast forward to adulthood, and when I came into AA, I felt the same way — like I hadn’t heard the recess bell of life. I just wanted to keep playing while everyone else moved on. The loss of jobs, relationships, and good things in life left me feeling completely alone and uncomfortable in my own skin.

Then one day, I heard another guy in a meeting share something that sounded just like my story. Something deep inside me said, “Hey, another guy did that too. Maybe there are more.” I decided to stick around to see how they got it back together again.

Some days, recovery can still be hard — living without the one thing that used to give me temporary connection to everyone else, even though it was fake. But in AA, I’ve found a real connection, and that brings real comfort. These days, when I reach out my hand to someone new, it’s not out of pity — it’s out of responsibility. And in that connection, something shifts. I get to give and receive at the same time.

When was the last time you reached out to help someone and ended up feeling helped yourself?
11-22.title: November 22 – Seek to Comfort

11-23.body:
November 23 – Seek to Understand

“Lord, grant that I may not so much seek to be understood as to understand. (Today)” — Prayer of St. Francis

There’s a scene in Rush Hour where Chris Tucker shouts at Jackie Chan, “Do you understand the words that are coming out of my mouth?!” He’s frustrated, loud, and completely missing the point. He’s talking at Jackie, not communicating with him. Most of us in recovery know that feeling. Trying so hard to be heard that real understanding slips through the cracks.

Fear doesn’t come walking through the front door. It hides under the words — in the hesitations, the eye rolls, the fast shut-downs. When that happens, a quiet prayer helps: “God, please let me have understanding here.” It slows me down enough to listen to more than words.

One of the most common exchanges in the rooms goes like this:
“Hey, how are you doing?”
“Fine.”
But underneath that “fine” often lives a story that never felt worth telling. A lot of us never felt heard—so we stopped trying. A gentle follow-up, “How are you really doing?” opens a door. When I pause and wait, people usually walk through it. That space doesn’t need to fix anything; it just gives someone a chance to feel connection.

Alcoholism steals voices. AA helps them return. Sometimes the best way to speak recovery is without words at all—by showing up, shaking a hand, sitting in a circle, and proving that this matters. When we show up together, we say it loud without ever saying a thing: It is important for me to be here. It might be important to you, too.

What’s something you wish people understood about you in early recovery—but you didn’t know how to say out loud?
11-23.title: November 23 – Seek to Understand

11-24.body:
November 24 – To Love

“To love than to be loved. (Today)” — Prayer of St. Francis

Early on in sobriety, I was confused as hell. This AA stuff didn’t come easy for me. People kept calling it a “simple program for complicated people,” and I thought, well… I guess I’m the complicated part.

I remember telling my sponsor, “Look, I’m not drinking. What’s the point of all this other stuff?” He paused — for what felt like way too long — then said, “You’re going to be a blessing for anyone you meet.”

I swear to God, that made zero sense back then. A blessing? Me? I wasn’t even a blessing to myself.

But fast-forward into contented sobriety, and I get it. The whole thing is simple now: we do no harm.

There’s a lady in a meeting who always reminds me, “If I can help you, I will. If I can harm you, I won’t.”
That’s the deal for me today. Everybody needs help. Everybody.

And I’ve got two choices: either be a dick about it… or not.

I’m not trying to be Mother Teresa over here. I’m just trying to participate in a way of living that keeps me away from alcohol and reasonably resentment-free. And when I do that — when I stay in the lane of kindness and usefulness, you know, the way God designed me to be — something wild happens: people are actually attracted to being around me.

Think about it. What does the AA program of action really do?

You get in here and give up the fight—powerlessness turns to power as soon as we do this.

You get some strength in regular meetings with other drunks to stay away from booze.

They help get you hooked up with a Higher Power.

They get you volunteering.

They get you wisdom eventually — the kind that slows you down so you’re not just firing off opinions like they’re facts.

They hand you a purpose: stay sober and helping other drunks stay alive today.

Somewhere in that mix, you become a human being that is loving towards others — others-centered instead of self-centered. And honestly?

That’s irresistible.

What’s one thing you do today that the old you would’ve never believed was part of staying sober?
11-24.title: November 24 – To Love

11-25.body:
November 25 — Excitement

“We are then in much less danger of… excitement.”

The character Lloyd in the movie Dumb and Dumber really nails this whole excitement thing. Alcoholics of my type can treat that movie like a documentary. All the dumb stuff I did in my drinking career fits right into that universe. Sure, the movie is absurd, and so were my decisions. Excitement can flip straight into psychotic wishful thinking if I’m not grounded in a Higher Power. In the Lamborghini scene, these guys are broke, unemployable, and barely holding it together—but the second Lloyd gets excited, he blows the cash on a Lamborghini so he can “fit in” with a ritzy crowd. Classic: excitement hits, fantasy kicks in, reality goes out the window. Man, I can relate.

The program gave me a tool that saves me before I end up in hot water again: “Thy will be done.” What would God have me do right now? If we pause and wait out that little adrenaline spike of excitement, we can usually make a decision that’s grounded, sane, and not just another self-centered stunt. It works. It really does.

What’s one “excitement moment” where you almost acted too fast—but paused long enough to let God get a word in?
11-25.title: November 25 — Excitement

11-26.body:
November 26 — Fear

“We are then in much less danger of… fear.”

Fear—what a sucky thing to have running the entire show. I once heard someone say fear stands for Forget Everything’s All Right, and man, that hits home. One little spark sets me off, and boom: I’m worked up, anxiety through the roof, inventing a whole disaster that doesn’t even exist. Alcoholics have a gift for turning a molehill into a mountain in half a second. For me, the fear usually circles the same three drains: not enough money, not enough sex, or not enough approval. It’s like my ego demands way more attention than I deserve.

I remember being at a meeting once, shaking hands with everyone as I walked around. One guy didn’t shake back—it looked like he shrugged me off. The fear hit instantly. What did I do wrong? Why doesn’t he like me? Should I switch meetings? Start my own meeting? Go home? Quit AA? My head went straight into panic mode. Later I mentioned it to a friend, and he said, “Dude… that guy is blind and mostly deaf.” Yeah. I felt like an idiot.

Thank God for Rule 62: Don’t take yourself too damn seriously. My ego can latch onto one imagined problem and ignore the twenty people who actually welcomed me. Fear sucks. But today I try to pause long enough to remember: “Thy will be done.” It pulls me back into reality, into something steadier than my imagination. It works. It really does.

When was the last time your ego demanded way more attention than you deserved—and what did you do about it?
11-26.title: November 26 — Fear

11-27.body:
November 27 — Anger“We are then in much less danger of… anger.”
I remember feeling anger… like, a lot. It was basically my default setting. I felt constantly frustrated with people and with my situation, and alcohol temporarily took the edge off—but like a boomerang, it always came back harder. At one point I even convinced myself that having a hot temper was a useful tool. That’s the insanity of it. I’d burned my nerves down so far that I was walking around like Joe Pesci in Goodfellas. One minute everything’s calm and people are laughing, and the next minute I assume someone’s motive and—boom—I’m snapping, yelling “Funny how?” while everyone at the table of life is trying to calm me down.
Sure, it’s entertaining when Pesci does it in a movie. When I did it in real life? Not so much.
I heard a guy in a meeting say you can tell how an alcoholic is doing by looking at the people around them—are they relaxed and happy, or nervous and jumpy? Yeah… that one hit me right between the eyes. My anger wasn’t just hurting me. It was leaking into the whole room.
Anger is really just me imposing my self-centeredness on the world—demanding everyone act the way I think they should. These days, when I feel that fuse getting short again, I try to pause just long enough to say, “Thy will be done.” That tiny pause is usually enough to get me out of my own head and back into something like sanity. I felt constantly frustrated with people and with my situation, and alcohol temporarily took the edge off—but like a boomerang, it always came back harder. At one point I even convinced myself that having a hot temper was a useful tool. That’s the insanity of it. I’d burned my nerves down so far that I was walking around like Joe Pesci in Goodfellas. One minute everything’s calm and people are laughing, and the next minute I assume someone’s motive and—boom—I’m snapping, yelling “Funny how?” while everyone at the table of life is trying to calm me down.

11-28.body:
November 28 — Worry

“We’re in much less danger of… worry.” — Alcoholics Anonymous

Bill W. drops that line so casually you almost miss it. Much less danger of...worry. In my drinking years, I was in constant danger of worry. I practically lived in the emergency room of my own imagination. And even sober, that old wiring still tries to fire up and tell me something’s wrong—even when nothing is wrong.

Bill follows it in the 12&12 with another line that hits even harder: “We have been talking about problems because we are problem people.” On the surface, it sounds like he’s talking about the messes we created while drinking. But I heard a guy in a meeting twist it just right: “In my ungrateful state, I don’t just have problems—I see problems.”

It’s like that kid in The Sixth Sense whispering, “I see dead people.” Same vibe. I see problems. Real ones, imaginary ones, recycled ones, ones I borrow from the past or the future—anything except the present moment where God actually lives. And once I spot them, man, I latch on. I obsess. I spin out. I pick the problem apart until it’s bigger than God.

The band The Growlers nailed it:
“Worry is a bully
That just won’t let me be
Trying to keep me busy
Tussling and struggling.”

That’s my alcoholic mind in its ungrateful mode—keeping me spiritually busy, wrestling with shadows, arguing with outcomes that haven’t even happened.

And here’s the sick part: sometimes I try to fill the hole in my soul with reasons it can’t be filled. Reasons the world is unfair. Reasons everything is about to fall apart. Reasons I’m not enough. That restless, irritable, discontent feeling sneaks up without warning, and worry is almost always the front door it walks through.

But there’s a little crowbar in the program that pops that door back open: “Thy will, not mine, be done.” One breath of surrender. One second of remembering that I don't have to be the director of the universe today. That quick prayer lets me step aside—so God can do His work through me instead of me wrestling Him for control like a toddler fighting over the steering wheel.

It works. It really does.

Where does worry still try to sneak into your sobriety, and how do you slow it down before it takes over your whole day?
11-28.title: November 28 — Worry

11-29.body:
November 29 — Self-Pity

“We’re in much less danger of… self-pity” — Alcoholics Anonymous

Self-pity — nasty, nasty stuff. It slides in quiet and settles heavy. For me, it shows up as that old fantasy that the world should somehow parent me, soothe me, fix me, notice me, and love me exactly how I want to be loved. But nobody on earth can do that perfectly. And when they don’t? Oh, man… I can turn into a grown two-year-old with a driver’s license and a resentment list.

I once heard a guy in a meeting say, “Don’t go up in your own head without a flashlight and a shotgun.” That makes perfect sense, because my unlit head is not a safe neighborhood. It’s where old narratives go to lift weights and bulk up. It’s where I convince myself I’m the ultimate victim, the forgotten one, the poor soul the universe overlooked on purpose.

That’s self-pity at work:
Poor me, poor me… pour me another drink.
Classic AA wisdom. And it’s dead-on. When self-pity runs unchecked, it doesn’t just warp how I see the world — it warps how I treat it. I start acting like the big bad mean old world is out to get me, or worse, out to withhold from me. That mindset is gasoline on the fire for every old behavior I swore I was done with.

But here’s the twist: if I can muster even a sliver of courage in that moment — and some days it takes real effort — I can soften just enough to whisper, “Thy will be done.” No Herculean spiritual effort. No dramatic surrender. Just a quiet willingness to stop fighting my own life. And in that tiny crack of surrender, light gets in. Enough light to break the spell of self-pity, enough light to remind me I’m not the victim I tell myself I am.

It works.
It really does.
11-29.title: November 29 — Self-Pity

11-30.body:
November 30 — Foolish Decisions
“We’re in much less danger of… foolish decisions” — Alcoholics Anonymous
My life is 80% ‘It’ll be fine’ and 20% ‘Why did I think that would be fine?’ Experience is just a sophisticated word for “Well… that was dumb.” That’s been the story of my life more times than I can count. Deep in my drinking career, I had a talent for making decisions that were both delusional and somehow perfectly reasonable to me at the time. I’d bulldoze ahead, convinced I had it all figured out, while the people around me slowly lost trust in my judgment. And honestly, that was valid. My decision-making process was basically hijacked: have a feeling, call it a plan, then act like God co-signed it. I couldn’t see any of this clearly until I got into this wonderful program that stripped away the illusion that I knew what was best for me.
These days, the simple prayer “Thy will be done” is the thing that grounds me. It reminds me to stay out of my own damn way and to avoid doing anything insane until the right answer becomes abundantly clear. That pause—just waiting without forcing anything—isn’t weakness; it’s spiritual sobriety. When I sit long enough for God to move instead of me scrambling to fix, force, or manipulate, the clarity that shows up is a thing of beauty. I’m connected to a Higher Power now, and whatever happens, happens. The evidence it was supposed to happen is the fact that it did.
So that’s the ticket to freedom for me: show up, show up sober, see what happens, help out when asked, and try like hell not to get in the way. It works. It really does.
What’s one “It’ll be fine” moment that taught you something you still use in your sobriety today?

12-01.body:
December 1 — Having Had a Spiritual Awakening

“It’s a new dawn, it’s a new day…” — Nina Simone

Having had a spiritual awakening… I chased that line like it was some magic password that would unlock sobriety. Every meeting I went to, every story I heard, I was listening for that one moment where the sky cracked open and angels high-fived me. It just didn't happen like that for me.

I don’t even know what happened in my own recovery. I just kept coming back, sitting my butt in the chair, and trying to keep an open mind about this whole not drinking thing. That’s it. No fireworks. No secret handshake. No guru moment. Just showing up when everything in me wanted to create excuses to skip a meeting.

I kept hearing about this “psychic change” that removes the desire to drink, but I’d never had one before, so how the hell was I supposed to learn it? Eventually I had to trust the process — which is a fancy way of saying “stop fighting and keep walking.”

Then one night… boom. Something shifted. Maybe I had one too many cups of AA coffee. Maybe I was honest one too many times. Maybe it was one too many prayers. Maybe I overdosed on that acceptance page in the Big Book. Who knows. All I know is: on Sunday I was still wanting a drink… and on Monday the desire was gone.

Gone.

And it hasn’t come back.

Wild stuff. No logic to it. No formula. Just grace disguised as another boring day in recovery. Sometimes the awakening isn’t big — it’s quiet, sneaky, and shows up after you’ve already given up trying to feel anything spiritual.

But it’s real. And it keeps you sober.

What was your ‘Sunday I still wanted to drink, Monday I didn’t’ moment?
12-01.title: December 1 — Having Had a Spiritual Awakening

12-02.body:
December 2 — Nothing Insures Immunity

“You can’t just kill. You have to find people, you have to help them. That’s the whole point.”
— Eastman to Morgan, The Walking Dead

There’s a moment in The Walking Dead where Morgan is completely out of his mind, trapped in his own fear and pain. Eastman doesn’t fix him with a lecture or a threat. He offers him a switch of the heart — a way back to being human. And it’s simple: Find people. Help them. Not just killing a population of zombies. That’s the point.

That line gets me, because it’s the same thing AA handed me. I used to think recovery was all about killing drinking by controlling myself — locking down the chaos, muscling through cravings, white-knuckling my way past every bad idea and pretending everything was fine. And sure, that works for about… two seconds. But it never brought any peace.

What actually changed me was this quiet, inconvenient truth: I’m supposed to help people.
Not fix them. Not preach at them. Not bully them into being sober.
Just help — the way someone helped me.

There’s something mystical about it. When I'm talking with another alcoholic, something switches on inside me that I can’t create on my own. Suddenly I’m not trapped in my head. Suddenly I’m useful. Suddenly I’m reminded why I’m still here.

The Big Book wasn’t lying — nothing insures immunity from drinking like working with the next person who’s still suffering. You can find them anywhere: detoxes, meetings, hospitals, a phone call you didn’t want to answer. Most days I walk away knowing the truth AA has been saying since page one: they helped me more than I helped them.

When’s the last time you thought you were helping someone else… and realized afterward that they were actually helping you stay sober?
12-02.title: December 2 — Nothing Insures Immunity

12-03.body:
December 3 — When You’re Out of Ideas

In Rocky II, there’s this moment where Rocky finally admits the truth: the old way isn’t working.
All the stubborn pride… all the “I’ll do it my way”… all the plans he keeps trying to force—none of it is getting him anywhere. He finally drops the act, looks at Adrian, and says what’s actually going on inside:
“I just want to prove I’m not a bum.”

And that’s the real turning point.
Not the training.
Not the fight.
The surrender.

Because once he lets go of being a hot-shot who thinks he can just muscle through everything, something big shifts: he actually becomes teachable. Mickey retrains him from the ground up — footwork, stance, slipping punches, switching hands, fighting smart instead of wild. Rocky becomes a better athlete because he stops trying to win on heart alone and finally learns how to do it right.

AA is the same way.
It’s not for people who “need” it.
I needed it for years while I kept trying to run my own brilliant strategies. I needed it every morning I swore I’d do better and drank anyway. I needed it every time I tried to out think this thing.
Needing it never changed a thing.

Recovery only started to open up when I was completely out of ideas.
When the old way collapsed.
AA worked best when I was out of ideas and wanted it.

When did you first realize your best ideas weren’t going to get you sober — and what changed once you became willing?
12-03.title: December 3 — When You’re Out of Ideas

12-04.body:
December 4 — We Got One!

“We got one!” — the way Janine yelled it in Ghostbusters.

When we approach someone still stuck in the disease, the first thing to remember is simple: we’re dealing with a very sick human being. Not a bad one. Maybe a doomed one. But still — a sick one.

So we slow down.
We get what information we can from somebody who actually knows the person — and we dodge gossip like our sobriety depends on it. We already know the disease is calling the shots, and we should know what comes along with that. Maybe they’ve done a hundred awful things… but honestly, who didn’t once they crossed their own line?

Then we tell the truth about ourselves:
How we were flying blind in our own lives until we learned we weren’t “bad people needing to be good,” but sick people needing to get well. That’s the doorway.

From there: read the room.
If he’s in a rotten mood, talk about hopelessness — your hopelessness.
If he’s lighter, go ahead and share a funny disaster story. The kind only a sober drunk can laugh about because we’re not living that way anymore.

After a while, outline the program in your own words — not like a lecture, not like a sales pitch — just one drunk talking to another.

And then leave.
We don’t chase.
We don’t hound.
Maybe a check-in? Sure.
But if the person wants what AA has, they’ll come find us. Willingness is born, not forced.

That’s the whole job:
Show up, be real, and get out of God’s way.

Who was the first AA member that approached you—or the first one you connected with—and what happened in that moment?
12-04.title: December 4 — We Got One!

12-05.body:
December 5 — AA Is the Way of Service

“For if an alcoholic failed to perfect and enlarge his spiritual life through work and self-sacrifice for others, he could not survive the certain trials and low spots ahead.”
—Bill’s Story, Alcoholics Anonymous

Yeah… that line.
Sometimes I wish Bill would’ve said something softer, something like: “If you want to get more spiritual, go pray harder, meditate longer, maybe buy a new journal and feel deep.” But he just doesn’t say that. Not once.

Instead, he hits us with the uncomfortable truth: spiritual growth isn’t a feeling — it’s work.
It’s service.
It’s sacrifice.
It’s showing up for someone who can’t pay you back.
It’s answering the phone when you’re tired, driving someone to a meeting when you’d rather nap, or telling the truth when the lie would be easier.

I can pretend all day to be “grateful.” I can talk about being blessed, highly favored, spiritually aligned, cosmically tuned — the most grateful alcoholic to ever wobble into a folding chair. But unless I’m doing something for someone else, all that gratitude is just talk. A puff of smoke. A spiritual Instagram filter.

The paradox of AA is that the thing I most wanted — to feel better — only came when I stopped trying to feel better. When I started trying to help you.
Not because I’m noble, but because it’s the only thing that works on the sickness I’ve got.

So here it is, the simple formula nobody wants to hear:

Service = Stay Sober.
Self = Suffer.

Bill wasn’t trying to be poetic. He was giving us survival instructions.

What’s one act of service someone did for you in early sobriety that taught you what this program actually was?
12-05.title: December 5 — AA Is the Way of Service

12-06.body:
December 6 — Don’t Think

We don’t think our way into gratitude — we act our way into thinking grateful.

I heard a guy in a meeting once talk about “thinking positively” and how that made his whole day better. Good for him. Truly. Except that for someone like me — the real alcoholic described on page 21 — that whole approach is completely backwards. Sometimes, maybe I can do that, most of the time, nope.

If thinking positively could’ve kept me sober, grateful, sane, and stable I would have been sober years before I ever crawled into AA.

But no. That’s not how it works for a lot of real alcoholics.

Today I get to act myself into right thinking.
Not the other way around.

If I want to feel grateful, I don’t sit around waiting for gratitude to magically bubble up inside me. I act grateful — I help, I serve, I show up, I say yes when it’s inconvenient — and somewhere along the way the thinking catches up.

For too long in recovery I had it completely upside down and wondered why I was miserable. I kept talking about thinking gratitude, journaling gratitude, visualizing gratitude… and then trying to force myself to “feel” grateful afterward. It was spiritual cosplay.

Then a guy in a talk called me out — lovingly, but directly.
I was feeling the need to “think grateful” and he said something to the effect of, “Well good for you, kid. I wish I could do that. But it don’t work like that for the real alcoholic. Why don’t you go try to be of service to anybody right now, get out of your own head, and see what that gives you.”

And he was right.
I had it completely backwards for way too long.
I’m glad I don’t today.

What’s one small action you can take today that would create gratitude instead of waiting to feel it?
12-06.title: December 6 — Don’t Think

12-07.body:
December 7 — Practicing These Principles

Practicing these principles is easy… when I’m in an AA meeting.
I’m centered, I’m patient, I’m kind, I’m practically glowing with spiritual goodwill.
A newcomer walks in and suddenly I’m Mother Teresa with a coffee cup.

But when I’m at home?
Whole different ballgame.

Let one family member leave a sink full of dishes and my brain immediately decides they left them for me — personally — just to disrespect my entire existence. Suddenly, I’m having a full internal meltdown over a fork. No one said anything, no one did anything, but my mind spins it into a cosmic attack on my dignity.

The good news is the program taught me a crucial survival skill:
I don’t have to vocalize every insane thought that flies through my head.

Nobody is out to get me.
Nobody is plotting against me with cereal bowls.
I’m glad I know that nowadays.

But occasionally, on a low-spiritual day — when my spiritual Wi-Fi is glitching — I can unintentionally open my mouth and start some shit. Just… boom. Chaos. Whoops.

Thankfully, I’ve got the rest of the Steps to clean that up.
I can admit where I was wrong, make it right, and move on instead of marinating in guilt or doubling down on pride.
That’s what “practicing these principles” actually looks like for me— not perfection, but correction.

Someone in a meeting once told me,
“If you can treat everyone in the world like a newcomer that just stumbled into their first AA meeting, you’ll be fine.”
So far?
So good. Even when my spiritual Wi-Fi is glitching.

Who’s the hardest person for you to practice these principles with — and what does ‘progress, not perfection’ look like with them today?
12-07.title: December 7 — Practicing These Principles

12-08.body:
December 8 — Cleared for Takeoff
Most of us don’t walk into AA on a winning streak. By the time we show up, almost everything is already gone — the family trust, the job, the money, the health, the reputation. And the Four Horsemen are all that’s left. At that point, the ego has nothing left to latch onto, and it freaks out. It scrambles for an identity, any identity, even if it’s built on fear, blame, or self-pity.
But here’s what becomes clear once you get a little sober and look back with honest eyes:
none of it was punishment.
Your life wasn’t falling apart — you were being cleared for takeoff.
It doesn’t feel like that at the time, of course. At the time it feels like destruction, like everything meaningful is being ripped away. But it’s really spiritual housecleaning — everything that used to shield us, distract us, or inflate us gets stripped away so we can finally hear the truth and accept help. Most of us only become willing once the old life collapses.
And here’s the solid truth we pass on: the Twelve Steps take care of those Four Horsemen when they’re worked thoroughly. They always have. That’s why we don’t have to reinvent the wheel. The Big Book gives clear, precise instructions. Our job — when we’re spiritually awake enough to guide someone — is to help the next guy walk the same path that was handed to us. No new systems, no shortcuts. Just willingness, honesty, and direction.
When your ego ran out of identities to hide behind, what opened up for you in recovery?

12-09.body:
December 9 — Papers
Every now and then someone walks into AA “on paper.” Court told them. Probation told them. Their job told them. A treatment center signed them out with a requirement. Basically, someone in authority looked at their life and said: “Yeah… you need AA.”
And here’s the funny part — not funny haha, but funny human:
Some alcoholics will look down on them for it.
Only in AA could people who burned their lives to the ground find a way to feel superior to somebody else who got sent here. It’s pure ego — nothing helpful, nothing spiritual, nothing in line with what we’re actually trying to do. Just another way to pretend we’re not as bad as we really were.
But the deeper truth?
People who show up “on paper” are often getting the biggest miracle of the room.
Someone, somewhere, cared enough — to interrupt their drinking long enough to get them in a folding chair. That’s grace wearing a badge or a clipboard.
And sometimes the person on papers thinks it’s all a misunderstanding.
Like they’re the only person in here who doesn’t belong.
But if life, courts, bosses, families, or judges are all pointing at AA…
it might be time to pay attention.
That kind of external pressure is often the only thing that cracks the denial open.
For the rest of us — the ones already sober — our job isn’t to judge.
It’s to welcome them.
No ego.
No identity games.
No spiritual ranking system.
Just one alcoholic showing another alcoholic the miracle happening in these rooms, even if they arrived here thinking the whole thing is a clerical error.
AA works because people helped us long before we understood what was happening.
The least we can do is show up the same way — steady, simple, helpful — especially for the guy who thinks he’s just here to get his sheet signed.
If you first came to AA “on paper,” what finally broke through your denial?
And if you didn’t — what helped you drop your ego and treat those who did as equals?

12-09.title: December 9 — Papers

12-10.body:
December 10 — Recovered
I love alcoholics.
We’ll argue about anything.
Coffee strength, meeting formats, where the chairs should go… but the granddaddy of all pointless debates is the age-old battle of “recovered” vs. “recovering.”
My God, man.
You’ll hear someone stand up and proudly declare,
“I’m a recovered alcoholic,”
and they’ll back it up with Big Book quotes, 1939 history, dictionary definitions, footnotes, and maybe a timeline if you let them. They’ll die on that hill with perfect sobriety diction.
Then someone across the room fires back,
“You’re recovering! You’re not cured! You’re not a ham!”
And suddenly we’re off to the races. Two perfectly sober adults arguing like toddlers over who gets the blue crayon.
Here’s the truth — and it’s disappointingly simple:
They’re both right.
Hope that satisfies anyone's fragile little AA ego.
I am a recovered alcoholic because I found a Power greater than myself that released me from a hopeless state of mind and body.
And I am recovering because I’m still learning every day how to trust and rely on that Power instead of my own self-will.
Everybody wins.
Everybody gets a ribbon.
We’re all here, hopefully sober — if that’s your goal — and if arguing about a word is what’s keeping you from drinking today, then hey… welcome to AA.
How do you describe yourself — recovered, recovering, or something else — and what does that word actually mean in your experience?

and they’ll back it up with Big Book quotes, 1939 history, dictionary definitions, footnotes, and maybe a timeline if you let them. They’ll die on that hill with perfect sobriety diction.
Then someone across the room fires back,
“You’re recovering! You’re not cured! You’re not a ham!”
And suddenly we’re off to the races. Two perfectly sober adults arguing like toddlers over who gets the blue crayon.
Here’s the truth — and it’s disappointingly simple:
They’re both right.
Hope that satisfies anyone's fragile little AA ego.
I am a recovered alcoholic because I found a Power greater than myself that released me from a hopeless state of mind and body.
And I am recovering because I’m still learning every day how to trust and rely on that Power instead of my own self-will.
Everybody wins.
Everybody gets a ribbon.
We’re all here, hopefully sober — if that’s your goal — and if arguing about a word is what’s keeping you from drinking today, then hey… welcome to AA.
How do you describe yourself — recovered, recovering, or something else — and what does that word actually mean in your experience?
