12-11.body:
December 11 — Foundation Stones Don’t Float

“It’s dangerous to go alone! Take this.”
— The Legend of Zelda, 1986

Helping others is the foundation stone of my recovery. Not the garnish. Not the side quest. Not the “good deed of the week” I trot out so I can feel like a decent human being for five minutes.

It’s the foundation stone — the piece the whole emotional house sits on. Without it, my mood collapses like a cheap lawn chair at a family reunion.

For a long time, I thought sprinkling a few kind acts around — like I was seasoning my life with random niceness — counted as spiritual growth. It worked just enough to convince me I was doing great while my insides were still running Windows 95.

But a kind act here and there? That’s maintenance-level stuff. That might keep me from drinking today, but it won’t give me the full spiritual charge that makes sobriety feel like something bigger than white-knuckling life.

If I want the real deal — the inner peace, the unexpected freedom, the sense that God is actually in the room and not just on break — then helping others can’t be occasional. It has to be daily.

Not grand gestures. Not saving the world. Just showing up. Listening when I’d rather argue. Being kind when my brain wants to be dramatic. Doing something small for someone else without making a big production out of it.

The Good Samaritan didn’t help because he was feeling holy. He helped because someone needed help. Simple, human, no spotlight.

And the wild part? Almost every time I show up for someone else, I’m the one who gets picked up. I’m the one who calms down. I’m the one who remembers I don’t have to wander through life acting like stubbornness is a personality trait.

Helping others is the foundation stone — and foundation stones don’t float. They keep me grounded when my brain wants to reboot into Chaos Mode.

What reminds you to look outside yourself during the day, especially when you really don’t feel like it?
12-11.title: December 11 — Foundation Stones Don’t Float

12-12.body:
December 12 — We’re the Can’ts, and That’s Okay

Assuming we’re spiritually fit, we can go anywhere liquor is served. Restaurants, weddings, cookouts, that one cousin’s house where every flat surface is a coaster — we’re allowed in all of it. But only if we’re not there to tease the disease. I heard a guy in a meeting say "I have a two drink limit, you have two drinks, and I'm out."

I used to think sobriety meant avoiding alcohol like it was radioactive. Like I had to scrub the world clean of beer logos and margarita specials just to stay safe. Like every bottle had a sniper scope on me. But that’s not the deal. We’re not here to ban alcohol, protest alcohol, or remodel the world to be AA-friendly. That’s not spiritual fitness — that’s spiritual paranoia with a gym membership.

The truth is way simpler: there are people who can drink, and there are people who can’t. Some people have the normally installed "off switch", some don't. That’s it. No moral ranking. No shame. No “I’m better than them because I don’t drink” nonsense. They’re the cans. We’re the can’ts. Owning that has saved my life more times than any rule, slogan, or motivational poster ever did.

Because once I stopped trying to negotiate with alcohol — stopped testing myself, stopped pretending I could “hang out with it” like we were still cool — everything got lighter. Spiritually fit doesn’t mean I’m bulletproof. It means I’m honest about where my feet are and what my disease does when it smells opportunity.

I don’t avoid places because there’s alcohol there. I avoid situations where I’m not right. When I’m tired, resentful, lonely, spiritually empty, or just trying to prove something. If I’m solid inside, I can be anywhere, as long as I have good reason to be there.

So yeah — some people can drink. Some people can’t. I’m a can’t. And accepting that doesn’t shrink my world. It frees it.

What helps you recognize the difference between being spiritually fit enough to be somewhere… and being somewhere you just don’t belong today?
12-12.title: December 12 — We’re the Can’ts, and That’s Okay

12-13.body:
December 13 - The Hardest Part of AA
Buried in Working With Others, Bill slips in a line so quietly it’s easy to miss: “Put yourself in the other man’s place.” No buildup. No explanation. Just that. And it might be the hardest suggestion in the entire Big Book.
Because that’s not sympathy or surface-level empathy. That’s a full stop on my self-centered way of thinking. It means I stop asking, Why doesn’t he get this? and start asking, What does this look like from inside his head? What is he afraid of? What is he protecting? What does he misunderstand? His fears, his obstinacy, his confusion, his agnosticism — the whole package.
That doesn’t come naturally to me. My default is judgment dressed up as concern. I want people to see things clearly, which usually means seeing them my way. Bill doesn’t tell me to fix the man. He tells me to stand where he’s standing.
That’s the move out of self and into others. And here’s the strange payoff: in the brief moments I actually try to do this, something loosens. I feel lighter. Less bound up. The bondage of self eases, not because I was right, but because I stopped making everything about me.
This practice doesn’t stay in AA. It spills into daily life — family, work, strangers, everyone who rubs me the wrong way. It’s hard. It’s uncomfortable. And it’s absolutely worth it.
When was the last time you realized you never really tried seeing a situation from the other person’s side?

12-14.body:
December 14 - Step Work When Nobody’s Around

Every so often, I get taken hostage by myself. One expectation slips in, turns into a resentment, and suddenly my whole world feels upside down. I’m trapped in the bondage of self again, replaying the same thoughts like they’re important.

The Big Book says to find an alcoholic to work with and get out of myself. That works. But sometimes it’s just not possible. I’m driving. I’m at work. I’m alone with my head, and that’s a dangerous neighborhood.

That’s when I use something an old sponsor taught me. When I can’t reach another alcoholic, I can still get out of myself by praying for other people — especially the ones I’m irritated with. She showed me how to take the Third Step Prayer and put someone else’s name in it, offering them to God instead of trying to manage them.

God, I offer [their name] to Thee — to build with them and to do with them as Thou wilt. Relieve them of the bondage of self, that they may better do Thy will. Take away their difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness to those they would help of Thy Power, Thy Love, and Thy Way of life. May they do Thy will always.

I don’t magically feel better, but something loosens. The resentment loses some power. I step out of the center for a minute, and that’s usually enough.

Thank God for the people in AA.

What’s something you do to get out of your head when you can’t reach another alcoholic?
12-14.title: December 14 - Step Work When Nobody’s Around

12-15.body:
December 15 - Two Things We Don’t Care About

There are two things we genuinely don’t care about in AA. The first is what your Higher Power is. Nobody should care — except for one small detail: it can’t be you. Other than that, call it God, Energy, Nature, Love, or Steve. If it keeps you sober and gets you out of self, you’re doing fine.

The second thing we don’t care about is how you like to have sex. That’s not our lane. Some people like it plain. Some people like it spicy, like they’re on an all-pepper diet. Either way, it’s none of our business. AA is not a lifestyle review committee.

We don’t avoid these topics because they’re taboo. We avoid them because we’re alcoholics. We have opinions, judgments, and hot takes on everything, and if we’re not careful, those things turn into resentments — and resentments are how we get sick all over again.

So we keep it simple. We’re here to help you get sober and learn how to deal with resentment when it shows up. The rest is God’s job. Our job is to stay out of the damn way.

What’s something you’ve learned to let go of in AA that you used to have a strong opinion about?
12-15.title: December 15 - Two Things We Don’t Care About

12-16.body:
December 16 — Wrong Number

Every now and then, the phone rings and it’s not the alcoholic. It’s a wife, a mom, a dad — someone worn down and scared. They’re not calling to chat, they’re calling to report. “He’s drinking again.” “She won’t stop.” Underneath it is the same fear: if this doesn’t end now, everything is going to fall apart.

Those of us who’ve lived with alcoholism understand something painful. Once an alcoholic starts drinking, triggering the allergy, they aren’t done until they’re done. Not when love begs. Not when consequences stack up. There’s no timeline that fear or affection can put on it.

So what’s left often isn’t solutions — it’s understanding. Listening without fixing. Letting someone say out loud how powerless and exhausted they are. Alcoholism spreads outward, and the people closest end up just as consumed and alone.

Sometimes support is simply recognizing the truth together, without promises or pressure, and letting connection do what control never could.

What’s something you understand about alcoholism now that you couldn’t see before?
12-16.title: December 16 — Wrong Number

12-17.body:
December 17 — What’s Next?

Luckily for me, the gift of desperation had me by the throat. Once I saw that the Steps had a way of returning drunks to something resembling respectful citizens, I was all in. I worked them hard and fast, not out of spiritual maturity, but because I wanted relief. I wanted the promises. I wanted a psychic change. I wanted that gorilla off my back. I wanted my family to look at me like I wasn’t a liability anymore. Honestly, I just had enough desire stacked up that drinking finally lost.

That kept me sober long enough for the right answers to start showing up.

After I finished the Steps for the first time, I looked at my sponsor and asked the most natural question in the world: “Okay… what’s next?” He told me to go home and write down everything I’d ever wanted to do in life. So I did. Travel the country. Get married. Be a real dad. A bunch of other stuff too. I brought the list back the next day and said, “Here it is. Now what?”

He leaned back, gave me one of those sponsor looks, and said, “Now go do it.”

Turns out sobriety wasn’t the finish line. It was the starting gate.

What is something you always wanted to do in life?
12-17.title: December 17 — What’s Next?

12-18.body:
December 18 — Traditions

We’ve probably all heard the line: the Steps keep you from committing suicide, and the Traditions keep you from committing homicide. Funny. Not funny. But there’s a truth hiding in there.

After I’d been around AA for a bit, I started to feel the ick again. Not enough to put a drink in my hand, but enough to get my head loud and uncomfortable. The kind of restless, irritated feeling that usually doesn’t end well if it goes unchecked. So I called my sponsor and told him what was going on.

He said he’d heard a guy share about applying the Traditions to his own life, not just to meetings. That stuck with me. If it was good enough for that guy, it was probably worth a look for me.

When I tried it on, things shifted. Unity started to matter more than being right. Group welfare looked a lot like not blowing up relationships just to feel justified. Anonymity felt less like secrecy and more like humility — letting my ego take a back seat so something else could breathe. Suddenly I wasn’t the center of every conversation or conflict anymore.

When I looked at my life the same way we look at a group, a whole other world opened up. Less tension. Fewer imaginary enemies. More room to stay sober and sane. Turns out the Traditions weren’t about controlling people — they were about keeping me from making a mess I’d later have to clean up.

Have you ever noticed your sobriety improve when you cared more about the whole than being right?
12-18.title: December 18 — Traditions

12-19.body:
December 19 — Humility

Bill writes a lot about humility, which makes sense, because it seems to come up in conversations more than I care to admit. My own self-centered ego is the enemy, and I can climb up on a pedestal faster than I’d like to believe. In the rooms, you’ll hear that alcoholics are “above average intelligence.” I’ve never heard that anywhere else in my life, but it sure sounds good when my ego’s looking for fuel.

Some days my imagination gets hijacked. I can walk out of an AA meeting and, within minutes, be mentally reorganizing how the entire country should be run. No information. No facts. Just pure opinion and confidence. It’s impressive, really, how quickly I can promote myself to expert on everything.

Then I remember something I heard in the rooms: the best I’m ever going to be is a guy in AA. Not less than. Not diminished. Just right-sized. There was a time I couldn’t stop drinking and didn’t know how. Learning this way of life didn’t qualify me to run the world — it taught me how to stay sober and be useful when asked.

I’m just a guy who knows where the Solution is. That’s it. If that service someday happens at a NATO conference, fine. But for now, my grand plans can sit quietly while I do the next right, ordinary thing. And honestly, I’m pretty content just being who I am today.

Where does your ego like to take you when it gets the microphone?
12-19.title: December 19 — Humility

12-20.body:
December 20 — They Don’t Like Me

At work the other day, a coworker said something like, “Everybody loves you here. You work hard, you don’t complain, and you just do what you’re asked without arguing.” My ego grabbed that sentence and took it for a ten-minute victory lap before I came back to my senses.

What landed wasn’t self-hatred — it was clarity. Left to my own devices, I’m not especially lovable. I’m a drunk who used to sit on a barstool, talk too much, take advantage of situations, and run my mouth like I had something important to say. That version of me didn’t earn much trust.

What people seem to respond to isn’t me — it’s what this program did with me. They like reliability. They like humility. They like someone who shows up, tries, listens, and doesn’t need to be the main character. Those are spiritual principles I practice imperfectly, but consistently enough to be useful.

And that usefulness does something unexpected — it rewards me with a quiet kind of happiness. Not the flashy kind my ego wants, just the kind that lets me sleep at night and come back tomorrow willing to try again.

So yeah… I’ll keep coming back.

Have you ever realized people weren’t responding to you, but to the principles you were practicing?
12-20.title: December 20 — They Don’t Like Me

12-21.body:
December 21 — Next!

Early sobriety resets your expectations fast. Once you start trying to help other drunks, you’re going to meet a lot of people. Some will listen. Some will swear they’re done. A lot of them will drink anyway.

Bill was frustrated early on because none of the people he tried to help stayed sober. What finally landed wasn’t their failure — it was that he did. He stayed sober. That’s when it clicked. Helping others wasn’t about results. It was about staying out of himself. Service became the foundation of his sobriety, not a scoreboard.

Sometimes you’ll spend days, weeks, even months with a drunk. Long talks. Big feelings. Then, in a heartbeat, he drinks and disappears. Sometimes he won’t answer the phone. Sometimes he won’t want to see you again. It can feel pointless, and yeah, your feelings might get hurt.

That’s when the instruction is simple and uncomfortable: Next! We don’t chase. We don’t argue. We don’t take it personally. We immediately look for another alcoholic to work with. Not because the last one didn’t matter, but because he already did his job. He kept you sober. He kept you out of your own head. He got you out of your own way.

Not everyone stays. But everyone helps. So don’t quit. Just keep moving. Next!

When working with others didn’t go the way you hoped, how did it affect your sobriety — and what helped you stay right-sized?
12-21.title: December 21 — Next!

12-22.body:
December 22 — The Gotta Dance

A lot of us come into AA full of self-will, even though alcohol just finished kicking our ass. We don’t walk in humbled — we walk in activated. We see the wreckage of our lives and treat it like a challenge to fix, not a message to slow down.

That’s when the “gotta” thinking shows up. I gotta get a new car. I gotta get a new girl. I gotta get a few thousand dollars in my bank account. I gotta get these people off my back. Gotta, gotta, gotta. It feels productive. It feels responsible. It even looks good from the outside.

You’re dancing with yourself like the world isn’t watching. You’re moving fast, making plans, stacking fixes, convinced momentum equals recovery. But if you’re not careful, you can gotta-dance your way right out the door of an AA meeting and never come back.

It happens. Not because people stop believing in sobriety — but because they start believing they’ve got it now. The danger isn’t wanting a better life. The danger is thinking you can build one on the same thinking that just burned the last one down.

Early on, the program asks for something painfully unglamorous: stop the music. Sit down. Let things be unfinished for a while. Stay close to the people who remember what it was like when alcohol was still winning.

Because the gotta dance doesn’t end in freedom. It usually ends in distance — from the rooms, from help, and eventually from honesty.

And the wild part? Nobody pushes you out. You dance yourself out.

What was something you thought you “had to have” in early sobriety that you later realized God had something better planned for?
12-22.title: December 22 — The Gotta Dance

12-23.body:
Dec 23 — Selfish vs. Self-Seeking

I was at a meeting once and heard a take on the whole self thing that finally stuck.

A lady leaned back in her chair and said:
Selfish is when I have something and you can’t have it.
Self-seeking is when you have something I want—and I’m coming to get it.

That pretty much covers my entire spiritual autobiography.

Different flavors, same illness. Whether I’m hoarding, grabbing, comparing, or plotting—it's all still me sitting in the middle of the universe, keeping score. Call it selfish, self-seeking, or just plain self-centeredness. Same umbrella. Same rain.

And here’s the annoying part: the fix is boringly simple.

Go help someone else.

Not to look good. Not to fix them. Not to earn points. Just to get out of my own head for five minutes. Make a call. Hold a door. Listen without correcting. Do something small that doesn’t benefit me at all.

I hate how well it works.

What’s the difference between selfish and self-seeking in your own life—and what’s one small way helping someone else has snapped you out of it?
12-23.title: Dec 23 — Selfish vs. Self-Seeking

12-24.body:
Dec 24 — Long Day
Holidays can be hard for alcoholics.
Not always loud-hard. Sometimes quiet-hard.
My alcoholism has this built-in sense of separation that loves to show up right on schedule. I didn’t do enough. They won’t like the gift. Crap—I forgot a gift. Family stuff. Old feelings. New expectations. On and on, like my head’s running a highlight reel of everything I’m supposedly doing wrong.
Restless, irritable, discontent.
It’s like my nervous system remembers the holidays even when I’m trying not to.
That’s a truth I’d rather avoid, but today I don’t have to. Because the great fact of my life now is this: I’ve been given something that actually works. The program of AA brings me back to sanity. I don’t have to drink to fit in. I don’t have to pretend I’m fine. I don’t have to be alone—even when I feel lonely.
There’s a meeting somewhere. There’s a phone I can pick up. And when things feel heavy, I’ve learned this too shall pass—even if it doesn’t feel like it in the moment.
I’m grateful for AA. It’s like a cast for a broken arm. It doesn’t make the arm perfect, but it holds it steady long enough to heal.
So during the holidays, I try to reach out a little more. Not just for me—but for you.
And somehow, in doing that, it helps me too.
What’s one way the holidays mess with your head—and what helps you stay grounded when that old restless, irritable, discontent feeling shows up?

12-24.title: Dec 24 — Long Day

12-25.body:
Dec 25 — Grace: The Greatest Gift

The greatest gift I’ve ever been given is the free gift of sobriety.

I didn’t earn it. I didn’t deserve it. It showed up anyway.

Grace has a habit of doing that—arriving right when I least expect it and right when I’m sure I’ve blown my chance. If you’re an alcoholic and not drinking for any length of time, that’s grace. A pause. Something stepping in between me and my old desire to hurt myself.

That moment matters.

Somewhere along the way, we were trusted with something big. Not perfection—but purpose. We were given strength we never had before, and a power that shows up exactly where we were weakest. The very thing that was destroying our lives is now the place where we can help others survive theirs.

That’s not an accident.

Sobriety gives me a reason to be here. It gives my life weight and direction. And the wild part is this: it’s the only gift I can keep as long as I give it away.

Today, I’m grateful. Not because life is perfect—but because I’m present for it.

What does sobriety mean to you today—and how have you seen grace show up when you least expected it?
12-25.title: Dec 25 — Grace: The Greatest Gift

12-26.body:
December 26 — The Alcoholism Is Winning

Someone once said, “Your alcoholism is winning.”
I remember thinking, What are you talking about? I’m not drinking.
End of conversation. Or so I thought.

What they meant was this: alcoholism isn’t just about alcohol. It’s the disease of more. More money. More attention. More comfort. More excitement. More relief. It grinds away at you quietly, day after day, until the mental side finally shrugs and says, “Screw it,” and you do the thing.

When I looked at it that way, a whole new part of the program opened up.
Not am I drinking? but where am I restless, irritable, and discontent—and trying to fix it with more?

Maybe it’s buying a new car, and two weeks later the color bugs me.
Maybe it’s chasing a new relationship when, if I’m honest, all I really wanted was sex.
Maybe it’s money, food, scrolling, projects, control, fixing other people, or proving I’m right—again.

None of those things are evil on their own. The danger is believing this one thing will finally settle me inside. That’s where the grind starts. That’s where the disease wins without ever opening a bottle.

And then came the follow-up I didn’t expect: be gentle with yourself.
This whole thing is delicate. Recovery isn’t about beating yourself into submission. It’s about noticing the grind earlier, pausing sooner, and remembering that peace usually shows up when I stop chasing “more” and let God do His job.

If alcoholism is winning, it doesn’t mean I’m failing.
It means I need to slow down, get honest, and handle this thing with care.

Where in your life have you noticed the disease of “more” trying to pass itself off as a solution—and what did you learn when it didn’t deliver?
12-26.title: December 26 — The Alcoholism Is Winning

12-27.body:
December 27 — Stinkin’ Thinkin’

Physicians who are familiar with alcoholism agree there is no such thing a
making a normal thinker out of an alcoholic. Science may one day accomplish this, but it hasn't
done so yet.

Despite all we can say, many who are real alcoholics are not going to believe they are in that
class. By every form of self- deception and experimentation, they will try to prove themselves
exceptions to the rule, therefore nonalcoholic. If anyone who is showing inability to control his thinking can do the right-about- face and think like a gentleman, our hats are off to him. Heaven
knows, we have tried hard enough and long enough to think like other people!

And there it is. That’s the problem.

My drinking wasn’t always the issue—my thinking was. Left alone, I can make a strong case for just about anything. I can justify it, dress it up, and call it reasonable without ever checking myself.

Something changes when two alcoholics get together. We may still be selfish, but at least we’re honest. Saying a thought out loud either exposes it or softens it. Sometimes I hear myself and quickly realize, Oh… that sounded better in my head. Sometimes someone else gently labels it for what it is: stinkin’ thinkin’.

That’s the gift. Not perfect thoughts—just honest ones, shared. Enough light to slow the lie down.

Left alone, my thinking runs wild.
With another alcoholic, it has to behave.

Glad I found you guys in AA.

What’s a thought that made total sense in your head—but not once you said it out loud?
12-27.title: December 27 — Stinkin’ Thinkin’

12-28.body:
December 28 – Say What?

I once heard someone mess up the Serenity Prayer in a meeting and say, “God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot say, the courage to say the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference.” Everyone laughed—but it stuck with me. Close enough to the real thing to hit home. Because when I’m angry or frustrated, this prayer is now my go-to, and what it really reminds me of is to watch my mouth.
Words matter. They land hard. Some of them don’t bounce—they stick for years. And when I’m running on untreated alcoholic thinking—delusional, selfish, convinced my wants are urgent and righteous—I can get sharp. I can get cruel. Alcoholics don’t always throw punches; sometimes we just throw sentences and walk away like nothing happened. Meanwhile, someone else is still carrying it.
This prayer slows me down. It reminds me that not everything I feel needs to be said, not everything I think is true, and not every moment is mine to control. Acceptance doesn’t just apply to people and situations—it applies to silence, restraint, and letting God handle outcomes I’m tempted to manage with words.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing I can do is shut up long enough for the wisdom part to catch up.
When you’re irritated or fired up, what helps you pause before saying something you might not be able to take back?

Acceptance doesn’t just apply to people and situations—it applies to silence, restraint, and letting God handle outcomes I’m tempted to manage with words.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing I can do is shut up long enough for the wisdom part to catch up.
When you’re irritated or fired up, what helps you pause before saying something you might not be able to take back?

I once heard someone mess up the Serenity Prayer in a meeting and say, “God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot say, the courage to say the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference.” Everyone laughed—but it stuck with me. Close enough to the real thing to hit home. Because when I’m angry or frustrated, this prayer is now my go-to, and what it really reminds me of is to watch my mouth.

Words matter. They land hard. Some of them don’t bounce—they stick for years. And when I’m running on untreated alcoholic thinking—delusional, selfish, convinced my wants are urgent and righteous—I can get sharp. I can get cruel. Alcoholics don’t always throw punches; sometimes we just throw sentences and walk away like nothing happened. Meanwhile, someone else is still carrying it.

This prayer slows me down. It reminds me that not everything I feel needs to be said, not everything I think is true, and not every moment is mine to control. Acceptance doesn’t just apply to people and situations—it applies to silence, restraint, and letting God handle outcomes I’m tempted to manage with words.

Sometimes the most spiritual thing I can do is shut up long enough for the wisdom part to catch up.

When you’re irritated or fired up, what helps you pause before saying something you might not be able to take back?
12-28.title: December 28 – Say What?

12-29.body:
December 29 — Everything… or Nothing

It really wasn’t until AA that I realized God is everything… or nothing. And which one I see is kind of up to me. If I want to notice God at work, I can. If I don’t, I don’t have to. Nobody forces it. For me, though, it’s all good. Even the stuff I used to call mistakes.

Because here’s what keeps happening: I try to do the next right thing, I get a little off course, I screw something up—and somehow that “mistake” ends up launching me forward. It turns into a lesson I couldn’t have learned any other way. A correction, not a punishment. A weird win.

I once heard a guy in a meeting say, “Grace is the free gift of auto-correct on your life.” That’s about the best definition I’ve ever heard. As long as I don’t throw in the towel and pick up a bottle, life keeps adjusting me—quietly, gently—toward something better than I had planned. I get experiences I never had before. A sense of fulfillment I never knew was missing. And when I look back, it all seems connected… even the wrong turns.

Where have you seen something you thought was a mistake turn into a correction—or even a gift—once you stayed sober and kept going?
12-29.title: December 29 — Everything… or Nothing

12-30.body:
AA has been very good to us. Recovery has taken many of us places we never imagined we'd see when our worlds were about the size of a barstool.

One time, I was about five hundred miles from home and got completely lost on a trail. No signal. No people. Just woods. I wandered around for hours, getting more turned around by the minute. Fear set in hard. I started saying the Serenity Prayer on a loop, not because I was calm, but because it was the only thing I had.

A lot of us know that feeling. Maybe we're not lost in the woods, but we're lost in our own heads. We start circling the same fears, the same resentments, the same problems. The harder we try to force our way out, the more lost we seem to become.

Eventually, I slowed down enough to actually ask for help. Not demand it. Not bargain. Just a simple, honest, "God, please help me." A few minutes later, a guy appeared on the trail like it was the most normal thing in the world. I asked him how to get out of the woods, and he gave me a few clear directions. I followed them, step by step, and I was out in no time—safe, steady, back on my way.

I waited around to thank him. He never came out. I've never seen him again.

But I think about that moment a lot. Most of the time, help shows up after we calm down, ask for it, and then actually follow simple directions.

When was a time you were "lost" in recovery, and what finally helped you find your way back?
12-30.title: December 30 — Out of the Woods

12-31.body:
I’ve finally tapped into something greater than myself, and it didn’t arrive with fireworks, resolutions, or a clean slate. It showed up quietly, right where I already was. When I look down at my coin and see the words To Thine Own Self Be True, I’m reminded of something simple and unsettling: nobody is coming to save me. That’s not bad news—it’s freedom. I don’t have to do this for anyone else, I don’t have to prove anything, I just have to be honest with myself. There’s a crack in the system of my drinking, there always has been, but I didn't find it until now—it is a small opening where truth sneaks in, a pause, a hesitation, a moment where I know deep down that the old way doesn’t work anymore. That crack is where grace gets in, and I’ve learned to exploit it. Nothing—absolutely nothing—is as important as staying sober just for today. That first genuine smile I’ve had in a long time will disappear, the small but real sense of integrity I’ve proven to myself will vanish, all of it gone the moment I take the first drink. So just for today, I hold onto this thought until my head hits the pillow. The opportunity is now. The time is now. I’ve tapped into something bigger than sitting on a barstool, bigger than noise, bigger than escape.

You ain’t seen nothing yet.

What’s your simple game plan to stay connected and stay sober today—who are you calling, where are you going, or what are you doing to make sure your head hits the pillow sober?
12-31.title: December 31 — To Thine Own Self Be True

08-08.title: August 8 - The Willingness to Be Willing
08-08.body:
Some amends are simpler to make than others. There are some we know we have to make, but we don’t want to because of the fear and chaos surrounding whatever situation we found ourselves in. We may be getting ready to become willing, but the fear feels like a brick wall standing in the way.

We can catastrophize about what might happen. We play out every possible consequence in our heads, usually imagining the worst. This is where we’ve learned to seek experience from a trusted friend. Someone who isn’t caught up in our fear can sometimes see a clear path where we can’t see one at all.

But what if we are absolutely not willing?

We’ve heard to pray for the willingness to be willing. It’s a start. We don’t have to pretend we’re ready when we’re not. We can simply ask God to help us become willing to become willing. After all, it’s in God’s hands anyway. We’re sober now. We’re trying to do the next right thing. Even a small attempt at willingness is going to get us farther than closing the door on the memory and trying to shut it off. We already know that usually doesn’t work.

Sometimes willingness doesn’t come all at once. Sometimes it starts with a prayer we have to say over and over again. But if we keep praying for the willingness to be willing, we may eventually find ourselves in a position to do the next right thing.

Today’s Question: Is there something I’m not willing to face yet, and am I willing to pray for the willingness to be willing?

08-09.title: August 9, 2026 - All
08-09.body:
Maybe there are some amends we’re unwilling to make. Maybe we tell ourselves the amend is going to stir up some sort of catastrophic consequence. Maybe we don’t feel good enough about ourselves to make the amend. Maybe we’re still holding onto something. Who really needs forgiven at this point?

Maybe we’re taking our God-given sobriety for granted. We think, think, think that we’re doing this for ourselves instead of remembering that we’re people learning how to live in God’s grace. So we put the amend on the shelf and say, “Nope, not going to do it.” Maybe that’s our ego trying to hold us back from a deeper connection with the Spiritual Solution.

Our overbearing egos love to be in charge. Why would they want to give up control now? They got us this far by convincing us that we know what’s best, that we can predict what’s going to happen, and that we’re safer listening to ourselves. Maybe this is just another place where our ego wants the final say.

So we connect with a trusted friend who has followed this path. We consider their experience. We don’t have to blindly do anything, and we don’t have to figure everything out today. Maybe they help us see something we couldn’t see on our own. Maybe we find a doorway in that works for us. Maybe we become willing to consider something we had already decided was impossible.

Maybe.

Is there an amend we’ve put on the shelf, and what might be keeping us from taking another look at it?
